\chapter*{CHAPTER XII: CURVATURE. RADIUS OF CURVATURE}

\textbf{99. Curvature.} The shape of a curve depends very largely upon the rate at which the direction of the tangent changes as the point of contact describes the curve. This rate of change of direction is called \textit{curvature} and is denoted by $K$. We now proceed to find its analytical expression, first for the simple case of the circle, and then for curves in general.

\textbf{100. Curvature of a circle.} Consider a circle of radius $R$. Let

$\tau =$ angle that the tangent at $P$ makes with $OX$, and

$\tau + \Delta\tau =$ angle made by the tangent at a neighboring point $P'$.

Then we say

\[ \Delta\tau = \textit{total curvature of arc } PP'. \]


If the point $P$ with its tangent be supposed to move along the curve to $P'$, the total curvature $(=\Delta\tau)$ would measure the total change in direction, or rotation, of the tangent; or, what is the same thing, the total change in direction of the arc itself. Denoting by $s$ the length of the arc of the curve measured from some fixed point (as $A$) to $P$, and by $\Delta s$ the length of the arc $PP'$, then the ratio

\[ \frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s} \]

measures the average change in direction per unit length of arc.$^*$ Since, from the figure,

\[ \Delta s = R \cdot \Delta\tau, \]

or

\[ \frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s} = \frac{1}{R}, \]

\noindent $^*$ Thus, if $\Delta\tau = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ radians $(= 30^\circ)$, and $\Delta s = 3$ centimeters, then $\dfrac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s} = \dfrac{\pi}{18}$ radians per centimeter $= 10^\circ$ per centimeter $=$ average rate of change of direction.

it is evident that this ratio is constant everywhere on the circle. This ratio is, by definition, the \textit{curvature of the circle}, and we have
\[ (38)\qquad K=\frac{1}{R}. \]
\textit{The curvature of a circle equals the reciprocal of its radius.}

\textbf{101. Curvature at a point.} Consider any curve. As in the last section,
\[ \Delta\tau = \textit{total curvature of the arc } PP', \]
and
\[ \frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s} = \textit{average curvature of the arc } PP'. \]
More important, however, than the notion of the average curvature of an arc is that of \textit{curvature at a point.} This is obtained as follows. Imagine $P'$ to approach $P$ along the curve; then the limiting value of
the average curvature $\left(=\dfrac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s}\right)$ as $P'$ approaches $P$ along the curve is defined as the curvature at $P$, that is,
\[ \textit{Curvature at a point} = \underset{\Delta s=0}{\text{limit}}\left(\frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s}\right)=\frac{d\tau}{ds}. \]
\[ (39)\qquad \therefore\ K=\frac{d\tau}{ds}=\textbf{curvature.} \]
Since the angle $\Delta\tau$ is measured in radians and the length of arc $\Delta s$ in units of length, it follows that \textit{the unit of curvature at a point is one radian per unit of length.}

\textbf{102. Formulas for curvature.} It is evident that if, in the last section, instead of measuring the angles which the tangents made with $OX$, we had denoted by $\tau$ and $\tau+\Delta\tau$ the angles made by the tangents with any arbitrarily fixed line, the different steps would in no wise have been changed, and consequently the results are entirely independent of the system of coördinates used. However, since the equations of the curves we shall consider are all given in either rectangular or polar coördinates, it is necessary to deduce formulas for $K$ in terms of both. We have
\[ \tan\tau=\frac{dy}{dx},\qquad \S\ 32,\ \text{p. } 31 \]
or
\[ \tau=\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{dy}{dx}. \]

Differentiating with respect to $x$, using \textbf{XX}

(A)
\[
\frac{d\tau}{dx}=\frac{\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}}{1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}}\cdot
\]
Also

(B)
\[
\frac{ds}{dx}=\left[1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}\cdot
\]
From (\textbf{24}), p. 134

Dividing $(A)$ by $(B)$ gives
\[
\frac{\dfrac{d\tau}{dx}}{\dfrac{ds}{dx}}=\frac{\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}}{\left[1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}\cdot
\]

But
\[
\frac{\dfrac{d\tau}{dx}}{\dfrac{ds}{dx}}=\frac{d\tau}{ds}=K.
\]
Hence

(\textbf{40})
\[
\mathbf{K}=\frac{\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}}{\left[1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}\cdot
\]

If the equation of the curve be given in polar coördinates, $K$ may be found as follows:

From (\textbf{B}), p. 84,
\[
\tau=\theta+\psi.\quad\text{Differentiating,}
\]

(C)
\[
\frac{d\tau}{d\theta}=1+\frac{d\psi}{d\theta}\cdot
\]

But
\[
\tan\psi=\frac{\rho}{\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}}\cdot
\]
From (\textbf{A}), p. 84
\[
\therefore\ \psi=\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{\rho}{\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}}\cdot
\]

Differentiating by \textbf{XX} with respect to $\theta$ and reducing,

(D)
\[
\frac{d\psi}{d\theta}=\frac{\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^{2}-\rho\,\dfrac{d^{2}\rho}{d\theta^{2}}}{\rho^{2}+\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^{2}}\cdot
\]

Substituting $(D)$ in $(C)$, we get
\[
(E)\qquad \frac{d\tau}{d\theta}=\frac{\rho^2-\rho\,\dfrac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}+2\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}{\rho^2+\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}.\quad\text{Also}
\]
\[
(F)\qquad \frac{ds}{d\theta}=\left[\rho^2+\left(\frac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]^{\frac12}.\qquad\text{From }\textbf{(30)}\text{, p. 136}
\]
Dividing $(E)$ by $(F)$ gives
\[
\frac{\dfrac{d\tau}{d\theta}}{\dfrac{ds}{d\theta}}=\frac{\rho^2-\rho\,\dfrac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}+2\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}{\left[\rho^2+\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]^{\frac32}}.
\]
But
\[
\frac{\dfrac{d\tau}{d\theta}}{\dfrac{ds}{d\theta}}=\frac{d\tau}{ds}=K.\quad\text{Hence}
\]
\[
(41)\qquad K=\frac{\rho^2-\rho\,\dfrac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}+2\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}{\left[\rho^2+\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]^{\frac32}}.
\]

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Find the curvature of the parabola $y^2=4px$ at the upper end of the latus rectum.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2p}{y};\qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\frac{2p}{y^2}\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{4p^2}{y^3}.
\]
Substituting in (40),
\[
K=-\frac{4p^2}{(y^2+4p^2)^{\frac32}},
\]
giving the curvature at \textit{any point}. At the upper end of the latus rectum $(p,\,2p)$
\[
K=-\frac{4p^2}{(4p^2+4p^2)^{\frac32}}=-\frac{4p^2}{16\sqrt{2}\,p^3}=-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}\,p}.\,{}^{*}\qquad \textit{Ans.}
\]

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 2. Find the curvature of the logarithmic spiral $\rho=e^{a\theta}$ at any point.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[
\frac{d\rho}{d\theta}=ae^{a\theta}=a\rho;\qquad \frac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}=a^2e^{a\theta}=a^2\rho.
\]
Substituting in (41),
\[
K=\frac{1}{\rho\sqrt{1+a^2}}.\qquad \textit{Ans.}
\]

${}^{*}$ While in our work it is generally only the numerical value of $K$ that is of importance, yet we can give a geometric meaning to its sign. Throughout our work we have taken the positive sign of the radical $\sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}$. Therefore $K$ will be positive or negative at the same time as $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$, that is (\S\ 85, p. 125), according as the curve is concave upwards or concave downwards.

In laying out the curves on a railroad it will not do, on account of the high speed of trains, to pass abruptly from a straight stretch of track to a circular curve. In order to make the change of direction gradual, engineers make use of \textit{transition curves} to connect the straight part of a track with a circular curve. Arcs of cubical parabolas are generally employed as transition curves.

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 3. The transition curve on a railway track has the shape of an arc of the cubical parabola $y=\frac{1}{3}x^3$. At what rate is a car on this track changing its direction (1 mi. = unit of length) when it is passing through (a) the point $(3,\,9)$? (b) the point $(2,\,\frac{8}{3})$? (c) the point $(1,\,\frac{1}{3})$?

\textbf{Solution.}
\[ \frac{dy}{dx}=x^2, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2x. \]

Substituting in (40),
\[ K=\frac{2x}{(1+x^4)^{\frac{3}{2}}}. \]

(a) At $(3,\,9)$,
\[ K=\frac{6}{(82)^{\frac{3}{2}}} \text{ radians per mile } = 28' \text{ per mile.} \]

(b) At $(2,\,\frac{8}{3})$,
\[ K=\frac{4}{(17)^{\frac{3}{2}}} \text{ radians per mile } = 3^\circ\ 16' \text{ per mile. } \textit{Ans.} \]

(c) At $(1,\,\frac{1}{3})$,
\[ K=\frac{2}{(2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ radians per mile } = 40^\circ\ 30' \text{ per mile. } \textit{Ans.} \]

\textbf{103. Radius of curvature.} By analogy with the circle (see (38), p. 156), the \textit{radius of curvature of a curve at a point} is defined as the reciprocal of the curvature of the curve at that point. Denoting the radius of curvature by $R$, we have
\[ R=\frac{1}{K};{}^{*} \]
or, substituting the values of $K$ from (40) and (41),
\[ R=\frac{\left[1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}}; \tag{42} \]
\[ R=\frac{\left[\rho^2+\left(\frac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\rho^2-\rho\,\dfrac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}+2\left(\frac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}.{}^{\dagger} \tag{43} \]

$^{*}$ Hence the radius of curvature will have the same sign as the curvature, that is, $+$ or $-$, according as the curve is concave upwards or concave downwards.

$\dagger$ In \S 98, p. 152, (43) is derived from (42) by transforming from rectangular to polar coördinates.


\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Find the radius of curvature at any point of the catenary $y = \frac{a}{2}\left(e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right)$.

\textbf{Solution.} \[ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{2}\left(e^{\frac{x}{a}} - e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right); \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{1}{2a}\left(e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right). \]

Substituting in (42),

\[ R = \frac{\left[1 + \left(\dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{a}} - e^{-\frac{x}{a}}}{2}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}}{2a}} = \frac{\left(\dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}}{2}\right)^{3}}{\dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}}{2a}} = \frac{a\left(e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right)^{2}}{4} = \frac{y^2}{a}. \quad \textit{Ans.} \]

If the equation of the curve is given in parametric form, find the first and second derivatives of $y$ with respect to $x$ from $(A)$ and $(B)$, pp. 150, 151, namely:

\[ (G) \qquad \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\dfrac{dy}{dt}}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}}, \text{ and} \]

\[ (H) \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{\dfrac{dx}{dt}\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2} - \dfrac{dy}{dt}\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}}{\left(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right)^{3}}; \]

and then substitute the results in (42).$^{*}$

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 2. Find the radius of curvature of the cycloid
\[ x = a(t - \sin t), \]
\[ y = a(1 - \cos t). \]

\textbf{Solution.} \[ \frac{dx}{dt} = a(1 - \cos t), \qquad \frac{dy}{dt} = a\sin t; \]
\[ \frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = a\sin t, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dt^2} = a\cos t. \]

Substituting in $(G)$ and $(H)$, and then in (42), p. 159, we get

\[ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t}, \quad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{a(1 - \cos t)\,a\cos t - a\sin t\,a\sin t}{a^3(1 - \cos t)^3} = -\frac{1}{a(1 - \cos t)^2}. \]

\[ R = \frac{\left[1 + \left(\dfrac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{-\dfrac{1}{a(1 - \cos t)^2}} = -2a\sqrt{2 - 2\cos t}. \quad \textit{Ans.} \]

$^{*}$ Substituting $(G)$ and $(H)$ in (42) gives $R = \dfrac{\left[\left(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{dy}{dt}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2} - \dfrac{dy}{dt}\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}}$.

\textbf{104. Circle of curvature.} Consider any point $P$ on the curve $C$. The tangent drawn to the curve at $P$ has the same slope as the curve itself at $P$ (\S\ 64, p. 73). In an analogous manner we may construct for each point of the curve a circle whose curvature is the same as the curvature of the curve itself at that point. To do this, proceed as follows. Draw the normal to the curve at $P$ on the concave side of the curve. Lay off on this normal the distance $PC =$ radius of curvature ($= R$) at $P$. With $C$ as a center draw the circle passing through $P$. The curvature of this circle is then
\[ K = \frac{1}{R}, \]
which also equals the curvature of the curve itself at $P$. The circle so constructed is called the \textit{circle of curvature} for the point $P$ on the curve.

In general, the circle of curvature of a curve at a point will cross the curve at that point. This is illustrated in the above figure.

Just as the tangent at $P$ shows the direction of the curve at $P$, so the circle of curvature at $P$ aids us very materially in forming a geometric concept of the curvature of the curve at $P$, the rate of change of direction of the curve and of the circle being the same at $P$.

In a subsequent section (\S\ 116) the circle of curvature will be defined as the limiting position of a secant circle, a definition analogous to that of the tangent given in \S\ 32, p. 31.


\textsc{Illustrative Example 4.} Find the radius of curvature at the point $(3, 4)$ on the equilateral hyperbola $xy = 12$, and draw the corresponding circle of curvature.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[ \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{y}{x}, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{2y}{x^2}. \]

For $(3, 4)$,
\[ \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{4}{3}, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{8}{9}. \]

\[ \therefore\ R = \frac{\left[1 + \frac{16}{9}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{8}{9}} = \frac{125}{24} = 5\frac{5}{24}. \]

The circle of curvature crosses the curve at two points.

\textbf{EXAMPLES} 

1. Find the radius of curvature for each of the following curves, at the point indicated; draw the curve and the corresponding circle of curvature:
(a) $b^2x^2 + a^2y^2 = a^2b^2$, $(a, 0)$. \textit{Ans.} $R = \frac{b^2}{a}$.
(b) $b^2x^2 + a^2y^2 = a^2b^2$, $(0, b)$. $R = \frac{a^2}{b}$.
(c) $y = x^4 - 4x^3 - 18x^2$, $(0, 0)$. $R = \frac{1}{36}$.
(d) $16y^2 = 4x^4 - x^6$, $(2, 0)$. $R = 2$.
(e) $y = x^3$, $(x_1, y_1)$. $R = \frac{(1 + 9x_1^4)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6x_1}$.
(f) $y^2 = x^3$, $(4, 8)$. $R = \frac{1}{3}(40)^{\frac{3}{2}}$.
(g) $y^2 = 8x$, $\left(\frac{9}{8}, 3\right)$. $R = 7\frac{13}{16}$.
(h) $\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{y}{b}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} = 1$, $(0, b)$. $R = \frac{a^2}{3b}$.
(i) $x^2 = 4ay$, $(0, 0)$. $R = 2a$.
(j) $(y - x^2)^2 = x^5$, $(0, 0)$. $R = \frac{1}{2}$.
(k) $b^2x^2 - a^2y^2 = a^2b^2$, $(x_1, y_1)$. $R = \frac{(b^4x_1^2 + a^4y_1^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{a^4b^4}$.
(l) $e^x = \sin y$, $(x_1, y_1)$.
(m) $y = \sin x$, $\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)$.
(n) $y = \cos x$, $\left(\frac{\pi}{4}, \sqrt{2}\right)$.
(o) $y = \log x$, $x = e$.
(p) $9y = x^3$, $x = 3$.
(q) $4y^2 = x^3$, $x = 4$.
(r) $x^2 - y^2 = a^2$, $y = 0$.
(s) $x^2 + 2y^2 = 9$, $(1, -2)$.

2. Determine the radius of curvature of the curve $a^2y = bx^2 + cx^2y$ at the origin. \textit{Ans.} $R = \frac{a^2}{2b}$.

3. Show that the radius of curvature of the witch $y^2 = -\frac{a^2(a - x)}{x}$ at the vertex is $\frac{a}{2}$.

4. Find the radius of curvature of the curve $y = \log \sec x$ at the point $(x_1, y_1)$. \textit{Ans.} $R = \sec x_1$.

5. Find $K$ at any point on the parabola $x^{\frac{1}{2}} + y^{\frac{1}{2}} = a^{\frac{1}{2}}$. \textit{Ans.} $K = \frac{a^{\frac{1}{2}}}{2(x + y)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$.

6. Find $R$ at any point on the hypocycloid $x^{\frac{2}{3}} + y^{\frac{2}{3}} = a^{\frac{2}{3}}$. \textit{Ans.} $R = 3(axy)^{\frac{1}{3}}$.

7. Find $R$ at any point on the cycloid $x = r\,\text{arc vers}\,\frac{y}{r} - \sqrt{2ry - y^2}$. \textit{Ans.} $R = 2\sqrt{2ry}$.

Find the radius of curvature of the following curves at any point:

8. The circle $\rho = a\sin\theta$. \textit{Ans.} $R = \frac{a}{2}$.

9. The spiral of Archimedes $\rho = a\theta$. $R = \frac{(\rho^2 + a^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\rho^2 + 2a^2}$.

10. The cardioid $\rho = a(1 - \cos\theta)$. $R = \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{2a\rho}$.

11. The lemniscate $\rho^2 = a^2\cos 2\theta$. $R = \frac{a^2}{3\rho}$.

12. The parabola $\rho = a\sec^2\frac{\theta}{2}$. $R = 2a\sec^3\frac{\theta}{2}$.

13. The curve $\rho = a\sin^3\frac{\theta}{3}$. $R = \frac{3}{4}a\sin^2\frac{\theta}{3}$.

14. The trisectrix $\rho = 2a\cos\theta - a$. \hfill \textit{Ans.} $R = \dfrac{a(5 - 4\cos\theta)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9 - 6\cos\theta}$.

15. The equilateral hyperbola $\rho^2\cos 2\theta = a^2$. \hfill \textit{Ans.} $R = \dfrac{\rho^3}{a^2}$.

16. The conic $\rho = \dfrac{a(1 - e^2)}{1 - e\cos\theta}$. \hfill \textit{Ans.} $R = \dfrac{a(1 - e^2)(1 - 2e\cos\theta + e^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{(1 - e\cos\theta)^3}$.

17. The curve $\left\{\begin{array}{l} x = 3t^2, \\ y = 3t - t^3. \end{array}\right.$ $t = 1$. \hfill \textit{Ans.} $R = 6$.

18. The hypocycloid $\left\{\begin{array}{l} x = a\cos^3 t, \\ y = a\sin^3 t. \end{array}\right.$ $t = t_1$. \hfill \textit{Ans.} $R = 3a\sin t_1\cos t_1$.

19. The curve $\left\{\begin{array}{l} x = a(\cos t + t\sin t), \\ y = a(\sin t - t\cos t). \end{array}\right.$ $t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. \hfill \textit{Ans.} $R = \dfrac{\pi a}{2}$.

20. The curve $\left\{\begin{array}{l} x = a(m\cos t + \cos mt), \\ y = a(m\sin t - \sin mt). \end{array}\right.$ $t = t_0$. \hfill \textit{Ans.} $R = \dfrac{4ma}{m - 1}\sin\left(\dfrac{m + 1}{2}\right)t_0$.

21. Find the radius of curvature for each of the following curves at the point indicated; draw the curve and the corresponding circle of curvature:
(a) $x = t^2$, $2y = t$; $t = 1$.
(b) $x = t^2$, $y = t^3$; $t = 1$.
(c) $x = \sin t$, $y = \cos 2t$; $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
(d) $x = 1 - t$, $y = t^3$; $t = 3$.
(e) $x = t$, $y = 6t^{-1}$; $t = 2$.
(f) $x = 2e^t$, $y = e^{-t}$; $t = 0$.
(g) $x = \sin t$, $y = 2\cos t$; $t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
(h) $x = t^3$, $y = t^2 + 2t$; $t = 1$.

22. An automobile race track has the form of the ellipse $x^2 + 16y^2 = 16$, the unit being one mile. At what rate is a car on this track changing its direction
(a) when passing through one end of the major axis?
(b) when passing through one end of the minor axis?
(c) when two miles from the minor axis?
(d) when equidistant from the minor and major axes?
\hfill \textit{Ans.} (a) 4 radians per mile; (b) $\frac{1}{16}$ radian per mile.

23. On leaving her dock a steamship moves on an arc of the semicubical parabola $4y^2 = x^3$. If the shore line coincides with the axis of $y$, and the unit of length is one mile, how fast is the ship changing its direction when one mile from the shore?
\hfill \textit{Ans.} $\frac{24}{125}$ radians per mile.

24. A battleship 400 ft. long has changed its direction $30^\circ$ while moving through a distance equal to its own length. What is the radius of the circle in which it is moving? \hfill \textit{Ans.} 764 ft.

25. At what rate is a bicycle rider on a circular track of half a mile diameter changing his direction? \hfill \textit{Ans.} 4 rad. per mile $= 43'$ per rod.

26. The origin being directly above the starting point, an aëroplane follows approximately the spiral $\rho = \theta$, the unit of length being one mile. How rapidly is the aëroplane turning at the instant it has circled the starting point once?

27. A railway track has curves of approximately the form of arcs from the following curves. At what rate will an engine change its direction when passing through the points indicated (1 mi. $=$ unit of length):
(a) $y = x^3$, $(2, 8)$?
(b) $y = x^2$, $(3, 9)$?
(c) $x^2 - y^2 = 8$, $(3, 1)$?
(d) $y = e^x$, $x = 0$?
(e) $y = \cos x$, $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$?
(f) $\rho\theta = 4$, $\theta = 1$?
chapters.text_markdown: # CHAPTER XII: CURVATURE. RADIUS OF CURVATURE **99. Curvature.** The shape of a curve depends very largely upon the rate at which the direction of the tangent changes as the point of contact describes the curve. This rate of change of direction is called *curvature* and is denoted by $K$. We now proceed to find its analytical expression, first for the simple case of the circle, and then for curves in general. **100. Curvature of a circle.** Consider a circle of radius $R$. Let $\tau =$ angle that the tangent at $P$ makes with $OX$, and $\tau + \Delta\tau =$ angle made by the tangent at a neighboring point $P'$. Then we say $$\Delta\tau = \textit{total curvature of arc } PP'.$$ If the point $P$ with its tangent be supposed to move along the curve to $P'$, the total curvature $(=\Delta\tau)$ would measure the total change in direction, or rotation, of the tangent; or, what is the same thing, the total change in direction of the arc itself. Denoting by $s$ the length of the arc of the curve measured from some fixed point (as $A$) to $P$, and by $\Delta s$ the length of the arc $PP'$, then the ratio $$\frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s}$$ measures the average change in direction per unit length of arc.$^*$ Since, from the figure, $$\Delta s = R \cdot \Delta\tau,$$ or $$\frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s} = \frac{1}{R},$$ $^*$ Thus, if $\Delta\tau = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ radians $(= 30^\circ)$, and $\Delta s = 3$ centimeters, then $\dfrac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s} = \dfrac{\pi}{18}$ radians per centimeter $= 10^\circ$ per centimeter $=$ average rate of change of direction. it is evident that this ratio is constant everywhere on the circle. This ratio is, by definition, the *curvature of the circle*, and we have $$(38)\qquad K=\frac{1}{R}.$$ *The curvature of a circle equals the reciprocal of its radius.* **101. Curvature at a point.** Consider any curve. As in the last section, $$\Delta\tau = \textit{total curvature of the arc } PP',$$ and $$\frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s} = \textit{average curvature of the arc } PP'.$$ More important, however, than the notion of the average curvature of an arc is that of *curvature at a point.* This is obtained as follows. Imagine $P'$ to approach $P$ along the curve; then the limiting value of the average curvature $\left(=\dfrac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s}\right)$ as $P'$ approaches $P$ along the curve is defined as the curvature at $P$, that is, $$\textit{Curvature at a point} = \underset{\Delta s=0}{\text{limit}}\left(\frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s}\right)=\frac{d\tau}{ds}.$$ $$(39)\qquad \therefore\ K=\frac{d\tau}{ds}=\textbf{curvature.}$$ Since the angle $\Delta\tau$ is measured in radians and the length of arc $\Delta s$ in units of length, it follows that *the unit of curvature at a point is one radian per unit of length.* **102. Formulas for curvature.** It is evident that if, in the last section, instead of measuring the angles which the tangents made with $OX$, we had denoted by $\tau$ and $\tau+\Delta\tau$ the angles made by the tangents with any arbitrarily fixed line, the different steps would in no wise have been changed, and consequently the results are entirely independent of the system of coördinates used. However, since the equations of the curves we shall consider are all given in either rectangular or polar coördinates, it is necessary to deduce formulas for $K$ in terms of both. We have $$\tan\tau=\frac{dy}{dx},\qquad \S\ 32,\ \text{p. } 31$$ or $$\tau=\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{dy}{dx}.$$ Differentiating with respect to $x$, using **XX** \(A\) $$\frac{d\tau}{dx}=\frac{\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}}{1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}}\cdot$$ Also \(B\) $$\frac{ds}{dx}=\left[1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}\cdot$$ From (**24**), p. 134 Dividing $(A)$ by $(B)$ gives $$\frac{\dfrac{d\tau}{dx}}{\dfrac{ds}{dx}}=\frac{\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}}{\left[1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}\cdot$$ But $$\frac{\dfrac{d\tau}{dx}}{\dfrac{ds}{dx}}=\frac{d\tau}{ds}=K.$$ Hence (**40**) $$\mathbf{K}=\frac{\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}}{\left[1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}\cdot$$ If the equation of the curve be given in polar coördinates, $K$ may be found as follows: From (**B**), p. 84, $$\tau=\theta+\psi.\quad\text{Differentiating,}$$ \(C\) $$\frac{d\tau}{d\theta}=1+\frac{d\psi}{d\theta}\cdot$$ But $$\tan\psi=\frac{\rho}{\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}}\cdot$$ From (**A**), p. 84 $$\therefore\ \psi=\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{\rho}{\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}}\cdot$$ Differentiating by **XX** with respect to $\theta$ and reducing, \(D\) $$\frac{d\psi}{d\theta}=\frac{\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^{2}-\rho\,\dfrac{d^{2}\rho}{d\theta^{2}}}{\rho^{2}+\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^{2}}\cdot$$ Substituting $(D)$ in $(C)$, we get $$(E)\qquad \frac{d\tau}{d\theta}=\frac{\rho^2-\rho\,\dfrac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}+2\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}{\rho^2+\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}.\quad\text{Also}$$ $$(F)\qquad \frac{ds}{d\theta}=\left[\rho^2+\left(\frac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]^{\frac12}.\qquad\text{From }\textbf{(30)}\text{, p. 136}$$ Dividing $(E)$ by $(F)$ gives $$\frac{\dfrac{d\tau}{d\theta}}{\dfrac{ds}{d\theta}}=\frac{\rho^2-\rho\,\dfrac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}+2\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}{\left[\rho^2+\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]^{\frac32}}.$$ But $$\frac{\dfrac{d\tau}{d\theta}}{\dfrac{ds}{d\theta}}=\frac{d\tau}{ds}=K.\quad\text{Hence}$$ $$(41)\qquad K=\frac{\rho^2-\rho\,\dfrac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}+2\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}{\left[\rho^2+\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]^{\frac32}}.$$ Illustrative Example 1. Find the curvature of the parabola $y^2=4px$ at the upper end of the latus rectum. **Solution.** $$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2p}{y};\qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\frac{2p}{y^2}\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{4p^2}{y^3}.$$ Substituting in (40), $$K=-\frac{4p^2}{(y^2+4p^2)^{\frac32}},$$ giving the curvature at *any point*. At the upper end of the latus rectum $(p,\,2p)$ $$K=-\frac{4p^2}{(4p^2+4p^2)^{\frac32}}=-\frac{4p^2}{16\sqrt{2}\,p^3}=-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}\,p}.\,{}^{*}\qquad \textit{Ans.}$$ Illustrative Example 2. Find the curvature of the logarithmic spiral $\rho=e^{a\theta}$ at any point. **Solution.** $$\frac{d\rho}{d\theta}=ae^{a\theta}=a\rho;\qquad \frac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}=a^2e^{a\theta}=a^2\rho.$$ Substituting in (41), $$K=\frac{1}{\rho\sqrt{1+a^2}}.\qquad \textit{Ans.}$$ ${}^{*}$ While in our work it is generally only the numerical value of $K$ that is of importance, yet we can give a geometric meaning to its sign. Throughout our work we have taken the positive sign of the radical $\sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}$. Therefore $K$ will be positive or negative at the same time as $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$, that is (§ 85, p. 125), according as the curve is concave upwards or concave downwards. In laying out the curves on a railroad it will not do, on account of the high speed of trains, to pass abruptly from a straight stretch of track to a circular curve. In order to make the change of direction gradual, engineers make use of *transition curves* to connect the straight part of a track with a circular curve. Arcs of cubical parabolas are generally employed as transition curves. Illustrative Example 3. The transition curve on a railway track has the shape of an arc of the cubical parabola $y=\frac{1}{3}x^3$. At what rate is a car on this track changing its direction (1 mi. = unit of length) when it is passing through (a) the point $(3,\,9)$? (b) the point $(2,\,\frac{8}{3})$? (c) the point $(1,\,\frac{1}{3})$? **Solution.** $$\frac{dy}{dx}=x^2, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2x.$$ Substituting in (40), $$K=\frac{2x}{(1+x^4)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.$$ \(a\) At $(3,\,9)$, $$K=\frac{6}{(82)^{\frac{3}{2}}} \text{ radians per mile } = 28' \text{ per mile.}$$ \(b\) At $(2,\,\frac{8}{3})$, $$K=\frac{4}{(17)^{\frac{3}{2}}} \text{ radians per mile } = 3^\circ\ 16' \text{ per mile. } \textit{Ans.}$$ \(c\) At $(1,\,\frac{1}{3})$, $$K=\frac{2}{(2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ radians per mile } = 40^\circ\ 30' \text{ per mile. } \textit{Ans.}$$ **103. Radius of curvature.** By analogy with the circle (see (38), p. 156), the *radius of curvature of a curve at a point* is defined as the reciprocal of the curvature of the curve at that point. Denoting the radius of curvature by $R$, we have $$R=\frac{1}{K};{}^{*}$$ or, substituting the values of $K$ from (40) and (41), $$R=\frac{\left[1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}}; \tag{42}$$ $$R=\frac{\left[\rho^2+\left(\frac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\rho^2-\rho\,\dfrac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}+2\left(\frac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}.{}^{\dagger} \tag{43}$$ $^{*}$ Hence the radius of curvature will have the same sign as the curvature, that is, $+$ or $-$, according as the curve is concave upwards or concave downwards. $\dagger$ In §98, p. 152, (43) is derived from (42) by transforming from rectangular to polar coördinates. Illustrative Example 1. Find the radius of curvature at any point of the catenary $y = \frac{a}{2}\left(e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right)$. **Solution.** $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{2}\left(e^{\frac{x}{a}} - e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right); \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{1}{2a}\left(e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right).$$ Substituting in (42), $$R = \frac{\left[1 + \left(\dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{a}} - e^{-\frac{x}{a}}}{2}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}}{2a}} = \frac{\left(\dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}}{2}\right)^{3}}{\dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}}{2a}} = \frac{a\left(e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right)^{2}}{4} = \frac{y^2}{a}. \quad \textit{Ans.}$$ If the equation of the curve is given in parametric form, find the first and second derivatives of $y$ with respect to $x$ from $(A)$ and $(B)$, pp. 150, 151, namely: $$(G) \qquad \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\dfrac{dy}{dt}}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}}, \text{ and}$$ $$(H) \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{\dfrac{dx}{dt}\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2} - \dfrac{dy}{dt}\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}}{\left(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right)^{3}};$$ and then substitute the results in (42).$^{*}$ Illustrative Example 2. Find the radius of curvature of the cycloid $$x = a(t - \sin t),$$ $$y = a(1 - \cos t).$$ **Solution.** $$\frac{dx}{dt} = a(1 - \cos t), \qquad \frac{dy}{dt} = a\sin t;$$ $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = a\sin t, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dt^2} = a\cos t.$$ Substituting in $(G)$ and $(H)$, and then in (42), p. 159, we get $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t}, \quad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{a(1 - \cos t)\,a\cos t - a\sin t\,a\sin t}{a^3(1 - \cos t)^3} = -\frac{1}{a(1 - \cos t)^2}.$$ $$R = \frac{\left[1 + \left(\dfrac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{-\dfrac{1}{a(1 - \cos t)^2}} = -2a\sqrt{2 - 2\cos t}. \quad \textit{Ans.}$$ $^{*}$ Substituting $(G)$ and $(H)$ in (42) gives $R = \dfrac{\left[\left(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{dy}{dt}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2} - \dfrac{dy}{dt}\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}}$. **104. Circle of curvature.** Consider any point $P$ on the curve $C$. The tangent drawn to the curve at $P$ has the same slope as the curve itself at $P$ (§ 64, p. 73). In an analogous manner we may construct for each point of the curve a circle whose curvature is the same as the curvature of the curve itself at that point. To do this, proceed as follows. Draw the normal to the curve at $P$ on the concave side of the curve. Lay off on this normal the distance $PC =$ radius of curvature ($= R$) at $P$. With $C$ as a center draw the circle passing through $P$. The curvature of this circle is then $$K = \frac{1}{R},$$ which also equals the curvature of the curve itself at $P$. The circle so constructed is called the *circle of curvature* for the point $P$ on the curve. In general, the circle of curvature of a curve at a point will cross the curve at that point. This is illustrated in the above figure. Just as the tangent at $P$ shows the direction of the curve at $P$, so the circle of curvature at $P$ aids us very materially in forming a geometric concept of the curvature of the curve at $P$, the rate of change of direction of the curve and of the circle being the same at $P$. In a subsequent section (§ 116) the circle of curvature will be defined as the limiting position of a secant circle, a definition analogous to that of the tangent given in § 32, p. 31. Illustrative Example 4. Find the radius of curvature at the point $(3, 4)$ on the equilateral hyperbola $xy = 12$, and draw the corresponding circle of curvature. **Solution.** $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{y}{x}, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{2y}{x^2}.$$ For $(3, 4)$, $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{4}{3}, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{8}{9}.$$ $$\therefore\ R = \frac{\left[1 + \frac{16}{9}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{8}{9}} = \frac{125}{24} = 5\frac{5}{24}.$$ The circle of curvature crosses the curve at two points. **EXAMPLES** 1\. Find the radius of curvature for each of the following curves, at the point indicated; draw the curve and the corresponding circle of curvature: (a) $b^2x^2 + a^2y^2 = a^2b^2$, $(a, 0)$. *Ans.* $R = \frac{b^2}{a}$. (b) $b^2x^2 + a^2y^2 = a^2b^2$, $(0, b)$. $R = \frac{a^2}{b}$. (c) $y = x^4 - 4x^3 - 18x^2$, $(0, 0)$. $R = \frac{1}{36}$. (d) $16y^2 = 4x^4 - x^6$, $(2, 0)$. $R = 2$. (e) $y = x^3$, $(x_1, y_1)$. $R = \frac{(1 + 9x_1^4)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6x_1}$. (f) $y^2 = x^3$, $(4, 8)$. $R = \frac{1}{3}(40)^{\frac{3}{2}}$. (g) $y^2 = 8x$, $\left(\frac{9}{8}, 3\right)$. $R = 7\frac{13}{16}$. (h) $\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{y}{b}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} = 1$, $(0, b)$. $R = \frac{a^2}{3b}$. (i) $x^2 = 4ay$, $(0, 0)$. $R = 2a$. (j) $(y - x^2)^2 = x^5$, $(0, 0)$. $R = \frac{1}{2}$. (k) $b^2x^2 - a^2y^2 = a^2b^2$, $(x_1, y_1)$. $R = \frac{(b^4x_1^2 + a^4y_1^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{a^4b^4}$. (l) $e^x = \sin y$, $(x_1, y_1)$. (m) $y = \sin x$, $\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)$. (n) $y = \cos x$, $\left(\frac{\pi}{4}, \sqrt{2}\right)$. (o) $y = \log x$, $x = e$. (p) $9y = x^3$, $x = 3$. (q) $4y^2 = x^3$, $x = 4$. (r) $x^2 - y^2 = a^2$, $y = 0$. (s) $x^2 + 2y^2 = 9$, $(1, -2)$. 2\. Determine the radius of curvature of the curve $a^2y = bx^2 + cx^2y$ at the origin. *Ans.* $R = \frac{a^2}{2b}$. 3\. Show that the radius of curvature of the witch $y^2 = -\frac{a^2(a - x)}{x}$ at the vertex is $\frac{a}{2}$. 4\. Find the radius of curvature of the curve $y = \log \sec x$ at the point $(x_1, y_1)$. *Ans.* $R = \sec x_1$. 5\. Find $K$ at any point on the parabola $x^{\frac{1}{2}} + y^{\frac{1}{2}} = a^{\frac{1}{2}}$. *Ans.* $K = \frac{a^{\frac{1}{2}}}{2(x + y)^{\frac{3}{2}}}$. 6\. Find $R$ at any point on the hypocycloid $x^{\frac{2}{3}} + y^{\frac{2}{3}} = a^{\frac{2}{3}}$. *Ans.* $R = 3(axy)^{\frac{1}{3}}$. 7\. Find $R$ at any point on the cycloid $x = r\,\text{arc vers}\,\frac{y}{r} - \sqrt{2ry - y^2}$. *Ans.* $R = 2\sqrt{2ry}$. Find the radius of curvature of the following curves at any point: 8\. The circle $\rho = a\sin\theta$. *Ans.* $R = \frac{a}{2}$. 9\. The spiral of Archimedes $\rho = a\theta$. $R = \frac{(\rho^2 + a^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\rho^2 + 2a^2}$. 10\. The cardioid $\rho = a(1 - \cos\theta)$. $R = \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{2a\rho}$. 11\. The lemniscate $\rho^2 = a^2\cos 2\theta$. $R = \frac{a^2}{3\rho}$. 12\. The parabola $\rho = a\sec^2\frac{\theta}{2}$. $R = 2a\sec^3\frac{\theta}{2}$. 13\. The curve $\rho = a\sin^3\frac{\theta}{3}$. $R = \frac{3}{4}a\sin^2\frac{\theta}{3}$. 14\. The trisectrix $\rho = 2a\cos\theta - a$. *Ans.* $R = \dfrac{a(5 - 4\cos\theta)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9 - 6\cos\theta}$. 15\. The equilateral hyperbola $\rho^2\cos 2\theta = a^2$. *Ans.* $R = \dfrac{\rho^3}{a^2}$. 16\. The conic $\rho = \dfrac{a(1 - e^2)}{1 - e\cos\theta}$. *Ans.* $R = \dfrac{a(1 - e^2)(1 - 2e\cos\theta + e^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{(1 - e\cos\theta)^3}$. 17\. The curve $\left\{\begin{array}{l} x = 3t^2, \\ y = 3t - t^3. \end{array}\right.$ $t = 1$. *Ans.* $R = 6$. 18\. The hypocycloid $\left\{\begin{array}{l} x = a\cos^3 t, \\ y = a\sin^3 t. \end{array}\right.$ $t = t_1$. *Ans.* $R = 3a\sin t_1\cos t_1$. 19\. The curve $\left\{\begin{array}{l} x = a(\cos t + t\sin t), \\ y = a(\sin t - t\cos t). \end{array}\right.$ $t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. *Ans.* $R = \dfrac{\pi a}{2}$. 20\. The curve $\left\{\begin{array}{l} x = a(m\cos t + \cos mt), \\ y = a(m\sin t - \sin mt). \end{array}\right.$ $t = t_0$. *Ans.* $R = \dfrac{4ma}{m - 1}\sin\left(\dfrac{m + 1}{2}\right)t_0$. 21\. Find the radius of curvature for each of the following curves at the point indicated; draw the curve and the corresponding circle of curvature: (a) $x = t^2$, $2y = t$; $t = 1$. (b) $x = t^2$, $y = t^3$; $t = 1$. (c) $x = \sin t$, $y = \cos 2t$; $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$. (d) $x = 1 - t$, $y = t^3$; $t = 3$. (e) $x = t$, $y = 6t^{-1}$; $t = 2$. Denoting by \(s\) the length of the arc of the curve measured from some fixed point (as \(A\)) to \(P\), and by \(\Delta s\) the length of the arc \(PP'\), then the ratio

\[\frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s}\]

measures the average change in direction per unit length of arc.\(^*\) Since, from the figure,

\[\Delta s = R \cdot \Delta\tau,\]

or

\[\frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s} = \frac{1}{R},\]

\(^*\) Thus, if \(\Delta\tau = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\) radians \((= 30^\circ)\), and \(\Delta s = 3\) centimeters, then \(\dfrac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s} = \dfrac{\pi}{18}\) radians per centimeter \(= 10^\circ\) per centimeter \(=\) average rate of change of direction.

it is evident that this ratio is constant everywhere on the circle. This ratio is, by definition, the curvature of the circle, and we have \[(38)\qquad K=\frac{1}{R}.\] The curvature of a circle equals the reciprocal of its radius.

101. Curvature at a point. Consider any curve. As in the last section, \[\Delta\tau = \textit{total curvature of the arc } PP',\] and \[\frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s} = \textit{average curvature of the arc } PP'.\] More important, however, than the notion of the average curvature of an arc is that of curvature at a point. This is obtained as follows. Imagine \(P'\) to approach \(P\) along the curve; then the limiting value of the average curvature \(\left(=\dfrac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s}\right)\) as \(P'\) approaches \(P\) along the curve is defined as the curvature at \(P\), that is, \[\textit{Curvature at a point} = \underset{\Delta s=0}{\text{limit}}\left(\frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta s}\right)=\frac{d\tau}{ds}.\] \[(39)\qquad \therefore\ K=\frac{d\tau}{ds}=\textbf{curvature.}\] Since the angle \(\Delta\tau\) is measured in radians and the length of arc \(\Delta s\) in units of length, it follows that the unit of curvature at a point is one radian per unit of length.

102. Formulas for curvature. It is evident that if, in the last section, instead of measuring the angles which the tangents made with \(OX\), we had denoted by \(\tau\) and \(\tau+\Delta\tau\) the angles made by the tangents with any arbitrarily fixed line, the different steps would in no wise have been changed, and consequently the results are entirely independent of the system of coördinates used. However, since the equations of the curves we shall consider are all given in either rectangular or polar coördinates, it is necessary to deduce formulas for \(K\) in terms of both. We have \[\tan\tau=\frac{dy}{dx},\qquad \S\ 32,\ \text{p. } 31\] or \[\tau=\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{dy}{dx}.\]

Differentiating with respect to \(x\), using XX

(A) \[\frac{d\tau}{dx}=\frac{\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}}{1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}}\cdot\] Also

(B) \[\frac{ds}{dx}=\left[1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}\cdot\] From (24), p. 134

Dividing \((A)\) by \((B)\) gives \[\frac{\dfrac{d\tau}{dx}}{\dfrac{ds}{dx}}=\frac{\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}}{\left[1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}\cdot\]

But \[\frac{\dfrac{d\tau}{dx}}{\dfrac{ds}{dx}}=\frac{d\tau}{ds}=K.\] Hence

(40) \[\mathbf{K}=\frac{\dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}}{\left[1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}\cdot\]

If the equation of the curve be given in polar coördinates, \(K\) may be found as follows:

From (B), p. 84, \[\tau=\theta+\psi.\quad\text{Differentiating,}\]

(C) \[\frac{d\tau}{d\theta}=1+\frac{d\psi}{d\theta}\cdot\]

But \[\tan\psi=\frac{\rho}{\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}}\cdot\] From (A), p. 84 \[\therefore\ \psi=\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{\rho}{\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}}\cdot\]

Differentiating by XX with respect to \(\theta\) and reducing,

(D) \[\frac{d\psi}{d\theta}=\frac{\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^{2}-\rho\,\dfrac{d^{2}\rho}{d\theta^{2}}}{\rho^{2}+\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^{2}}\cdot\]

Substituting \((D)\) in \((C)\), we get \[(E)\qquad \frac{d\tau}{d\theta}=\frac{\rho^2-\rho\,\dfrac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}+2\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}{\rho^2+\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}.\quad\text{Also}\] \[(F)\qquad \frac{ds}{d\theta}=\left[\rho^2+\left(\frac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]^{\frac12}.\qquad\text{From }\textbf{(30)}\text{, p. 136}\] Dividing \((E)\) by \((F)\) gives \[\frac{\dfrac{d\tau}{d\theta}}{\dfrac{ds}{d\theta}}=\frac{\rho^2-\rho\,\dfrac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}+2\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}{\left[\rho^2+\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]^{\frac32}}.\] But \[\frac{\dfrac{d\tau}{d\theta}}{\dfrac{ds}{d\theta}}=\frac{d\tau}{ds}=K.\quad\text{Hence}\] \[(41)\qquad K=\frac{\rho^2-\rho\,\dfrac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}+2\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}{\left[\rho^2+\left(\dfrac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]^{\frac32}}.\]

Illustrative Example 1. Find the curvature of the parabola \(y^2=4px\) at the upper end of the latus rectum.

Solution. \[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2p}{y};\qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\frac{2p}{y^2}\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{4p^2}{y^3}.\] Substituting in (40), \[K=-\frac{4p^2}{(y^2+4p^2)^{\frac32}},\] giving the curvature at any point. At the upper end of the latus rectum \((p,\,2p)\) \[K=-\frac{4p^2}{(4p^2+4p^2)^{\frac32}}=-\frac{4p^2}{16\sqrt{2}\,p^3}=-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}\,p}.\,{}^{*}\qquad \textit{Ans.}\]

Illustrative Example 2. Find the curvature of the logarithmic spiral \(\rho=e^{a\theta}\) at any point.

Solution. \[\frac{d\rho}{d\theta}=ae^{a\theta}=a\rho;\qquad \frac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}=a^2e^{a\theta}=a^2\rho.\] Substituting in (41), \[K=\frac{1}{\rho\sqrt{1+a^2}}.\qquad \textit{Ans.}\]

\({}^{*}\) While in our work it is generally only the numerical value of \(K\) that is of importance, yet we can give a geometric meaning to its sign. Throughout our work we have taken the positive sign of the radical \(\sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}\). Therefore \(K\) will be positive or negative at the same time as \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\), that is (§ 85, p. 125), according as the curve is concave upwards or concave downwards.

In laying out the curves on a railroad it will not do, on account of the high speed of trains, to pass abruptly from a straight stretch of track to a circular curve. In order to make the change of direction gradual, engineers make use of transition curves to connect the straight part of a track with a circular curve. Arcs of cubical parabolas are generally employed as transition curves.

Illustrative Example 3. The transition curve on a railway track has the shape of an arc of the cubical parabola \(y=\frac{1}{3}x^3\). At what rate is a car on this track changing its direction (1 mi. = unit of length) when it is passing through (a) the point \((3,\,9)\)? (b) the point \((2,\,\frac{8}{3})\)? (c) the point \((1,\,\frac{1}{3})\)?

Solution. \[\frac{dy}{dx}=x^2, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2x.\]

Substituting in (40), \[K=\frac{2x}{(1+x^4)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.\]

(a) At \((3,\,9)\), \[K=\frac{6}{(82)^{\frac{3}{2}}} \text{ radians per mile } = 28' \text{ per mile.}\]

(b) At \((2,\,\frac{8}{3})\), \[K=\frac{4}{(17)^{\frac{3}{2}}} \text{ radians per mile } = 3^\circ\ 16' \text{ per mile. } \textit{Ans.}\]

(c) At \((1,\,\frac{1}{3})\), \[K=\frac{2}{(2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ radians per mile } = 40^\circ\ 30' \text{ per mile. } \textit{Ans.}\]

103. Radius of curvature. By analogy with the circle (see (38), p. 156), the radius of curvature of a curve at a point is defined as the reciprocal of the curvature of the curve at that point. Denoting the radius of curvature by \(R\), we have \[R=\frac{1}{K};{}^{*}\] or, substituting the values of \(K\) from (40) and (41), \[R=\frac{\left[1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}}; \tag{42}\] \[R=\frac{\left[\rho^2+\left(\frac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\rho^2-\rho\,\dfrac{d^2\rho}{d\theta^2}+2\left(\frac{d\rho}{d\theta}\right)^2}.{}^{\dagger} \tag{43}\]

\(^{*}\) Hence the radius of curvature will have the same sign as the curvature, that is, \(+\) or \(-\), according as the curve is concave upwards or concave downwards.

\(\dagger\) In §98, p. 152, (43) is derived from (42) by transforming from rectangular to polar coördinates.

Illustrative Example 1. Find the radius of curvature at any point of the catenary \(y = \frac{a}{2}\left(e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right)\).

Solution. \[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{2}\left(e^{\frac{x}{a}} - e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right); \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{1}{2a}\left(e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right).\]

Substituting in (42),

\[R = \frac{\left[1 + \left(\dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{a}} - e^{-\frac{x}{a}}}{2}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}}{2a}} = \frac{\left(\dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}}{2}\right)^{3}}{\dfrac{e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}}{2a}} = \frac{a\left(e^{\frac{x}{a}} + e^{-\frac{x}{a}}\right)^{2}}{4} = \frac{y^2}{a}. \quad \textit{Ans.}\]

If the equation of the curve is given in parametric form, find the first and second derivatives of \(y\) with respect to \(x\) from \((A)\) and \((B)\), pp. 150, 151, namely:

\[(G) \qquad \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\dfrac{dy}{dt}}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}}, \text{ and}\]

\[(H) \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{\dfrac{dx}{dt}\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2} - \dfrac{dy}{dt}\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}}{\left(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right)^{3}};\]

and then substitute the results in (42).\(^{*}\)

Illustrative Example 2. Find the radius of curvature of the cycloid \[x = a(t - \sin t),\] \[y = a(1 - \cos t).\]

Solution. \[\frac{dx}{dt} = a(1 - \cos t), \qquad \frac{dy}{dt} = a\sin t;\] \[\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = a\sin t, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dt^2} = a\cos t.\]

Substituting in \((G)\) and \((H)\), and then in (42), p. 159, we get

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t}, \quad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{a(1 - \cos t)\,a\cos t - a\sin t\,a\sin t}{a^3(1 - \cos t)^3} = -\frac{1}{a(1 - \cos t)^2}.\]

\[R = \frac{\left[1 + \left(\dfrac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{-\dfrac{1}{a(1 - \cos t)^2}} = -2a\sqrt{2 - 2\cos t}. \quad \textit{Ans.}\]

\(^{*}\) Substituting \((G)\) and \((H)\) in (42) gives \(R = \dfrac{\left[\left(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{dy}{dt}\right)^{2}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2} - \dfrac{dy}{dt}\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}}\).

104. Circle of curvature. Consider any point \(P\) on the curve \(C\). The tangent drawn to the curve at \(P\) has the same slope as the curve itself at \(P\) (§ 64, p. 73). In an analogous manner we may construct for each point of the curve a circle whose curvature is the same as the curvature of the curve itself at that point. To do this, proceed as follows. Draw the normal to the curve at \(P\) on the concave side of the curve. Lay off on this normal the distance \(PC =\) radius of curvature (\(= R\)) at \(P\). With \(C\) as a center draw the circle passing through \(P\). The curvature of this circle is then \[K = \frac{1}{R},\] which also equals the curvature of the curve itself at \(P\). The circle so constructed is called the circle of curvature for the point \(P\) on the curve.

In general, the circle of curvature of a curve at a point will cross the curve at that point. This is illustrated in the above figure.

Just as the tangent at \(P\) shows the direction of the curve at \(P\), so the circle of curvature at \(P\) aids us very materially in forming a geometric concept of the curvature of the curve at \(P\), the rate of change of direction of the curve and of the circle being the same at \(P\).

In a subsequent section (§ 116) the circle of curvature will be defined as the limiting position of a secant circle, a definition analogous to that of the tangent given in § 32, p. 31.

Illustrative Example 4. Find the radius of curvature at the point \((3, 4)\) on the equilateral hyperbola \(xy = 12\), and draw the corresponding circle of curvature.

Solution. \[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{y}{x}, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{2y}{x^2}.\]

For \((3, 4)\), \[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{4}{3}, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{8}{9}.\]

\[\therefore\ R = \frac{\left[1 + \frac{16}{9}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{8}{9}} = \frac{125}{24} = 5\frac{5}{24}.\]

The circle of curvature crosses the curve at two points.

EXAMPLES

1. Find the radius of curvature for each of the following curves, at the point indicated; draw the curve and the corresponding circle of curvature: (a) \(b^2x^2 + a^2y^2 = a^2b^2\), \((a, 0)\). Ans. \(R = \frac{b^2}{a}\). (b) \(b^2x^2 + a^2y^2 = a^2b^2\), \((0, b)\). \(R = \frac{a^2}{b}\). (c) \(y = x^4 - 4x^3 - 18x^2\), \((0, 0)\). \(R = \frac{1}{36}\). (d) \(16y^2 = 4x^4 - x^6\), \((2, 0)\). \(R = 2\). (e) \(y = x^3\), \((x_1, y_1)\). \(R = \frac{(1 + 9x_1^4)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6x_1}\). (f) \(y^2 = x^3\), \((4, 8)\). \(R = \frac{1}{3}(40)^{\frac{3}{2}}\). (g) \(y^2 = 8x\), \(\left(\frac{9}{8}, 3\right)\). \(R = 7\frac{13}{16}\). (h) \(\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{y}{b}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}} = 1\), \((0, b)\). \(R = \frac{a^2}{3b}\). (i) \(x^2 = 4ay\), \((0, 0)\). \(R = 2a\). (j) \((y - x^2)^2 = x^5\), \((0, 0)\). \(R = \frac{1}{2}\). (k) \(b^2x^2 - a^2y^2 = a^2b^2\), \((x_1, y_1)\). \(R = \frac{(b^4x_1^2 + a^4y_1^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{a^4b^4}\). (l) \(e^x = \sin y\), \((x_1, y_1)\). (m) \(y = \sin x\), \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)\). (n) \(y = \cos x\), \(\left(\frac{\pi}{4}, \sqrt{2}\right)\). (o) \(y = \log x\), \(x = e\). (p) \(9y = x^3\), \(x = 3\). (q) \(4y^2 = x^3\), \(x = 4\). (r) \(x^2 - y^2 = a^2\), \(y = 0\). (s) \(x^2 + 2y^2 = 9\), \((1, -2)\).

2. Determine the radius of curvature of the curve \(a^2y = bx^2 + cx^2y\) at the origin. Ans. \(R = \frac{a^2}{2b}\).

3. Show that the radius of curvature of the witch \(y^2 = -\frac{a^2(a - x)}{x}\) at the vertex is \(\frac{a}{2}\).

4. Find the radius of curvature of the curve \(y = \log \sec x\) at the point \((x_1, y_1)\). Ans. \(R = \sec x_1\).

5. Find \(K\) at any point on the parabola \(x^{\frac{1}{2}} + y^{\frac{1}{2}} = a^{\frac{1}{2}}\). Ans. \(K = \frac{a^{\frac{1}{2}}}{2(x + y)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\).

6. Find \(R\) at any point on the hypocycloid \(x^{\frac{2}{3}} + y^{\frac{2}{3}} = a^{\frac{2}{3}}\). Ans. \(R = 3(axy)^{\frac{1}{3}}\).

7. Find \(R\) at any point on the cycloid \(x = r\,\text{arc vers}\,\frac{y}{r} - \sqrt{2ry - y^2}\). Ans. \(R = 2\sqrt{2ry}\).

Find the radius of curvature of the following curves at any point:

8. The circle \(\rho = a\sin\theta\). Ans. \(R = \frac{a}{2}\).

9. The spiral of Archimedes \(\rho = a\theta\). \(R = \frac{(\rho^2 + a^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\rho^2 + 2a^2}\).

10. The cardioid \(\rho = a(1 - \cos\theta)\). \(R = \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{2a\rho}\).

11. The lemniscate \(\rho^2 = a^2\cos 2\theta\). \(R = \frac{a^2}{3\rho}\).

12. The parabola \(\rho = a\sec^2\frac{\theta}{2}\). \(R = 2a\sec^3\frac{\theta}{2}\).

13. The curve \(\rho = a\sin^3\frac{\theta}{3}\). \(R = \frac{3}{4}a\sin^2\frac{\theta}{3}\).

14. The trisectrix \(\rho = 2a\cos\theta - a\). Ans. \(R = \dfrac{a(5 - 4\cos\theta)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9 - 6\cos\theta}\).

15. The equilateral hyperbola \(\rho^2\cos 2\theta = a^2\). Ans. \(R = \dfrac{\rho^3}{a^2}\).

16. The conic \(\rho = \dfrac{a(1 - e^2)}{1 - e\cos\theta}\). Ans. \(R = \dfrac{a(1 - e^2)(1 - 2e\cos\theta + e^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{(1 - e\cos\theta)^3}\).

17. The curve \(\left\{\begin{array}{l} x = 3t^2, \\ y = 3t - t^3. \end{array}\right.\) \(t = 1\). Ans. \(R = 6\).

18. The hypocycloid \(\left\{\begin{array}{l} x = a\cos^3 t, \\ y = a\sin^3 t. \end{array}\right.\) \(t = t_1\). Ans. \(R = 3a\sin t_1\cos t_1\).

19. The curve \(\left\{\begin{array}{l} x = a(\cos t + t\sin t), \\ y = a(\sin t - t\cos t). \end{array}\right.\) \(t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Ans. \(R = \dfrac{\pi a}{2}\).

20. The curve \(\left\{\begin{array}{l} x = a(m\cos t + \cos mt), \\ y = a(m\sin t - \sin mt). \end{array}\right.\) \(t = t_0\). Ans. \(R = \dfrac{4ma}{m - 1}\sin\left(\dfrac{m + 1}{2}\right)t_0\).

21. Find the radius of curvature for each of the following curves at the point indicated; draw the curve and the corresponding circle of curvature: (a) \(x = t^2\), \(2y = t\); \(t = 1\). (b) \(x = t^2\), \(y = t^3\); \(t = 1\). (c) \(x = \sin t\), \(y = \cos 2t\); \(t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\). (d) \(x = 1 - t\), \(y = t^3\); \(t = 3\). (e) \(x = t\), \(y = 6t^{-1}\); \(t = 2\). (f) \(x = 2e^t\), \(y = e^{-t}\); \(t = 0\). (g) \(x = \sin t\), \(y = 2\cos t\); \(t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). (h) \(x = t^3\), \(y = t^2 + 2t\); \(t = 1\).

22. An automobile race track has the form of the ellipse \(x^2 + 16y^2 = 16\), the unit being one mile. At what rate is a car on this track changing its direction (a) when passing through one end of the major axis? (b) when passing through one end of the minor axis? (c) when two miles from the minor axis? (d) when equidistant from the minor and major axes? Ans. (a) 4 radians per mile; (b) \(\frac{1}{16}\) radian per mile.

23. On leaving her dock a steamship moves on an arc of the semicubical parabola \(4y^2 = x^3\). If the shore line coincides with the axis of \(y\), and the unit of length is one mile, how fast is the ship changing its direction when one mile from the shore? Ans. \(\frac{24}{125}\) radians per mile.

24. A battleship 400 ft. long has changed its direction \(30^\circ\) while moving through a distance equal to its own length. What is the radius of the circle in which it is moving? Ans. 764 ft.

25. At what rate is a bicycle rider on a circular track of half a mile diameter changing his direction? Ans. 4 rad. per mile \(= 43'\) per rod.

26. The origin being directly above the starting point, an aëroplane follows approximately the spiral \(\rho = \theta\), the unit of length being one mile. How rapidly is the aëroplane turning at the instant it has circled the starting point once?

27. A railway track has curves of approximately the form of arcs from the following curves. At what rate will an engine change its direction when passing through the points indicated (1 mi. \(=\) unit of length): (a) \(y = x^3\), \((2, 8)\)? (b) \(y = x^2\), \((3, 9)\)? (c) \(x^2 - y^2 = 8\), \((3, 1)\)? (d) \(y = e^x\), \(x = 0\)? (e) \(y = \cos x\), \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\)? (f) \(\rho\theta = 4\), \(\theta = 1\)?

\chapter*{CHAPTER XIII: THEOREM OF MEAN VALUE. INDETERMINATE FORMS}

\textbf{105. Rolle's Theorem.} Let $y=f(x)$ be a continuous single-valued function of $x$, vanishing for $x=a$ and $x=b$, and suppose that $f'(x)$ changes continuously when $x$ varies from $a$ to $b$. The function will then be represented graphically by a continuous curve as in the figure. Geometric intuition shows us at once that for \textit{at least one value of $x$ between $a$ and $b$} the tangent is parallel to the axis of $X$ (as at $P$); that is, the slope is .zero. This illustrates \textbf{Rolle's Theorem}:

\textit{If $f(x)$ vanishes when $x=a$ and $x=b$, and $f(x)$ and $f'(x)$ are continuous for all values of $x$ from $x=a$ to $x=b$, then $f'(x)$ will be zero for at least one value of $x$ between $a$ and $b$.}

This theorem is obviously true, because as $x$ increases from $a$ to $b$, $f(x)$ cannot always increase or always decrease as $x$ increases, since $f(a)=0$ and $f(b)=0$. Hence for at least one value of $x$ between $a$ and $b$, $f(x)$ must cease to increase and begin to decrease, or else cease to decrease and begin to increase; and for that particular value of $x$ the first derivative must be zero (\S\ 81, p. 108).

That Rolle's Theorem does not apply when $f(x)$ or $f'(x)$ are discontinuous is illustrated as follows:

Fig. $a$ shows the graph of a function which is discontinuous ($=\infty$) for $x=c$, a value lying between $a$ and $b$. Fig. $b$ shows a continuous function whose first derivative is discontinuous ($=\infty$) for such an intermediate value $x=c$. In either case it is seen that at no point on the graph between $x=a$ and $x=b$ does the tangent (or curve) become parallel to $OX$.

\textbf{106. The Theorem of Mean Value.}$^{*}$ Consider the quantity $Q$ defined by the equation

\[
(A)\qquad \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}=Q,\ \text{or}
\]

\[
(B)\qquad f(b)-f(a)-(b-a)\,Q=0.
\]

Let $F(x)$ be a function formed by replacing $b$ by $x$ in the left-hand member of $(B)$; that is,

\[
(C)\qquad F(x)=f(x)-f(a)-(x-a)\,Q.
\]

From $(B)$, \quad $F(b)=0$, and from $(C)$, $F(a)=0$;

therefore, by Rolle's Theorem (p. 164) $F'(x)$ must be zero for at least one value of $x$ \textit{between $a$ and $b$}, say for $x_1$. But by differentiating $(C)$ we get

\[
F'(x)=f'(x)-Q.
\]

Therefore, since \quad $F'(x_1)=0$, then also $f'(x)-Q=0$,

and

\[
Q=f'(x_1).
\]

Substituting this value of $Q$ in $(A)$, we get the \textbf{Theorem of Mean Value,}

\[
\textbf{(44)}\qquad \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}=f'(x_1),\qquad a<x_1<b
\]

where in general all we know about $x_1$ is that it lies \textit{between $a$ and $b$}.

\textbf{The Theorem of Mean Value interpreted Geometrically.} Let the curve in the figure be the locus of

\[
y=f(x).
\]


Take $OC=a$ and $OD=b$; then $f(a)=CA$ and $f(b)=DB$, giving $AE=b-a$ and $EB=f(b)-f(a)$.

Therefore the slope of the chord $AB$ is

\[
(D)\qquad \tan EAB=\frac{EB}{AE}=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
\]

There is at least one point on the curve between $A$ and $B$ (as $P$) where the tangent (or curve) is parallel to the chord $AB$. If the abscissa of $P$ is $x_1$, the slope at $P$ is

\[
(E)\qquad \tan t=f'(x_1)=\tan EAB.
\]

$^{*}$ Also called the \textit{Law of the Mean.}


Equating $(D)$ and $(E)$, we get
\[
\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}=f'(x_1),
\]
which is the Theorem of Mean Value.

The student should draw curves (as the one on p. 164) to show that there may be more than one such point in the interval; and curves to illustrate, on the other hand, that the theorem may not be true if $f(x)$ becomes discontinuous for any value of $x$ between $a$ and $b$ (Fig. $a$, p. 164), or if $f'(x)$ becomes discontinuous (Fig. $b$, p. 164).

Clearing (\textbf{44}) of fractions, we may also write the theorem in the form
\[
(\textbf{45})\qquad f(b)=f(a)+(b-a)f'(x_1).
\]

Let $b=a+\Delta a$; then $b-a=\Delta a$, and since $x_1$ is a number lying between $a$ and $b$, we may write
\[
x_1=a+\theta\cdot\Delta a,
\]
where $\theta$ is a positive proper fraction. Substituting in (\textbf{45}), we get \textit{another form of the} \textbf{Theorem of Mean Value.}
\[
(\textbf{46})\qquad f(a+\Delta a)-f(a)=\Delta a f'(a+\theta\cdot\Delta a). \qquad 0<\theta<1
\]

\textbf{107. The Extended Theorem of Mean Value.}$^{*}$ Following the method of the last section, let $R$ be defined by the equation
\[
(A)\qquad f(b)-f(a)-(b-a)f'(a)-\tfrac{1}{2}(b-a)^2R=0.
\]

Let $F(x)$ be a function formed by replacing $b$ by $x$ in the left-hand member of $(A)$; that is,
\[
(B)\qquad F(x)=f(x)-f(a)-(x-a)f'(a)-\tfrac{1}{2}(x-a)^2R.
\]

From $(A)$, \quad $F(b)=0$; and from $(B)$, $F(a)=0$; therefore, by Rolle's Theorem (p. 164), at least one value of $x$ between $a$ and $b$, say $x_1$, will cause $F'(x)$ to vanish. Hence, since
\[
F'(x)=f'(x)-f'(a)-(x-a)R, \text{ we get}
\]
\[
F'(x_1)=f'(x_1)-f'(a)-(x_1-a)R=0.
\]

Since $F'(x_1)=0$ and $F'(a)=0$, it is evident that $F'(x)$ also satisfies the conditions of Rolle's Theorem, so that \textit{its derivative}, namely $F''(x)$, must vanish for at least one value of $x$ between $a$ and $x_1$, say $x_2$, and therefore $x_2$ also lies between $a$ and $b$. But
\[
F''(x)=f''(x)-R; \text{ therefore } F''(x_2)=f''(x_2)-R=0,
\]
and
\[
R=f''(x_2).
\]

$^{*}$ Also called the \textit{Extended Law of the Mean.}

Substituting this result in $(A)$, we get
\[
(C)\quad f(b)=f(a)+(b-a)f'(a)+\frac{1}{\underline{|2}}(b-a)^{2}f''(x_{2}).\qquad a<x_{2}<b
\]
In the same manner, if we define $S$ by means of the equation
\[
f(b)-f(a)-(b-a)f'(a)-\frac{1}{\underline{|2}}(b-a)^{2}f''(a)-\frac{1}{\underline{|3}}(b-a)^{3}S=0,
\]
we can derive the equation
\[
(D)\quad f(b)=f(a)+(b-a)f'(a)+\frac{1}{\underline{|2}}(b-a)^{2}f''(a)
\]
\[
\qquad+\frac{1}{\underline{|3}}(b-a)^{3}f'''(x_{3}),\qquad\qquad a<x_{3}<b
\]
where $x_{3}$ lies between $a$ and $b$.

By continuing this process we get the general result,
\[
(E)\quad f(b)=f(a)+\frac{(b-a)}{\underline{|1}}f'(a)+\frac{(b-a)^{2}}{\underline{|2}}f''(a)
\]
\[
\qquad+\frac{(b-a)^{3}}{\underline{|3}}f'''(a)+\cdots+\frac{(b-a)^{n-1}}{\underline{|n-1}}f^{(n-1)}(a)
\]
\[
\qquad+\frac{(b-a)^{n}}{\underline{|n}}f^{(n)}(x_{1}),\qquad\qquad a<x_{1}<b
\]
where $x_{1}$ lies between $a$ and $b$. $(E)$ is called the \textit{Extended Theorem of Mean Value.}

\textbf{108. Maxima and minima treated analytically.} By making use of the results of the last two sections we can now give a general discussion of \textit{maxima and minima of functions of a single independent variable.}

Given the function $f(x)$. Let $h$ be a positive number as small as we please; then the definitions given in \S\ 82, p. 109, may be stated as follows:

If, for all values of $x$ different from $a$ in the interval $[a-h,\ a+h]$,
\[
(A)\qquad f(x)-f(a)=\textit{a negative number,}
\]
then $f(x)$ is said to be a \textit{maximum when $x=a$.}

If, on the other hand,
\[
(B)\qquad f(x)-f(a)=\textit{a positive number,}
\]
then $f(x)$ is said to be a \textit{minimum when $x=a$.}

Consider the following cases:

I. \textit{Let $f'(a)\neq 0$.}

From (\textbf{45}), p. 166, replacing $b$ by $x$ and transposing $f(a)$,
\[
(C)\qquad f(x)-f(a)=(x-a)f'(x_{1}).\qquad\qquad a<x_{1}<\mathbf{x}
\]

Since $f'(a) \neq 0$, and $f'(x)$ is assumed as continuous, $h$ may be chosen so small that $f'(x)$ will have the same sign as $f'(a)$ for all values of $x$ in the interval $[a-h,\, a+h]$. Therefore $f'(x_1)$ has the same sign as $f'(a)$ (Chap. III). But $x-a$ changes sign according as $x$ is less or greater than $a$. Therefore, from $(C)$, the difference
\[ f(x)-f(a) \]
will also change sign, and, by $(A)$ and $(B)$, $f(a)$ will be neither a maximum nor a minimum. This result agrees with the discussion in \S\ 82, where it was shown that \textit{for all values of $x$ for which $f(x)$ is a maximum or a minimum, the first derivative $f'(x)$ must vanish.}

II. \textit{Let $f'(a)=0$, and $f''(a) \neq 0$.}

From $(C)$, p. 167, replacing $b$ by $x$ and transposing $f(a)$,
\[ (D) \qquad f(x)-f(a)=\frac{(x-a)^2}{\underline{|2}}\,f''(x_2). \qquad a<x_2<x \]

Since $f''(a) \neq 0$, and $f''(x)$ is assumed as continuous, we may choose our interval $[a-h,\, a+h]$ so small that $f''(x_2)$ will have the same sign as $f''(a)$ (Chap. III). Also $(x-a)^2$ does not change sign. Therefore the second member of $(D)$ will not change sign, and the difference
\[ f(x)-f(a) \]
will have the same sign for all values of $x$ in the interval $[a-h,\, a+h]$, and, moreover, \textit{this sign will be the same as the sign of $f''(a)$.} It therefore follows from our definitions $(A)$ and $(B)$ that

\textit{$(E)$ $f(a)$ is a maximum if $f'(a)=0$ and $f''(a)=$ a negative number;}

\textit{$(F)$ $f(a)$ is a minimum if $f'(a)=0$ and $f''(a)=$ a positive number.}

These conditions are the same as (\textbf{21}) and (\textbf{22}), p. 113.

III. \textit{Let $f'(a)=f''(a)=0$, and $f'''(a) \neq 0$.}

From $(D)$, p. 167, replacing $b$ by $x$ and transposing $f(a)$,
\[ (G) \qquad f(x)-f(a)=\frac{1}{\underline{|3}}(x-a)^3 f'''(x_3). \qquad a<x_3<x \]

As before, $f'''(x_3)$ will have the same sign as $f'''(a)$. But $(x-a)^3$ changes its sign from $-$ to $+$ as $x$ increases through $a$. Therefore the difference
\[ f(x)-f(a) \]
must change sign, and $f(a)$ is neither a maximum nor a minimum.


IV. \textit{Let $f'(a)=f''(a)=\cdots=f^{(n-1)}(a)=0$, and $f^{(n)}(a)\neq 0$.}

By continuing the process as illustrated in I, II, and III, it is seen that if the first derivative of $f(x)$ which does not vanish for $x=a$ is of \textbf{even order} $(=n)$, then

\textbf{(47)} \quad \textbf{$f(a)$ is a maximum if $f^{(n)}(a)=$ a negative number;}

\textbf{(48)} \quad \textbf{$f(a)$ is a minimum if $f^{(n)}(a)=$ a positive number.}$^{*}$

If the first derivative of $f(x)$ which does not vanish for $x=a$ is of \textbf{odd order, then $f(a)$ will be neither a maximum nor a minimum.}

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Examine $x^3-9x^2+24x-7$ for maximum and minimum values.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[ f(x)=x^3-9x^2+24x-7. \]
\[ f'(x)=3x^2-18x+24. \]
Solving
\[ 3x^2-18x+24=0 \]
gives the critical values $x=2$ and $x=4$. \quad $\therefore f'(2)=0$, and $f'(4)=0$.

Differentiating again, \quad $f''(x)=6x-18.$

Since $f''(2)=-6$, we know from (47) that $f(2)=13$ is a maximum.

Since $f''(4)=+6$, we know from (48) that $f(4)=9$ is a minimum.

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 2. Examine $e^x+2\cos x+e^{-x}$ for maximum and minimum values.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[ f(x)=e^x+2\cos x+e^{-x}, \]
\[ f'(x)=e^x-2\sin x-e^{-x}=0,\ \text{for } x=0,\dagger \]
\[ f''(x)=e^x-2\cos x+e^{-x}=0,\ \text{for } x=0, \]
\[ f'''(x)=e^x+2\sin x-e^{-x}=0,\ \text{for } x=0, \]
\[ f^{\mathrm{iv}}(x)=e^x+2\cos x+e^{-x}=4,\ \text{for } x=0. \]
Hence, from (48), $f(0)=4$ is a minimum.

\textsc{Examples}

Examine the following functions for maximum and minimum values, using the method of the last section:

1. $3x^4-4x^3+1$. \hfill \textit{Ans.} $x=1$ gives min. $=0$; $x=0$ gives neither.

2. $x^3-6x^2+12x+48$. \hfill $x=2$ gives neither.

3. $(x-1)^2(x+1)^3$. \hfill $x=1$ gives min. $=0$; $x=\frac{1}{5}$ gives max.; $x=-1$ gives neither.

4. Investigate $x^5-5x^4+5x^3-1$, at $x=1$ and $x=3$.

5. Investigate $x^3-3x^2+3x+7$, at $x=1$.

6. Show that if the first derivative of $f(x)$ which does not vanish for $x=a$ is of odd order $(=n)$, then $f(x)$ is an increasing or decreasing function when $x=a$, according as $f^{(n)}(a)$ is positive or negative.

$^{*}$ As in \S 82, a critical value $x=a$ is found by placing the first derivative equal to zero and solving the resulting equation for real roots.

$\dagger$ $x=0$ is the only root of the equation $e^x-2\sin x-e^{-x}=0$.

\textbf{109. Indeterminate forms.} When, for a particular value of the independent variable, a function takes on one of the forms
\[
\frac{0}{0},\quad \frac{\infty}{\infty},\quad 0\cdot\infty,\quad \infty-\infty,\quad 0^{0},\quad \infty^{0},\quad 1^{\infty},
\]
it is said to be \textit{indeterminate}, and the function is \textit{not} defined for that value of the independent variable by the given analytical expression. For example, suppose we have
\[
y=\frac{f(x)}{F(x)},
\]
where for some value of the variable, as $x=a$,
\[
f(a)=0,\qquad F(a)=0.
\]
For this value of $x$ our function is \textit{not} defined and we may therefore assign to it any value we please. It is evident from what has gone before (Case II, p. 15) that it is desirable to assign to the function a value that will make it continuous when $x=a$ whenever it is possible to do so.

\textbf{110. Evaluation of a function taking on an indeterminate form.} If when $x=a$ the function $f(x)$ assumes an indeterminate form, then
\[
\mathop{\text{limit}}_{x=a} f(x)^{*}
\]
\textit{is taken as the value of $f(x)$ for $x=a$.}

The assumption of this limiting value makes $f(x)$ continuous for $x=a$. This agrees with the theorem under Case II, p. 15, and also with our practice in Chapter III, where several functions assuming the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ were evaluated. Thus, for $x=2$ the function $\frac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}$ assumes the form $\frac{0}{0}$, but
\[
\mathop{\text{limit}}_{x=2} \frac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}=4.
\]
Hence 4 is taken as the value of the function for $x=2$. Let us now illustrate graphically the fact that if we assume 4 as the value of the function for $x=2$, then the function is continuous for $x=2$.

Let
\[
y=\frac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}.
\]
This equation may also be written in the form
\[
y(x-2)=(x-2)(x+2);
\]
or,
\[
(x-2)(y-x-2)=0.
\]

$^{*}$ The calculation of this limiting value is called \textit{evaluating the indeterminate form.}


Placing each factor separately equal to zero, we have
\[ x = 2, \text{ and } y = x + 2. \]

In plotting, the loci of these equations are found to be the two lines $AB$ and $CD$ respectively. Since there are infinitely many points on the line $AB$ having the abscissa 2, it is clear that when $x = 2$ $(= OM)$, the value of $y$ (or the function) may be taken as any number whatever; but when $x$ is different from 2, it is seen from the graph of the function that the corresponding value of $y$ (or the function) is always found from
\[ y = x + 2, \]
the equation of the line $CD$. Also, on $CD$, when $x = 2$, we get
\[ y = MP = 4, \]
which we saw was also the limiting value of $y$ (or the function) for $x = 2$; and it is evident from geometrical considerations that if we assume 4 as the value of the function for $x = 2$, then the function is continuous for $x = 2$.


Similarly, several of the examples given in Chapter III illustrate how the limiting values of many functions assuming indeterminate forms may be found by employing suitable algebraic or trigonometric transformations, and how in general these limiting values make the corresponding functions continuous at the points in question. The most general methods, however, for evaluating indeterminate forms depend on differentiation.

\textbf{111. Evaluation of the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$.} Given a function of the form $\dfrac{f(x)}{F(x)}$ such that $f(a) = 0$ and $F(a) = 0$; that is, the function takes on the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}$ when $a$ is substituted for $x$. It is then required to find
\[ \mathop{\text{limit}}_{x=a} \frac{f(x)}{F(x)}. \]


Draw the graphs of the functions $f(x)$ and $F(x)$. Since, by hypothesis, $f(a) = 0$ and $F(a) = 0$, these graphs intersect at $(a, 0)$.

Applying the Theorem of Mean Value to each of these functions (replacing $b$ by $x$), we get
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
f(x)=f(a)+(x-a)f'(x_1), & \qquad a<x_1<x \\
F(x)=F(a)+(x-a)\,F'(x_2). & \qquad a<x_2<x
\end{array}
\]
Since $f(a)=0$ and $F(a)=0$, we get, after canceling out $(x-a)$,
\[
\frac{f(x)}{F(x)}=\frac{f'(x_1)}{F'(x_2)}.
\]
Now let $x \doteq a$; then $x_1 \doteq a$, $x_2 \doteq a$, and
\[
\mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{x=a} f'(x_1)=f'(a), \qquad \mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{x=a} F'(x_2)=F'(a).
\]
\textbf{(49)}
\[
\mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{x=a}\frac{f(x)}{F(x)}=\frac{f'(a)}{F'(a)}. \qquad\qquad F'(a)\neq 0
\]
\textbf{Rule for evaluating the indeterminate form} $\frac{0}{0}$. \textit{Differentiate the numerator for a new numerator and the denominator for a new denominator.}$^{*}$ \textit{The value of this new fraction for the assigned value}$^{\dagger}$ \textit{of the variable will be the limiting value of the original fraction.}

In case it so happens that
\[
f'(a)=0 \text{ and } F'(a)=0,
\]
that is, the first derivatives also vanish for $x=a$, then we still have the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$, and the theorem can be applied anew to the ratio
\[
\frac{f'(x)}{F'(x)},
\]
giving us
\[
\mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{x=a}\frac{f(x)}{F(x)}=\frac{f''(a)}{F''(a)}.
\]
When also $f''(a)=0$ and $F''(a)=0$, we get in the same manner
\[
\mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{x=a}\frac{f(x)}{F(x)}=\frac{f'''(a)}{F'''(a)},
\]
and so on.

It may be necessary to repeat this process several times.

$^{*}$ The student is warned against the very careless but common mistake of differentiating the whole expression as a fraction by VII.

$^{\dagger}$ If $a=\infty$, the substitution $x=\frac{1}{z}$ reduces the problem to the evaluation of the limit for $z=0$.

Thus
\[
\mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{x=\infty}\frac{f(x)}{F(x)}
=\mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{z=0}\frac{-f'\!\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)\frac{1}{z^2}}{-F'\!\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)\frac{1}{z^2}}
=\mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{z=0}\frac{f'\!\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)}{F'\!\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)}
=\mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{x=\infty}\frac{f'(x)}{F'(x)}.
\]

Therefore the rule holds in this case also.


\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Evaluate $\frac{f(x)}{F(x)} = \frac{x^3 - 3x + 2}{x^3 - x^2 - x + 1}$ when $x = 1$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[ \frac{f(1)}{F(1)} = \left.\frac{x^3 - 3x + 2}{x^3 - x^2 - x + 1}\right]_{x=1} = \frac{1 - 3 + 2}{1 - 1 - 1 + 1} = \frac{0}{0}. \quad \therefore \text{ indeterminate.} \]
\[ \frac{f'(1)}{F'(1)} = \left.\frac{3x^2 - 3}{3x^2 - 2x - 1}\right]_{x=1} = \frac{3 - 3}{3 - 2 - 1} = \frac{0}{0}. \quad \therefore \text{ indeterminate.} \]
\[ \frac{f''(1)}{F''(1)} = \left.\frac{6x}{6x - 2}\right]_{x=1} = \frac{6}{6 - 2} = \frac{3}{2}. \quad \textit{Ans.} \]

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 2. Evaluate $\underset{x=0}{\text{limit}}\ \frac{e^x - e^{-x} - 2x}{x - \sin x}$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[ \frac{f(0)}{F(0)} = \left.\frac{e^x - e^{-x} - 2x}{x - \sin x}\right]_{x=0} = \frac{1 - 1 - 0}{0 - 0} = \frac{0}{0}. \quad \therefore \text{ indeterminate.} \]
\[ \frac{f'(0)}{F'(0)} = \left.\frac{e^x + e^{-x} - 2}{1 - \cos x}\right]_{x=0} = \frac{1 + 1 - 2}{1 - 1} = \frac{0}{0}. \quad \therefore \text{ indeterminate.} \]
\[ \frac{f''(0)}{F''(0)} = \left.\frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{\sin x}\right]_{x=0} = \frac{1 - 1}{0} = \frac{0}{0}. \quad \therefore \text{ indeterminate.} \]
\[ \frac{f'''(0)}{F'''(0)} = \left.\frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{\cos x}\right]_{x=0} = \frac{1 + 1}{1} = 2. \quad \textit{Ans.} \]

\textbf{EXAMPLES}

1. $\underset{x=4}{\text{limit}}\ \frac{x^2 - 16}{x^2 + x - 20}$. \textit{Ans.} $\frac{8}{9}$.
