\chapter*{CHAPTER XV: PARTIAL DIFFERENTIATION}

\textbf{122. Continuous functions of two or more independent variables.} A function $f(x,\,y)$ of two independent variables $x$ and $y$ is defined as continuous for the values $(a,\,b)$ of $(x,\,y)$ when
\[
\mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{\substack{x=a\\ y=b}} f(x,\,y)=f(a,\,b),
\]
no matter in what way $x$ and $y$ approach their respective limits $a$ and $b$. This definition is sometimes roughly summed up in the statement that \textit{a very small change in one or both of the independent variables shall produce a very small change in the value of the function.}$^{*}$

We may illustrate this geometrically by considering the surface represented by the equation
\[
z=f(x,\,y).
\]

Consider a fixed point $P$ on the surface where $x=a$ and $y=b$.

Denote by $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ the increments of the independent variables $x$ and $y$, and by $\Delta z$ the corresponding increment of the dependent variable $z$, the coördinates of $P'$ being

\[
(x+\Delta x,\ y+\Delta y,\ z+\Delta z).
\]

At $P$ the value of the function is
\[
z=f(a,\,b)=MP.
\]

If the function is continuous at $P$, then however $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ may approach the limit zero, $\Delta z$ will also approach the limit zero. That is, $M'P'$ will approach coincidence with $MP$, the point $P'$ approaching the point $P$ on the surface from any direction whatever.

A similar definition holds for a continuous function of more than two independent variables.

In what follows, only values of the independent variables are considered for which a function is continuous.

$^{*}$ This will be better understood if the student again reads over \S\ 18, p. 14, on continuous functions of a single variable.

\textbf{123. Partial derivatives.} Since $x$ and $y$ are independent in
\[ z = f(x,\, y), \]
$x$ may be supposed to vary while $y$ remains constant, or the reverse.

The derivative of $z$ with respect to $x$ when $x$ varies and $y$ remains constant\,$^{*}$ is called the \textit{partial derivative of $z$ with respect to $x$}, and is denoted by the symbol $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$. We may then write
\[ (A)\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{\Delta x = 0}\left[\frac{f(x + \Delta x,\, y) - f(x,\, y)}{\Delta x}\right]. \]

Similarly, when $x$ remains constant\,$^{*}$ and $y$ varies, \textit{the partial derivative of $z$ with respect to $y$} is
\[ (B)\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{\Delta y = 0}\left[\frac{f(x,\, y + \Delta y) - f(x,\, y)}{\Delta y}\right]. \]

$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ is also written $\frac{\partial}{\partial x} f(x,\, y)$, or $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$.

Similarly, $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ is also written $\frac{\partial}{\partial y} f(x,\, y)$, or $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$.

In order to avoid confusion the round $\partial^{\dagger}$ has been generally adopted to indicate partial differentiation. Other notations, however, which are in use are
\[ \left(\frac{dz}{dx}\right),\ \left(\frac{dz}{dy}\right);\ f'_x(x,\, y),\ f'_y(x,\, y);\ f_x(x,\, y),\ f_y(x,\, y);\ D_x f,\ D_y f;\ z_x,\ z_y. \]

Our notation may be extended to a function of any number of independent variables. Thus, if
\[ u = F(x,\, y,\, z), \]
then we have the three partial derivatives
\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y},\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial z};\ \text{or,}\ \frac{\partial F}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial F}{\partial y},\ \frac{\partial F}{\partial z}. \]

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Find the partial derivatives of $z = ax^2 + 2\,bxy + cy^2$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[ \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 2\,ax + 2\,by, \text{ treating } y \text{ as a constant,} \]
\[ \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = 2\,bx + 2\,cy, \text{ treating } x \text{ as a constant.} \]

$^{*}$ The constant values are substituted in the function before differentiating.

$\dagger$ Introduced by Jacobi (1804--1851).

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 2. Find the partial derivatives of $u = \sin (ax + by + cz)$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = a \cos (ax + by + cz), \text{ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants,} \]
\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = b \cos (ax + by + cz), \text{ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants,} \]
\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial z} = c \cos (ax + by + cz), \text{ treating $y$ and $x$ as constants.} \]

Again turning to the function
\[ z = f(x, y), \]
we have, by $(A)$, p. 191, defined $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ as the limit of the ratio of the increment of the function ($y$ being constant) to the increment of $x$, as the increment of $x$ approaches the limit zero. Similarly, $(B)$, p. 191, has defined $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}$. It is evident, however, that if we look upon these partial derivatives from the point of view of \S\ 94, p. 141, then
\[ \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \]
may be considered as the ratio of the time rates of change of $z$ and $x$ when $y$ is constant, and
\[ \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \]
as the ratio of the time rates of change of $z$ and $y$ when $x$ is constant.

\textbf{124. Partial derivatives interpreted geometrically.} Let the equation of the surface shown in the figure be
\[ z = f(x, y). \]


Pass a plane $EFGH$ through the point $P$ (where $x = a$ and $y = b$) on the surface parallel to the $XOZ$-plane. Since the equation of this plane is
\[ y = b, \]
the equation of the section $JPK$ cut out of the surface is
\[ z = f(x, b), \]
if we consider $EF$ as the axis of $Z$ and $EH$ as the axis of $X$. In this plane $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ means the same as $\frac{dz}{dx}$, and we have
\[ \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \mathit{tan}\ MTP \]
\[ = \mathit{slope\ of\ section\ JK\ at\ P.} \]

Similarly, if we pass the plane $BCD$ through $P$ parallel to the $YOZ$-plane, its equation is $x=a,$
and for the section $DPI$, $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ means the same as $\dfrac{dz}{dy}$. Hence
\[ \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \frac{dz}{dy} = -\tan MT'P = \text{slope of section } DI \text{ at } P. \]

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Given the ellipsoid $\dfrac{x^2}{24}+\dfrac{y^2}{12}+\dfrac{z^2}{6}=1$; find the slope of the section of the ellipsoid made (a) by the plane $y=1$ at the point where $x=4$ and $z$ is positive; (b) by the plane $x=2$ at the point where $y=3$ and $z$ is positive.

\textbf{Solution.} Considering $y$ as constant,
\[ \frac{2x}{24}+\frac{2z}{6}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=0, \text{ or } \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{x}{4z}. \]
When $x$ is constant,
\[ \frac{2y}{12}+\frac{2z}{6}\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=0, \text{ or } \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{y}{2z}. \]

(a) When $y=1$ and $x=4$, $z=\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$. $\therefore \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}$. \textit{Ans.}

(b) When $x=2$ and $y=3$, $z=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. $\therefore \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\dfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{2}$. \textit{Ans.}

\textbf{EXAMPLES} 

1. $u=x^3+3x^2y-y^3$. \textit{Ans.} $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=3x^2+6xy$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=3x^2-3y^2$.

2. $u=Ax^2+Bxy+Cy^2+Dx+Ey+F$. $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=2Ax+By+D$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=Bx+2Cy+E$.

3. $u=(ax^2+by^2+cz^2)^n$. $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\dfrac{2anxu}{ax^2+by^2+cz^2}$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=\dfrac{2bnyu}{ax^2+by^2+cz^2}$.

4. $u=\text{arc sin}\,\dfrac{x}{y}$. $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y^2-x^2}}$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=-\dfrac{x}{y\sqrt{y^2-x^2}}$.

5. $u=x^y$. $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=yx^{y-1}$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=x^y\log x$.

6. $u=ax^3y^2z+bxy^3z^4+cy^6+dxz^3$. $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=3ax^2y^2z+by^3z^4+dz^3$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=2ax^3yz+3bxy^2z^4+6cy^5$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z}=ax^3y^2+4bxy^3z^3+3dxz^2$.


7. $u = x^3y^2 - 2\,xy^4 + 3\,x^2y^3$; show that $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 5\,u$.

8. $u = \dfrac{xy}{x+y}$; show that $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = u$.

9. $u = (y-z)\,(z-x)\,(x-y)$; show that $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} = 0$.

10. $u = \log\,(e^x + e^y)$; show that $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 1$.

11. $u = \dfrac{e^{xy}}{e^x + e^y}$; show that $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = (x+y-1)\,u$.

12. $u = x^y y^x$; show that $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = (x + y + \log u)\,u$.

13. $u = \log\,(x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3\,xyz)$; show that $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} = \dfrac{3}{x+y+z}$.

14. $u = e^x \sin y + e^y \sin x$; show that
\[
\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)^2 = e^{2x} + e^{2y} + 2\,e^{x+y}\sin\,(x+y).
\]

15. $u = \log\,(\tan x + \tan y + \tan z)$; show that
\[
\sin 2\,x\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \sin 2\,y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} + \sin 2\,z\frac{\partial u}{\partial z} = 2.
\]

16. Let $y$ be the altitude of a right circular cone and $x$ the radius of its base. Show (a) that if the base remains constant, the volume changes $\frac{1}{3}\pi x^2$ times as fast as the altitude; (b) that if the altitude remains constant, the volume changes $\frac{2}{3}\pi xy$ times as fast as the radius of the base.

17. A point moves on the elliptic paraboloid $z = \dfrac{x^2}{9} + \dfrac{y^2}{4}$ and also in a plane parallel to the $XOZ$-plane. When $x = 3$ ft. and is increasing at the rate of 9 ft. per second, find (a) the time rate of change of $z$; (b) the magnitude of the velocity of the point; (c) the direction of its motion.
\textit{Ans.} (a) $v_z = 6$ ft. per sec.; (b) $v = 3\sqrt{13}$ ft. per sec.; (c) $\tau = \arctan \frac{2}{3}$, the angle made with the $XOY$-plane.

18. If, on the surface of Ex. 17, the point moves in a plane parallel to the plane $YOZ$, find, when $y = 2$ and increases at the rate of 5 ft. per sec., (a) the time rate of change of $z$; (b) the magnitude of the velocity of the point; (c) the direction of its motion.
\textit{Ans.} (a) 5 ft. per sec.; (b) $5\sqrt{2}$ ft. per sec.; (c) $\tau = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, the angle made with the plane $XOY$.

\textbf{125. Total derivatives.} We have already considered the differentiation of a function of one function of a single independent variable. Thus, if
\[
y = f(v) \text{ and } v = \phi(x),
\]
it was shown that
\[
\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{dv}\cdot\frac{dv}{dx}.
\]

We shall next consider a function of two variables, both of which depend on a single independent variable. Consider the function
\[ u = f(x,\, y), \]
where $x$ and $y$ are functions of a third variable $t$.

Let $t$ take on the increment $\Delta t$, and let $\Delta x$, $\Delta y$, $\Delta u$ be the corresponding increments of $x$, $y$, $u$ respectively. Then the quantity
\[ \Delta u = f(x + \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y) - f(x,\, y) \]
is called the \textit{total increment} of $u$.

Adding and subtracting $f(x,\, y + \Delta y)$ in the second member,
\[ (A)\ \ \Delta u = [f(x + \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y) - f(x,\, y + \Delta y)] + [f(x,\, y + \Delta y) - f(x,\, y)]. \]

Applying the Theorem of Mean Value (\textbf{46}), p. 166, to each of the two differences on the right-hand side of $(A)$, we get, for the first difference,
\[ (B)\ \ f(x + \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y) - f(x,\, y + \Delta y) = f_x'(x + \theta_1 \cdot \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y)\,\Delta x. \]
[$a = x$, $\Delta a = \Delta x$, and since $x$ varies while $y + \Delta y$ remains constant, we get the partial derivative with respect to $x$.]

For the second difference we get
\[ (C)\ \ f(x,\, y + \Delta y) - f(x,\, y) = f_y'(x,\, y + \theta_2 \cdot \Delta y)\,\Delta y. \]
[$a = y$, $\Delta a = \Delta y$, and since $y$ varies while $x$ remains constant, we get the partial derivative with respect to $y$.]

Substituting $(B)$ and $(C)$ in $(A)$ gives
\[ (D)\ \ \Delta u = f_x'(x + \theta_1 \cdot \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y)\,\Delta x + f_y'(x,\, y + \theta_2 \cdot \Delta y)\,\Delta y, \]
where $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are positive proper fractions. Dividing $(D)$ by $\Delta t$,
\[ (E)\ \ \frac{\Delta u}{\Delta t} = f_x'(x + \theta_1 \cdot \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y)\,\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} + f_y'(x,\, y + \theta_2 \cdot \Delta y)\,\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta t}. \]

Now let $\Delta t$ approach zero as a limit, then
\[ (F)\ \ \frac{du}{dt} = f_x'(x,\, y)\,\frac{dx}{dt} + f_y'(x,\, y)\,\frac{dy}{dt}. \]
[Since $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ converge to zero with $\Delta t$, we get
$\underset{\Delta t = 0}{\text{limit}}\, f_x'(x + \theta_1 \cdot \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y) = f_x'(x,\, y)$, and $\underset{\Delta t = 0}{\text{limit}}\, f_y'(x,\, y + \theta_2 \cdot \Delta y) = f_y'(x,\, y)$,
$f_x'(x,\, y)$ and $f_y'(x,\, y)$ being assumed continuous.]

Replacing $f(x,\, y)$ by $u$ in $(F)$, we get the \textit{total derivative}
\[ (\textbf{51})\ \ \frac{du}{dt} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\,\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\,\frac{dy}{dt}. \]

In the same way, if
\[ u = f(x, y, z), \]
and $x$, $y$, $z$ are all functions of $t$, we get
\[ (52)\qquad \frac{du}{dt} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\frac{dz}{dt}, \]
and so on for any number of variables.$^{*}$

In (51) we may suppose $t = x$; then $y$ is a function of $x$, and $u$ is really a function of the one variable $x$, giving
\[ (53)\qquad \frac{du}{dx} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dx}. \]
In the same way, from (52) we have
\[ (54)\qquad \frac{du}{dx} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\cdot\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\cdot\frac{dz}{dx}. \]
The student should observe that $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{du}{dx}$ have quite different meanings. The partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$ is formed on the supposition that the \textit{particular variable $x$ alone varies}, while
\[ \frac{du}{dx} = \mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{\Delta x = 0}\left(\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x}\right), \]
where $\Delta u$ is the \textit{total increment of $u$ caused by changes in all the variables}, these increments being due to the change $\Delta x$ in the independent variable. In contradistinction to partial derivatives, $\dfrac{du}{dt}$, $\dfrac{du}{dx}$ are called \textit{total derivatives} with respect to $t$ and $x$ respectively.$^\dagger$

$^{*}$ This is really only a special case of a general theorem which may be stated as follows:
If $u$ is a function of the independent variables $x$, $y$, $z$, $\cdots$, each of these in turn being a function of the independent variables $r$, $s$, $t$, $\cdots$, then (with certain assumptions as to continuity)
\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial r} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial r} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial r} + \cdots, \]
and similar expressions hold for $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial s}$, $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t}$, etc.

$^\dagger$ It should be observed that $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$ has a perfectly definite value for any point $(x, y)$, while $\dfrac{du}{dx}$ depends not only on the point $(x, y)$, but also on the particular direction chosen to reach that point. Hence

$\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$ is called a point function; while

$\dfrac{du}{dx}$ is not called a point function unless it is agreed to approach the point from some particular direction.


\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Given $u = \sin\frac{x}{y}$, $x = e^{t}$, $y = t^{2}$; find $\frac{du}{dt}$.

\textbf{Solution.} $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{y}\cos\frac{x}{y}$, $\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\frac{x}{y^{2}}\cos\frac{x}{y}$; $\frac{dx}{dt} = e^{t}$, $\frac{dy}{dt} = 2t$.

Substituting in (51), \quad $\frac{du}{dt} = (t-2)\frac{e^{t}}{t^{3}}\cos\frac{e^{t}}{t^{2}}$. \textit{Ans.}

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 2. Given $u = e^{ax}(y-z)$, $y = a\sin x$, $z = \cos x$; find $\frac{du}{dx}$.

\textbf{Solution.} $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = ae^{ax}(y-z)$, $\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = e^{ax}$, $\frac{\partial u}{\partial z} = -e^{ax}$; $\frac{dy}{dx} = a\cos x$, $\frac{dz}{dx} = -\sin x$.

Substituting in (54),
\[
\frac{du}{dx} = ae^{ax}(y-z) + ae^{ax}\cos x + e^{ax}\sin x = e^{ax}(a^{2}+1)\sin x. \quad \textit{Ans.}
\]

\textsc{Note.} In examples like the above, $u$ could, by substitution, be found explicitly in terms of the independent variable and then differentiated directly, but generally this process would be longer and in many cases could not be used at all.

Formulas (51) and (52) are very useful in all applications involving time rates of change of functions of two or more variables. The process is practically the same as that outlined in the rule given on p. 141, except that, instead of differentiating with respect to $t$ (Third Step), we find the partial derivatives and substitute in (51) or (52). Let us illustrate by an example.

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 3. The altitude of a circular cone is 100 inches, and decreasing at the rate of 10 inches per second; and the radius of the base is 50 inches, and increasing at the rate of 5 inches per second. At what rate is the volume changing?


\textbf{Solution.} Let $x$ = radius of base, $y$ = altitude; then $u = \frac{1}{3}\pi x^{2}y$ = volume, $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{2}{3}\pi xy$, $\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \frac{1}{3}\pi x^{2}$. Substitute in (51),
\[
\frac{du}{dt} = \frac{2}{3}\pi xy\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{1}{3}\pi x^{2}\frac{dy}{dt}.
\]
But \quad $x = 50$, $y = 100$, $\frac{dx}{dt} = 5$, $\frac{dy}{dt} = -10$.

$\therefore\ \frac{du}{dt} = \frac{2}{3}\pi\cdot 5000\cdot 5 - \frac{1}{3}\pi\cdot 2500\cdot 10 = 15.15$ cu. ft. per sec., increase. \textit{Ans.}

\textbf{126. Total differentials.} Multiplying (51) and (52) through by $dt$, we get

(55)
\[
du = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}dy,
\]

(56)
\[
du = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}dy + \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}dz;
\]

and so on.$^{*}$ Equations (55) and (56) define the quantity $du$, which is called a \textit{total differential of $u$} or a \textit{complete differential},

and
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}dx,\quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}dy,\quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}dz
\]

$^{*}$ A geometric interpretation of this result will be given on p. 264.

are called \textit{partial differentials.} These partial differentials are sometimes denoted by $d_xu$, $d_yu$, $d_zu$, so that (\textbf{56}) is also written
\[ du = d_xu + d_yu + d_zu. \]
\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Given $u = \text{arc tan}\,\dfrac{y}{x}$, find $du$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = -\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}. \]
Substituting in (55),
\[ du = \frac{x\,dy - y\,dx}{x^2+y^2}.\ \textit{Ans.} \]

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 2. The base and altitude of a rectangle are 5 and 4 inches respectively. At a certain instant they are increasing continuously at the rate of 2 inches and 1 inch per second respectively. At what rate is the area of the rectangle increasing at that instant?

\textbf{Solution.} Let $x$ = base, $y$ = altitude; then $u = xy$ = area, $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} = y$, $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = x$.

Substituting in (51),
\[ (A)\qquad \frac{du}{dt} = y\,\frac{dx}{dt} + x\,\frac{dy}{dt}. \]
But \quad $x = 5$ in., $y = 4$ in., $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2$ in. per sec., $\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 1$ in. per sec.
\[ \therefore\ \frac{du}{dt} = (8 + 5) \text{ sq. in. per sec.} = 13 \text{ sq. in. per sec.}\quad \textit{Ans.} \]

\textsc{Note.} Considering $du$ as an infinitesimal increment of area due to the infinitesimal increments $dx$ and $dy$, $du$ is evidently the sum of two thin strips added on to the two
sides. For, in $du = y\,dx + x\,dy$ (multiplying $(A)$ by $dt$),
\[ y\,dx = \text{area of vertical strip, and} \]
\[ x\,dy = \text{area of horizontal strip.} \]
But the total increment $\Delta u$ due to the increments $dx$ and $dy$ is evidently
\[ \Delta u = y\,dx + x\,dy + dx\,dy. \]
Hence the small rectangle in the upper right-hand corner ($= dx\,dy$) is evidently the difference between $\Delta u$ and $du$.
This figure illustrates the fact that the total increment and the total differential of a function of several variables are not in general equal.

\textbf{127. Differentiation of implicit functions.} The equation
\[ (A)\qquad f(x,\,y) = 0 \]
defines either $x$ or $y$ as an implicit function of the other.$^{*}$ It represents any equation containing $x$ and $y$ when all its terms have been transposed to the first member. Let
\[ (B)\qquad u = f(x,\,y); \]
then
\[ \frac{du}{dx} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\,\frac{dy}{dx}. \qquad (\textbf{53}),\ \text{p. } 196 \]

$^{*}$ We assume that a small change in the value of $x$ causes only a small change in the value of $y$.


But from $(A)$, \quad $f(x,\,y)=0$. $\therefore u=0$ and $\dfrac{du}{dx}=0$; that is,

$(C)$
\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dx}=0. \]

Solving for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$,${}^{*}$ we get

\textbf{(57)}
\[ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}}{\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}},\qquad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\neq 0 \]

a formula for differentiating implicit functions. This formula in the form $(C)$ is equivalent to the process employed in \S\ 62, p. 69, for differentiating implicit functions, and all the examples on p. 70 may be solved by using formula (\textbf{57}). Since

$(D)$
\[ f(x,\,y)=0 \]

for all admissible values of $x$ and $y$, we may say that (\textbf{57}) gives \textit{the relative time rates of change of $x$ and $y$ which keep $f(x,\,y)$ from changing at all.} Geometrically this means that the point $(x,\,y)$ must move on the curve whose equation is $(D)$, and (\textbf{57}) determines the direction of its motion at any instant. Since
\[ u=f(x,\,y), \]
we may write (\textbf{57}) in the form

\textbf{(57\,$a$)}
\[ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}}{\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}}.\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\neq 0 \]

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Given $x^2y^4+\sin y=0$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.

\textbf{Solution.} Let $f(x,\,y)=x^2y^4+\sin y$.

$\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}=2\,xy^4$, \quad $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}=4\,x^2y^3+\cos y$. \quad $\therefore$ from (57\,$a$), $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{2\,xy^4}{4\,x^2y^3+\cos y}$. \quad \textit{Ans.}

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 2. If $x$ increases at the rate of 2 inches per second as it passes through the value $x=3$ inches, at what rate must $y$ change when $y=1$ inch, in order that the function $2\,xy^2-3\,x^2y$ shall remain constant?

\textbf{Solution.} Let $f(x,\,y)=2\,xy^2-3\,x^2y$; then
\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=2\,y^2-6\,xy,\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=4\,xy-3\,x^2. \]

Substituting in (57\,$a$),
\[ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{2\,y^2-6\,xy}{4\,xy-3\,x^2},\ \text{or}\ \frac{\dfrac{dy}{dt}}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}}=-\frac{2\,y^2-6\,xy}{4\,xy-3\,x^2}. \qquad \text{By (33), p. 141} \]

But $x=3$, $y=1$, $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2$. $\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dt}=-\,2\frac{2}{15}$ ft. per second. \textit{Ans.}

${}^{*}$ It is assumed that $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}$ exist.

Let $P$ be the point $(x,\,y,\,z)$ on the surface given by the equation
\[ (E)\qquad u = F(x,\,y,\,z) = 0, \]
and let $PC$ and $AP$ be sections made by planes through $P$ parallel to the $YOZ$- and $XOZ$-planes respectively. Along the curve $AP$, $y$ is constant; therefore, from $(E)$, $z$ is an implicit function of $x$ alone, and we have, from $(57\,a)$,
\[ (58)\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = -\frac{\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial x}}{\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial z}}, \]
giving the slope at $P$ of the curve $AP$, \S\ 122, p. 190.

$\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ is used instead of $\dfrac{dz}{dx}$ in the first member, since $z$ was originally, from $(E)$, an implicit function of $x$ and $y$; but $(58)$ is deduced on the hypothesis that $y$ remains constant.

Similarly, the slope at $P$ of the curve $PC$ is
\[ (59)\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -\frac{\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial y}}{\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial z}}. \]

\textbf{EXAMPLES} 

Find the total derivatives, using (51), (52), or (53), in the following six examples:

1. $u = z^2 + y^3 + zy,\ z = \sin x,\ y = e^x.$ \textit{Ans.} $\dfrac{du}{dx} = 3\,e^{3x} + e^x(\sin x + \cos x) + \sin 2x.$

2. $u = \operatorname{arc\,tan}(xy),\ y = e^x.$ \textit{Ans.} $\dfrac{du}{dx} = \dfrac{e^x(1+x)}{1 + x^2e^{2x}}.$

3. $u = \log(a^2 - \rho^2),\ \rho = a\sin\theta.$ $\dfrac{du}{d\theta} = -\,2\tan\theta.$

4. $u = v^2 + vy,\ v = \log s,\ y = e^s.$ $\dfrac{du}{ds} = \dfrac{2v + y}{s} + ve^s.$

5. $u = \operatorname{arc\,sin}(r - s),\ r = 3\,t,\ s = 4\,t^3.$ $\dfrac{du}{dt} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}}.$

6. $u = \dfrac{e^{ax}(y - z)}{a^2 + 1},\ y = a\sin x,\ z = \cos x.$ $\dfrac{du}{dx} = e^{ax}\sin x.$

Using (55) or (56), find the total differentials in the next eight examples:

7. $u = by^2x + cx^2 + gy^3 + ex.$ \textit{Ans.} $du = (by^2 + 2\,cx + e)\,dx + (2\,byx + 3\,gy^2)\,dy.$

8. $u = \log x^y.$ $du = \dfrac{y}{x}\,dx + \log x\,dy.$


9. $u = y^{\sin x}$. \textit{Ans.} $du = y^{\sin x}\log y \cos x\,dx + \dfrac{\sin x}{y^{\operatorname{covers}\,x}}\,dy$.

10. $u = x^{\log y}$. $du = u\left(\dfrac{\log y}{x}\,dx + \dfrac{\log x}{y}\,dy\right)$.

11. $u = \dfrac{s+t}{s-t}$. $du = \dfrac{2\,(s\,dt - t\,ds)}{(s-t)^2}$.

12. $u = \sin{(pq)}$. $du = \cos{(pq)}\,[q\,dp + p\,dq]$.

13. $u = x^{yz}$. $du = x^{yz-1}(yz\,dx + zx\log x\,dy + xy\log x\,dz)$.

14. $u = \tan^2\phi\,\tan^2\theta\,\tan^2\psi$. $du = 4u\left(\dfrac{d\phi}{\sin 2\,\phi} + \dfrac{d\theta}{\sin 2\,\theta} + \dfrac{d\psi}{\sin 2\,\psi}\right)$.

15. Assuming the characteristic equation of a perfect gas to be
\[ vp = Rt, \]
where $v$ = volume, $p$ = pressure, $t$ = absolute temperature, and $R$ a constant, what is the relation between the differentials $dv$, $dp$, $dt$? \textit{Ans.} $v\,dp + p\,dv = R\,dt$.

16. Using the result in the last example as applied to air, suppose that in a given case we have found by actual experiment that
\[ t = 300^\circ\ \mathrm{C.},\ p = 2000\ \mathrm{lb.\ per\ sq.\ ft.},\ v = 14.4\ \mathrm{cubic\ feet.} \]
Find the change in $p$, assuming it to be uniform, when $t$ changes to $301^\circ$ C., and $v$ to $14.5$ cubic feet. $R = 96$. \textit{Ans.} $-\ 7.22$ lb. per sq. ft.

17. One side of a triangle is 8 ft. long, and increasing 4 inches per second; another side is 5 ft., and decreasing 2 inches per second. The included angle is $60^\circ$, and increasing $2^\circ$ per second. At what rate is the area of the triangle changing? \textit{Ans.} Increasing 71.05 sq. in. per sec.

18. At what rate is the side opposite the given angle in the last example increasing? \textit{Ans.} 4.93 in. per sec.

19. One side of a rectangle is 10 in. and increasing 2 in. per sec. The other side is 15 in. and decreasing 1 in. per sec. At what rate is the area changing at the end of two seconds? \textit{Ans.} Increasing 12 sq. in. per sec.

20. The three edges of a rectangular parallelepiped are 3, 4, 5 inches, and are each increasing at the rate of .02 in. per min. At what rate is the volume changing?

21. A boy starts flying a kite. If it moves horizontally at the rate of 2 ft. a sec. and rises at the rate of 5 ft. a sec., how fast is the string being paid out? \textit{Ans.} 5.38 ft. a sec.

22. A man standing on a dock is drawing in the painter of a boat at the rate of 2 ft. a sec. His hands are 6 ft. above the bow of the boat. How fast is the boat moving when it is 8 ft. from the dock? \textit{Ans.} $\frac{5}{2}$ ft. a sec.

23. The volume and the radius of a cylindrical boiler are expanding at the rate of 1 cu. ft. and .001 ft. per min. respectively. How fast is the length of the boiler changing when the boiler contains 60 cu. ft. and has a radius of 2 ft.? \textit{Ans.} .078 ft. a min.

24. Water is running out of an opening in the vertex of a conical filtering glass, 8 inches high and 6 inches across the top, at the rate of .005 cu. in. per hour. How fast is the surface of the water falling when the depth of the water is 4 inches?

25. A covered water tank is made of sheet iron in the form of an inverted cone of altitude 8 ft. surmounted by a cylinder of altitude 5 ft. The diameter is 6 ft. If the sun's heat is increasing the diameter at the rate of .002 ft. per min., the altitude of the cylinder at the rate of .003 ft. per min., and the altitude of the cone at the rate of .0025 ft. per minute, at what rate is (a) the volume increasing; (b) the total area increasing?

In the remaining examples find $\frac{dy}{dx}$, using formula (57 a):

26. $(x^2 + y^2)^2 - a^2(x^2 - y^2) = 0.$ \textit{Ans.} $\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y}\cdot\frac{2(x^2 + y^2) - a^2}{2(x^2 + y^2) + a^2}.$

27. $e^y - e^x + xy = 0.$ $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{e^x - y}{e^y + x}.$

28. $\sin(xy) - e^{xy} - x^2y = 0.$ $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y[\cos(xy) - e^{xy} - 2x]}{x[x + e^{xy} - \cos(xy)]}.$


\textbf{128. Successive partial derivatives.} Consider the function
\[ u = f(x, y); \]
then, in general,
\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \quad\text{and}\quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} \]
are functions of both $x$ and $y$, and may be differentiated again with respect to either independent variable, giving \textit{successive partial derivatives.} Regarding $x$ alone as varying, we denote the results by
\[ \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2},\ \frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial x^3},\ \frac{\partial^4 u}{\partial x^4},\ \ldots,\ \frac{\partial^n u}{\partial x^n}, \]
or, when $y$ alone varies,
\[ \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2},\ \frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial y^3},\ \frac{\partial^4 u}{\partial y^4},\ \ldots,\ \frac{\partial^n u}{\partial y^n}, \]
the notation being similar to that employed for functions of a single variable.

If we differentiate $u$ with respect to $x$, regarding $y$ as constant, and then this result with respect to $y$, regarding $x$ as constant, we obtain
\[ \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right), \text{ which we denote by } \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y\,\partial x}. \]

Similarly, if we differentiate twice with respect to $x$ and then once with respect to $y$, the result is denoted by the symbol
\[ \frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial y\,\partial x^2}. \]


\textbf{129. Order of differentiation immaterial.} Consider the function $f(x,\,y)$. Changing $x$ into $x+\Delta x$ and keeping $y$ constant, we get from the Theorem of Mean Value, (\textbf{46}), p. 166,

\[
(A)\quad f(x+\Delta x,\,y)-f(x,\,y)=\Delta x\cdot f'_x\,(x+\theta\cdot\Delta x,\,y).\qquad 0<\theta<1
\]

[$a=x$, $\Delta a=\Delta x$, and since $x$ varies while $y$ remains constant, we get the partial derivative with respect to $x$.]

If we now change $y$ to $y+\Delta y$ and keep $x$ and $\Delta x$ constant, the total increment of the left-hand member of $(A)$ is

\[
(B)\quad [f(x+\Delta x,\,y+\Delta y)-f(x,\,y+\Delta y)]-[f(x+\Delta x,\,y)-f(x,\,y)].
\]

The total increment of the right-hand member of $(A)$ found by the Theorem of Mean Value, (\textbf{46}), p. 166, is

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
(C)\quad \Delta x f'_x\,(x+\theta\cdot\Delta x,\,y+\Delta y)-\Delta x f'_x\,(x+\theta\cdot\Delta x,\,y) & \qquad 0<\theta_1<1\\[1ex]
\qquad\qquad =\Delta y\Delta x f''_{yx}\,(x+\theta_1\cdot\Delta x,\,y+\theta_2\cdot\Delta y). & \qquad 0<\theta_2<1
\end{array}
\]

[$a=y$, $\Delta a=\Delta y$, and since $y$ varies while $x$ and $\Delta x$ remain constant, we get the partial derivative with respect to $y$.]

Since the increments $(B)$ and $(C)$ must be equal,

\[
\begin{array}{l}
(D)\quad [f(x+\Delta x,\,y+\Delta y)-f(x,\,y+\Delta y)]-[f(x+\Delta x,\,y)-f(x,\,y)]\\[1ex]
\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad =\Delta y\Delta x f''_{yx}\,(x+\theta_1\cdot\Delta x,\,y+\theta_2\cdot\Delta y).
\end{array}
\]

In the same manner, if we take the increments in the reverse order,

\[
\begin{array}{l}
(E)\quad [f(x+\Delta x,\,y+\Delta y)-f(x+\Delta x,\,y)]-[f(x,\,y+\Delta y)-f(x,\,y)]\\[1ex]
\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad =\Delta x\Delta y f''_{xy}\,(x+\theta_3\cdot\Delta x,\,y+\theta_4\cdot\Delta y),
\end{array}
\]

$\theta_3$ and $\theta_4$ also lying between zero and unity.

The left-hand members of $(D)$ and $(E)$ being identical, we have

\[
(F)\quad f''_{yx}\,(x+\theta_1\cdot\Delta x,\,y+\theta_2\cdot\Delta y)=f''_{xy}\,(x+\theta_3\cdot\Delta x,\,y+\theta_4\cdot\Delta y).
\]

Taking the limit of both sides as $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ approach zero as limits, we have

\[
(G)\qquad f''_{yx}\,(x,\,y)=f''_{xy}\,(x,\,y),
\]

since these functions are assumed continuous. Placing

\[
u=f(x,\,y),
\]

$(G)$ may be written

\[
(\textbf{60})\qquad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y\partial x}=\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x\partial y}.
\]

That is, \textit{the operations of differentiating with respect to $x$ and with respect to $y$ are commutative.}

This may be easily extended to higher derivatives. For instance, since (\textbf{58}) is true,
\[
\frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial x^2 \partial y} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y}\right) = \frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial x \partial y \partial x} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x \partial y}\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right) = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial y \partial x}\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right) = \frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial y \partial x^2}.
\]
Similarly for functions of three or more variables.

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Given $u = x^3 y - 3\,x^2 y^3$; verify $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y \partial x} = \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y}$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 3\,x^2 y - 6\,x y^3, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y \partial x} = 3\,x^2 - 18\,x y^2,
\]
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = x^3 - 9\,x^2 y^2, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y} = 3\,x^2 - 18\,x y^2 ; \text{ hence verified.}
\]

\textbf{EXAMPLES} 

1. $u = \cos{(x + y)}$; \hfill verify $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y \partial x} = \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y}$.

2. $u = \dfrac{y^2 + x^2}{y^2 - x^2}$; \hfill verify $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y \partial x} = \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y}$.

3. $u = y \log{(1 + xy)}$; \hfill verify $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y \partial x} = \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y}$.

4. $u = \operatorname{arc\,tan} \dfrac{r}{s}$; \hfill verify $\dfrac{\partial^3 u}{\partial r^2 \partial s} = \dfrac{\partial^3 u}{\partial s \partial r^2}$.

5. $u = \sin{(\theta^2 \phi)}$; \hfill verify $\dfrac{\partial^3 u}{\partial \theta \partial \phi^2} = \dfrac{\partial^3 u}{\partial \phi^2 \partial \theta}$.

6. $u = 6\,e^{xy} y^2 z + 3\,e^{yz} x^2 z^2 + 2\,e^{zx} x^3 y - xyz$; show that $\dfrac{\partial^4 u}{\partial x^2 \partial y \partial z} = 12\,(e^{xy} y + e^{yz} z + e^{zx} x)$.

7. $u = e^{xyz}$; show that $\dfrac{\partial^3 u}{\partial x \partial y \partial z} = (1 + 3\,xyz + x^2 y^2 z^2)u$.

8. $u = \dfrac{x^2 y^2}{x + y}$; show that $x\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + y\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y} = 2\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$.

9. $u = (x^2 + y^2)^{\frac{1}{3}}$; show that $3\,x\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y} + 3\,y\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 0$.

10. $u = y^2 z^2 e^{\frac{x}{2}} + z^2 x^2 e^{\frac{y}{2}} + x^2 y^2 e^{\frac{z}{2}}$; show that $\dfrac{\partial^6 u}{\partial x^2 \partial y^2 \partial z^2} = e^{\frac{x}{2}} + e^{\frac{y}{2}} + e^{\frac{z}{2}}$.

11. $u = (x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$; show that $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial z^2} = 0$.
chapters.text_markdown: # CHAPTER XV: PARTIAL DIFFERENTIATION **122. Continuous functions of two or more independent variables.** A function $f(x,\,y)$ of two independent variables $x$ and $y$ is defined as continuous for the values $(a,\,b)$ of $(x,\,y)$ when $$\mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{\substack{x=a\\ y=b}} f(x,\,y)=f(a,\,b),$$ no matter in what way $x$ and $y$ approach their respective limits $a$ and $b$. This definition is sometimes roughly summed up in the statement that *a very small change in one or both of the independent variables shall produce a very small change in the value of the function.*$^{*}$ We may illustrate this geometrically by considering the surface represented by the equation $$z=f(x,\,y).$$ Consider a fixed point $P$ on the surface where $x=a$ and $y=b$. Denote by $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ the increments of the independent variables $x$ and $y$, and by $\Delta z$ the corresponding increment of the dependent variable $z$, the coördinates of $P'$ being $$(x+\Delta x,\ y+\Delta y,\ z+\Delta z).$$ At $P$ the value of the function is $$z=f(a,\,b)=MP.$$ If the function is continuous at $P$, then however $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ may approach the limit zero, $\Delta z$ will also approach the limit zero. That is, $M'P'$ will approach coincidence with $MP$, the point $P'$ approaching the point $P$ on the surface from any direction whatever. A similar definition holds for a continuous function of more than two independent variables. In what follows, only values of the independent variables are considered for which a function is continuous. $^{*}$ This will be better understood if the student again reads over § 18, p. 14, on continuous functions of a single variable. **123. Partial derivatives.** Since $x$ and $y$ are independent in $$z = f(x,\, y),$$ $x$ may be supposed to vary while $y$ remains constant, or the reverse. The derivative of $z$ with respect to $x$ when $x$ varies and $y$ remains constant $^{*}$ is called the *partial derivative of $z$ with respect to $x$*, and is denoted by the symbol $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$. We may then write $$(A)\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{\Delta x = 0}\left[\frac{f(x + \Delta x,\, y) - f(x,\, y)}{\Delta x}\right].$$ Similarly, when $x$ remains constant $^{*}$ and $y$ varies, *the partial derivative of $z$ with respect to $y$* is $$(B)\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{\Delta y = 0}\left[\frac{f(x,\, y + \Delta y) - f(x,\, y)}{\Delta y}\right].$$ $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ is also written $\frac{\partial}{\partial x} f(x,\, y)$, or $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$. Similarly, $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ is also written $\frac{\partial}{\partial y} f(x,\, y)$, or $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$. In order to avoid confusion the round $\partial^{\dagger}$ has been generally adopted to indicate partial differentiation. Other notations, however, which are in use are $$\left(\frac{dz}{dx}\right),\ \left(\frac{dz}{dy}\right);\ f'_x(x,\, y),\ f'_y(x,\, y);\ f_x(x,\, y),\ f_y(x,\, y);\ D_x f,\ D_y f;\ z_x,\ z_y.$$ Our notation may be extended to a function of any number of independent variables. Thus, if $$u = F(x,\, y,\, z),$$ then we have the three partial derivatives $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial y},\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial z};\ \text{or,}\ \frac{\partial F}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial F}{\partial y},\ \frac{\partial F}{\partial z}.$$ Illustrative Example 1. Find the partial derivatives of $z = ax^2 + 2\,bxy + cy^2$. **Solution.** $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 2\,ax + 2\,by, \text{ treating } y \text{ as a constant,}$$ $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = 2\,bx + 2\,cy, \text{ treating } x \text{ as a constant.}$$ $^{*}$ The constant values are substituted in the function before differentiating. $\dagger$ Introduced by Jacobi (1804--1851). Illustrative Example 2. Find the partial derivatives of $u = \sin (ax + by + cz)$. **Solution.** $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = a \cos (ax + by + cz), \text{ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants,}$$ $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = b \cos (ax + by + cz), \text{ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants,}$$ $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial z} = c \cos (ax + by + cz), \text{ treating $y$ and $x$ as constants.}$$ Again turning to the function $$z = f(x, y),$$ we have, by $(A)$, p. 191, defined $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ as the limit of the ratio of the increment of the function ($y$ being constant) to the increment of $x$, as the increment of $x$ approaches the limit zero. Similarly, $(B)$, p. 191, has defined $\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}$. It is evident, however, that if we look upon these partial derivatives from the point of view of § 94, p. 141, then $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$$ may be considered as the ratio of the time rates of change of $z$ and $x$ when $y$ is constant, and $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}$$ as the ratio of the time rates of change of $z$ and $y$ when $x$ is constant. **124. Partial derivatives interpreted geometrically.** Let the equation of the surface shown in the figure be $$z = f(x, y).$$ Pass a plane $EFGH$ through the point $P$ (where $x = a$ and $y = b$) on the surface parallel to the $XOZ$-plane. Since the equation of this plane is $$y = b,$$ the equation of the section $JPK$ cut out of the surface is $$z = f(x, b),$$ if we consider $EF$ as the axis of $Z$ and $EH$ as the axis of $X$. In this plane $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ means the same as $\frac{dz}{dx}$, and we have $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \mathit{tan}\ MTP$$ $$= \mathit{slope\ of\ section\ JK\ at\ P.}$$ Similarly, if we pass the plane $BCD$ through $P$ parallel to the $YOZ$-plane, its equation is $x=a,$ and for the section $DPI$, $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ means the same as $\dfrac{dz}{dy}$. Hence $$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \frac{dz}{dy} = -\tan MT'P = \text{slope of section } DI \text{ at } P.$$ Illustrative Example 1. Given the ellipsoid $\dfrac{x^2}{24}+\dfrac{y^2}{12}+\dfrac{z^2}{6}=1$; find the slope of the section of the ellipsoid made (a) by the plane $y=1$ at the point where $x=4$ and $z$ is positive; (b) by the plane $x=2$ at the point where $y=3$ and $z$ is positive. **Solution.** Considering $y$ as constant, $$\frac{2x}{24}+\frac{2z}{6}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=0, \text{ or } \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{x}{4z}.$$ When $x$ is constant, $$\frac{2y}{12}+\frac{2z}{6}\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=0, \text{ or } \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{y}{2z}.$$ \(a\) When $y=1$ and $x=4$, $z=\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$. $\therefore \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}$. *Ans.* \(b\) When $x=2$ and $y=3$, $z=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. $\therefore \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\dfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{2}$. *Ans.* **EXAMPLES** 1\. $u=x^3+3x^2y-y^3$. *Ans.* $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=3x^2+6xy$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=3x^2-3y^2$. 2\. $u=Ax^2+Bxy+Cy^2+Dx+Ey+F$. $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=2Ax+By+D$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=Bx+2Cy+E$. 3\. $u=(ax^2+by^2+cz^2)^n$. $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\dfrac{2anxu}{ax^2+by^2+cz^2}$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=\dfrac{2bnyu}{ax^2+by^2+cz^2}$. 4\. $u=\text{arc sin}\,\dfrac{x}{y}$. $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y^2-x^2}}$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=-\dfrac{x}{y\sqrt{y^2-x^2}}$. 5\. $u=x^y$. $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=yx^{y-1}$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=x^y\log x$. 6\. $u=ax^3y^2z+bxy^3z^4+cy^6+dxz^3$. $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}=3ax^2y^2z+by^3z^4+dz^3$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}=2ax^3yz+3bxy^2z^4+6cy^5$; $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z}=ax^3y^2+4bxy^3z^3+3dxz^2$. 7\. $u = x^3y^2 - 2\,xy^4 + 3\,x^2y^3$; show that $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 5\,u$. 8\. $u = \dfrac{xy}{x+y}$; show that $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = u$. 9\. $u = (y-z)\,(z-x)\,(x-y)$; show that $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} = 0$. 10\. $u = \log\,(e^x + e^y)$; show that $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 1$. 11\. $u = \dfrac{e^{xy}}{e^x + e^y}$; Total derivatives.** We have already considered the differentiation of a function of one function of a single independent variable. Thus, if $$y = f(v) \text{ and } v = \phi(x),$$ it was shown that $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{dv}\cdot\frac{dv}{dx}.$$ We shall next consider a function of two variables, both of which depend on a single independent variable. Consider the function $$u = f(x,\, y),$$ where $x$ and $y$ are functions of a third variable $t$. Let $t$ take on the increment $\Delta t$, and let $\Delta x$, $\Delta y$, $\Delta u$ be the corresponding increments of $x$, $y$, $u$ respectively. Then the quantity $$\Delta u = f(x + \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y) - f(x,\, y)$$ is called the *total increment* of $u$. Adding and subtracting $f(x,\, y + \Delta y)$ in the second member, $$(A)\ \ \Delta u = [f(x + \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y) - f(x,\, y + \Delta y)] + [f(x,\, y + \Delta y) - f(x,\, y)].$$ Applying the Theorem of Mean Value (**46**), p. 166, to each of the two differences on the right-hand side of $(A)$, we get, for the first difference, $$(B)\ \ f(x + \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y) - f(x,\, y + \Delta y) = f_x'(x + \theta_1 \cdot \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y)\,\Delta x.$$ \[a = x, \Delta a = \Delta x, and since x varies while y + \Delta y remains constant, we get the partial derivative with respect to x.\] For the second difference we get $$(C)\ \ f(x,\, y + \Delta y) - f(x,\, y) = f_y'(x,\, y + \theta_2 \cdot \Delta y)\,\Delta y.$$ \[a = y, \Delta a = \Delta y, and since y varies while x remains constant, we get the partial derivative with respect to y.\] Substituting $(B)$ and $(C)$ in $(A)$ gives $$(D)\ \ \Delta u = f_x'(x + \theta_1 \cdot \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y)\,\Delta x + f_y'(x,\, y + \theta_2 \cdot \Delta y)\,\Delta y,$$ where $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are positive proper fractions. Dividing $(D)$ by $\Delta t$, $$(E)\ \ \frac{\Delta u}{\Delta t} = f_x'(x + \theta_1 \cdot \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y)\,\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} + f_y'(x,\, y + \theta_2 \cdot \Delta y)\,\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta t}.$$ Now let $\Delta t$ approach zero as a limit, then $$(F)\ \ \frac{du}{dt} = f_x'(x,\, y)\,\frac{dx}{dt} + f_y'(x,\, y)\,\frac{dy}{dt}.$$ \[Since \Delta x and \Delta y converge to zero with \Delta t, we get \underset{\Delta t = 0}{\text{limit}}\, f_x'(x + \theta_1 \cdot \Delta x,\, y + \Delta y) = f_x'(x,\, y), and \underset{\Delta t = 0}{\text{limit}}\, f_y'(x,\, y + \theta_2 \cdot \Delta y) = f_y'(x,\, y), f_x'(x,\, y) and f_y'(x,\, y) being assumed continuous.\] Replacing $f(x,\, y)$ by $u$ in $(F)$, we get the *total derivative* $$(\textbf{51})\ \ \frac{du}{dt} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\,\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\,\frac{dy}{dt}.$$ In the same way, if $$u = f(x, y, z),$$ and $x$, $y$, $z$ are all functions of $t$, we get $$(52)\qquad \frac{du}{dt} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\frac{dz}{dt},$$ and so on for any number of variables.$^{*}$ In (51) we may suppose $t = x$; then $y$ is a function of $x$, and $u$ is really a function of the one variable $x$, giving $$(53)\qquad \frac{du}{dx} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dx}.$$ In the same way, from (52) we have $$(54)\qquad \frac{du}{dx} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\cdot\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\cdot\frac{dz}{dx}.$$ The student should observe that $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{du}{dx}$ have quite different meanings. The partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$ is formed on the supposition that the *particular variable $x$ alone varies*, while $$\frac{du}{dx} = \mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{\Delta x = 0}\left(\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x}\right),$$ where $\Delta u$ is the *total increment of $u$ caused by changes in all the variables*, these increments being due to the change $\Delta x$ in the independent variable. In contradistinction to partial derivatives, $\dfrac{du}{dt}$, $\dfrac{du}{dx}$ are called *total derivatives* with respect to $t$ and $x$ respectively.$^\dagger$ $^{*}$ This is really only a special case of a general theorem which may be stated as follows: If $u$ is a function of the independent variables $x$, $y$, $z$, $\cdots$, each of these in turn being a function of the independent variables $r$, $s$, $t$, $\cdots$, then (with certain assumptions as to continuity) $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial r} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial r} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial r} + \cdots,$$ and similar expressions hold for $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial s}$, $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t}$, etc. $^\dagger$ It should be observed that $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$ has a perfectly definite value for any point $(x, y)$, while $\dfrac{du}{dx}$ depends not only on the point $(x, y)$, but also on the particular direction chosen to reach that point. Hence $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$ is called a point function; while $\dfrac{du}{dx}$ is not called a point function unless it is agreed to approach the point from some particular direction. Illustrative Example 1. Given $u = \sin\frac{x}{y}$, $x = e^{t}$, $y = t^{2}$; find $\frac{du}{dt}$. **Solution.** $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{y}\cos\frac{x}{y}$, $\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\frac{x}{y^{2}}\cos\frac{x}{y}$; $\frac{dx}{dt} = e^{t}$, $\frac{dy}{dt} = 2t$. Substituting in (51), $\frac{du}{dt} = (t-2)\frac{e^{t}}{t^{3}}\cos\frac{e^{t}}{t^{2}}$. *Ans.* Illustrative Example 2. Given $u = e^{ax}(y-z)$, $y = a\sin x$, $z = \cos x$; find $\frac{du}{dx}$. **Solution.** $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = ae^{ax}(y-z)$, $\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = e^{ax}$, $\frac{\partial u}{\partial z} = -e^{ax}$; $\frac{dy}{dx} = a\cos x$, $\frac{dz}{dx} = -\sin x$. Substituting in (54), $$\frac{du}{dx} = ae^{ax}(y-z) + ae^{ax}\cos x + e^{ax}\sin x = e^{ax}(a^{2}+1)\sin x. \quad \textit{Ans.}$$ Note. In examples like the above, $u$ could, by substitution, be found explicitly in terms of the independent variable and then differentiated directly, but generally this process would be longer and in many cases could not be used at all. Formulas (51) and (52) are very useful in all applications involving time rates of change of functions of two or more variables. The process is practically the same as that outlined in the rule given on p. 141, except that, instead of differentiating with respect to $t$ (Third Step), we find the partial derivatives and substitute in (51) or (52). Let us illustrate by an example. Illustrative Example 3. The altitude of a circular cone is 100 inches, and decreasing at the rate of 10 inches per second; and the radius of the base is 50 inches, and increasing at the rate of 5 inches per second. At what rate is the volume changing? **Solution.** Let $x$ = radius of base, $y$ = altitude; then $u = \frac{1}{3}\pi x^{2}y$ = volume, $\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{2}{3}\pi xy$, $\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \frac{1}{3}\pi x^{2}$. Substitute in (51), $$\frac{du}{dt} = \frac{2}{3}\pi xy\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{1}{3}\pi x^{2}\frac{dy}{dt}.$$ But $x = 50$, $y = 100$, $\frac{dx}{dt} = 5$, $\frac{dy}{dt} = -10$. $\therefore\ \frac{du}{dt} = \frac{2}{3}\pi\cdot 5000\cdot 5 - \frac{1}{3}\pi\cdot 2500\cdot 10 = 15.15$ cu. ft. per sec., increase. *Ans.* **126. Total differentials.** Multiplying (51) and (52) through by $dt$, we get \(55\) $$du = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}dy,$$ \(56\) $$du = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}dy + \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}dz;$$ and so on.$^{*}$ Equations (55) and (56) define the quantity $du$, which is called a *total differential of $u$* or a *complete differential*, and $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}dx,\quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}dy,\quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial z}dz$$ $^{*}$ A geometric interpretation of this result will be given on p. 264. are called *partial differentials.* These partial differentials are sometimes denoted by $d_xu$, $d_yu$, $d_zu$, so that (**56**) is also written $$du = d_xu + d_yu + d_zu.$$ Illustrative Example 1. Given $u = \text{arc tan}\,\dfrac{y}{x}$, find $du$. **Solution.** $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = -\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}, \quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}.$$ Substituting in (55), $$du = \frac{x\,dy - y\,dx}{x^2+y^2}.\ \textit{Ans.}$$ Illustrative Example 2. The base and altitude of a rectangle are 5 and 4 inches respectively. At a certain instant they are increasing continuously at the rate of 2 inches and 1 inch per second respectively. At what rate is the area of the rectangle increasing at that instant? **Solution.** Let $x$ = base, $y$ = altitude; then $u = xy$ = area, $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} = y$, $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = x$. Substituting in (51), $$(A)\qquad \frac{du}{dt} = y\,\frac{dx}{dt} + x\,\frac{dy}{dt}.$$ But $x = 5$ in., $y = 4$ in., $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2$ in. per sec., $\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 1$ in. per sec. $$\therefore\ \frac{du}{dt} = (8 + 5) \text{ sq. in. per sec.} = 13 \text{ sq. in. per sec.}\quad \textit{Ans.}$$ Note. Considering $du$ as an infinitesimal increment of area due to the infinitesimal increments $dx$ and $dy$, $du$ is evidently the sum of two thin strips added on to the two sides. For, in $du = y\,dx + x\,dy$ (multiplying $(A)$ by $dt$), $$y\,dx = \text{area of vertical strip, and}$$ $$x\,dy = \text{area of horizontal strip.}$$ But the total increment $\Delta u$ due to the increments $dx$ and $dy$ is evidently $$\Delta u = y\,dx + x\,dy + dx\,dy.$$ Hence the small rectangle in the upper right-hand corner ($= dx\,dy$) is evidently the difference between $\Delta u$ and $du$. This figure illustrates the fact that the total increment and the total differential of a function of several variables are not in general equal. **127. Differentiation of implicit functions.** The equation $$(A)\qquad f(x,\,y) = 0$$ defines either $x$ or $y$ as an implicit function of the other.$^{*}$ It represents any equation containing $x$ and $y$ when all its terms have been transposed to the first member. Let $$(B)\qquad u = f(x,\,y);$$ then $$\frac{du}{dx} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\,\frac{dy}{dx}. \qquad (\textbf{53}),\ \text{p. } 196$$ $^{*}$ We assume that a small change in the value of $x$ causes only a small change in the value of $y$. But from $(A)$, $f(x,\,y)=0$. $\therefore u=0$ and $\dfrac{du}{dx}=0$; that is, $(C)$ $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dx}=0.$$ Solving for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$,${}^{*}$ we get **(57)** $$\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}}{\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}},\qquad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\neq 0$$ a formula for differentiating implicit functions. This formula in the form $(C)$ is equivalent to the process employed in § 62, p. 69, for differentiating implicit functions, and all the examples on p. 70 may be solved by using formula (**57**). Since $(D)$ $$f(x,\,y)=0$$ for all admissible values of $x$ and $y$, we may say that (**57**) gives *the relative time rates of change of $x$ and $y$ which keep $f(x,\,y)$ from changing at all.* Geometrically this means that the point $(x,\,y)$ must move on the curve whose equation is $(D)$, and (**57**) determines the direction of its motion at any instant. Since $$u=f(x,\,y),$$ we may write (**57**) in the form **(57 $a$)** $$\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}}{\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}}.\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\neq 0$$ Illustrative Example 1. Given $x^2y^4+\sin y=0$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$. **Solution.** Let $f(x,\,y)=x^2y^4+\sin y$. $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}=2\,xy^4$, $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}=4\,x^2y^3+\cos y$. $\therefore$ from (57 $a$), $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{2\,xy^4}{4\,x^2y^3+\cos y}$. *Ans.* Illustrative Example 2. If $x$ increases at the rate of 2 inches per second as it passes through the value $x=3$ inches, at what rate must $y$ change when $y=1$ inch, in order that the function $2\,xy^2-3\,x^2y$ shall remain constant? **Solution.** Let $f(x,\,y)=2\,xy^2-3\,x^2y$; then $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=2\,y^2-6\,xy,\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=4\,xy-3\,x^2.$$ Substituting in (57 $a$), $$\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{2\,y^2-6\,xy}{4\,xy-3\,x^2},\ \text{or}\ \frac{\dfrac{dy}{dt}}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}}=-\frac{2\,y^2-6\,xy}{4\,xy-3\,x^2}. \qquad \text{By (33), p. 141}$$ But $x=3$, $y=1$, $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2$. $\therefore\ \dfrac{dy}{dt}=-\,2\frac{2}{15}$ ft. per second. *Ans.* ${}^{*}$ It is assumed that $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y}$ exist. Let $P$ be the point $(x,\,y,\,z)$ on the surface given by the equation $$(E)\qquad u = F(x,\,y,\,z) = 0,$$ and let $PC$ and $AP$ be sections made by planes through $P$ parallel to the $YOZ$- and $XOZ$-planes respectively. Along the curve $AP$, $y$ is constant; therefore, from $(E)$, $z$ is an implicit function of $x$ alone, and we have, from $(57\,a)$, $$(58)\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = -\frac{\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial x}}{\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial z}},$$ giving the slope at $P$ of the curve $AP$, § 122, p. 190. $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ is used instead of $\dfrac{dz}{dx}$ in the first member, since $z$ was originally, from $(E)$, an implicit function of $x$ and $y$; but $(58)$ is deduced on the hypothesis that $y$ remains constant. Similarly, the slope at $P$ of the curve $PC$ is $$(59)\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -\frac{\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial y}}{\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial z}}.$$ **EXAMPLES** Find the total derivatives, using (51), (52), or (53), in the following six examples: 1\. $u = z^2 + y^3 + zy,\ z = \sin x,\ y = e^x.$ *Ans.* $\dfrac{du}{dx} = 3\,e^{3x} + e^x(\sin x + \cos x) + \sin 2x.$ 2\. $u = \operatorname{arc\,tan}(xy),\ y = e^x.$ *Ans.* $\dfrac{du}{dx} = \dfrac{e^x(1+x)}{1 + x^2e^{2x}}.$ 3\. $u = \log(a^2 - \rho^2),\ \rho = a\sin\theta.$ $\dfrac{du}{d\theta} = -\,2\tan\theta.$ 4\. $u = v^2 + vy,\ v = \log s,\ y = e^s.$ $\dfrac{du}{ds} = \dfrac{2v + y}{s} + ve^s.$ 5\. $u = \operatorname{arc\,sin}(r - s),\ r = 3\,t,\ s = 4\,t^3.$ $\dfrac{du}{dt} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{1 - t^2}}.$ 6\. $u = \dfrac{e^{ax}(y - z)}{a^2 + 1},\ y = a\sin x,\ z = \cos x.$ $\dfrac{du}{dx} = e^{ax}\sin x.$ Using (55) or (56), find the total differentials in the next eight examples: 7\. $u = by^2x + cx^2 + gy^3 + ex.$ *Ans.* $du = (by^2 + 2\,cx + e)\,dx + (2\,byx + 3\,gy^2)\,dy.$ 8\. $u = \log x^y.$ $du = \dfrac{y}{x}\,dx + \log x\,dy.$ 9\. $u = y^{\sin x}$. *Ans.* $du = y^{\sin x}\log y \cos x\,dx + \dfrac{\sin x}{y^{\operatorname{covers}\,x}}\,dy$. 10\. $u = x^{\log y}$. $du = u\left(\dfrac{\log y}{x}\,dx + \dfrac{\log x}{y}\,dy\right)$. 11\. $u = \dfrac{s+t}{s-t}$. $du = \dfrac{2\,(s\,dt - t\,ds)}{(s-t)^2}$. 12\. $u = \sin{(pq)}$. $du = \cos{(pq)}\,[q\,dp + p\,dq]$. 13\. $u = x^{yz}$. $du = x^{yz-1}(yz\,dx + zx\log x\,dy + xy\log x\,dz)$. 14\. $u = \tan^2\phi\,\tan^2\theta\,\tan^2\psi$. $du = 4u\left(\dfrac{d\phi}{\sin 2\,\phi} + \dfrac{d\theta}{\sin 2\,\theta} + \dfrac{d\psi}{\sin 2\,\psi}\right)$. 15\. Successive partial derivatives.** Consider the function $$u = f(x, y);$$ then, in general, $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \quad\text{and}\quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}$$ are functions of both $x$ and $y$, and may be differentiated again with respect to either independent variable, giving *successive partial derivatives.* Regarding $x$ alone as varying, we denote the results by $$\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2},\ \frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial x^3},\ \frac{\partial^4 u}{\partial x^4},\ \ldots,\ \frac{\partial^n u}{\partial x^n},$$ or, when $y$ alone varies, $$\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2},\ \frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial y^3},\ \frac{\partial^4 u}{\partial y^4},\ \ldots,\ \frac{\partial^n u}{\partial y^n},$$ the notation being similar to that employed for functions of a single variable. If we differentiate $u$ with respect to $x$, regarding $y$ as constant, and then this result with respect to $y$, regarding $x$ as constant, we obtain $$\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right), \text{ which we denote by } \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y\,\partial x}.$$ Similarly, if we differentiate twice with respect to $x$ and then once with respect to $y$, the result is denoted by the symbol $$\frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial y\,\partial x^2}.$$ **129. Order of differentiation immaterial.** Consider the function $f(x,\,y)$. Changing $x$ into $x+\Delta x$ and keeping $y$ constant, we get from the Theorem of Mean Value, (**46**), p. 166, $$(A)\quad f(x+\Delta x,\,y)-f(x,\,y)=\Delta x\cdot f'_x\,(x+\theta\cdot\Delta x,\,y).\qquad 0<\theta<1$$ \[a=x, \Delta a=\Delta x, and since x varies while y remains constant, we get the partial derivative with respect to x.\] If we now change $y$ to $y+\Delta y$ and keep $x$ and $\Delta x$ constant, the total increment of the left-hand member of $(A)$ is $$(B)\quad [f(x+\Delta x,\,y+\Delta y)-f(x,\,y+\Delta y)]-[f(x+\Delta x,\,y)-f(x,\,y)].$$ The total increment of the right-hand member of $(A)$ found by the Theorem of Mean Value, (**46**), p. 166, is $$\begin{array}{ll} (C)\quad \Delta x f'_x\,(x+\theta\cdot\Delta x,\,y+\Delta y)-\Delta x f'_x\,(x+\theta\cdot\Delta x,\,y) & \qquad 0<\theta_1<1\\[1ex] \qquad\qquad =\Delta y\Delta x f''_{yx}\,(x+\theta_1\cdot\Delta x,\,y+\theta_2\cdot\Delta y). & \qquad 0<\theta_2<1 \end{array}$$ \[a=y, \Delta a=\Delta y, and since y varies while x and \Delta x remain constant, we get the partial derivative with respect to y.\] Since the increments $(B)$ and $(C)$ must be equal, $$\begin{array}{l} (D)\quad [f(x+\Delta x,\,y+\Delta y)-f(x,\,y+\Delta y)]-[f(x+\Delta x,\,y)-f(x,\,y)]\\[1ex] \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad =\Delta y\Delta x f''_{yx}\,(x+\theta_1\cdot\Delta x,\,y+\theta_2\cdot\Delta y). \end{array}$$ In the same manner, if we take the increments in the reverse order, $$\begin{array}{l} (E)\quad [f(x+\Delta x,\,y+\Delta y)-f(x+\Delta x,\,y)]-[f(x,\,y+\Delta y)-f(x,\,y)]\\[1ex] \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad =\Delta x\Delta y f''_{xy}\,(x+\theta_3\cdot\Delta x,\,y+\theta_4\cdot\Delta y), \end{array}$$ $\theta_3$ and $\theta_4$ also lying between zero and unity. The left-hand members of $(D)$ and $(E)$ being identical, we have $$(F)\quad f''_{yx}\,(x+\theta_1\cdot\Delta x,\,y+\theta_2\cdot\Delta y)=f''_{xy}\,(x+\theta_3\cdot\Delta x,\,y+\theta_4\cdot\Delta y).$$ Taking the limit of both sides as $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ approach zero as limits, we have $$(G)\qquad f''_{yx}\,(x,\,y)=f''_{xy}\,(x,\,y),$$ since these functions are assumed continuous. Placing $$u=f(x,\,y),$$ $(G)$ may be written $$(\textbf{60})\qquad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y\partial x}=\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x\partial y}.$$ That is, *the operations of differentiating with respect to $x$ and with respect to $y$ are commutative.* This may be easily extended to higher derivatives. For instance, since (**58**) is true, $$\frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial x^2 \partial y} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y}\right) = \frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial x \partial y \partial x} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x \partial y}\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right) = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial y \partial x}\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right) = \frac{\partial^3 u}{\partial y \partial x^2}.$$ Similarly for functions of three or more variables. Illustrative Example 1. Given $u = x^3 y - 3\,x^2 y^3$; verify $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y \partial x} = \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y}$. **Solution.** $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 3\,x^2 y - 6\,x y^3, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y \partial x} = 3\,x^2 - 18\,x y^2,$$ $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = x^3 - 9\,x^2 y^2, \quad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y} = 3\,x^2 - 18\,x y^2 ; \text{ hence verified.}$$ **EXAMPLES** 1\. $u = \cos{(x + y)}$; verify $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y \partial x} = \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y}$. 2\. $u = \dfrac{y^2 + x^2}{y^2 - x^2}$; verify $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y \partial x} = \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y}$. 3\. $u = y \log{(1 + xy)}$; verify $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y \partial x} = \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y}$. 4\. $u = \operatorname{arc\,tan} \dfrac{r}{s}$; verify $\dfrac{\partial^3 u}{\partial r^2 \partial s} = \dfrac{\partial^3 u}{\partial s \partial r^2}$. 5\. $u = \sin{(\theta^2 \phi)}$; verify $\dfrac{\partial^3 u}{\partial \theta \partial \phi^2} = \dfrac{\partial^3 u}{\partial \phi^2 \partial \theta}$. 6\. $u = 6\,e^{xy} y^2 z + 3\,e^{yz} x^2 z^2 + 2\,e^{zx} x^3 y - xyz$; show that $\dfrac{\partial^4 u}{\partial x^2 \partial y \partial z} = 12\,(e^{xy} y + e^{yz} z + e^{zx} x)$. 7\. $u = e^{xyz}$; show that $\dfrac{\partial^3 u}{\partial x \partial y \partial z} = (1 + 3\,xyz + x^2 y^2 z^2)u$. 8\. $u = \dfrac{x^2 y^2}{x + y}$; show that $x\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + y\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y} = 2\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}$. 9\. $u = (x^2 + y^2)^{\frac{1}{3}}$; show that $3\,x\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x \partial y} + 3\,y\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 0$. 10\. $u = y^2 z^2 e^{\frac{x}{2}} + z^2 x^2 e^{\frac{y}{2}} + x^2 y^2 e^{\frac{z}{2}}$; show that $\dfrac{\partial^6 u}{\partial x^2 \partial y^2 \partial z^2} = e^{\frac{x}{2}} + e^{\frac{y}{2}} + e^{\frac{z}{2}}$. 11\. $u = (x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$; show that $\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial z^2} = 0$.
