CHAPTER XX: APPLICATIONS TO GEOMETRY OF SPACE

160. Tangent line and normal plane to a skew curve whose equations are given in parametric form. The student is already familiar with the parametric representation of a plane curve. In order to extend this notion to curves in space, let the coördinates of any point \(P\,(x,\,y,\,z)\) on a skew curve be given as functions of some fourth variable which we shall denote by \(t\), thus,

\[(A)\quad x=\phi\,(t),\quad y=\psi\,(t),\quad z=\chi\,(t).\]

The elimination of the parameter \(t\) between these equations two by two will give us the equations of the projecting cylinders of the curve on the coördinate planes.

Let the point \(P(x,\,y,\,z)\) correspond to the value \(t\) of the parameter, and the point \(P'(x+\Delta x,\,y+\Delta y,\,z+\Delta z)\) correspond to the value \(t+\Delta t\); \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\), \(\Delta z\) being the increments of \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) due to the increment \(\Delta t\) as found from equations \((A)\). From Analytic Geometry of three dimensions we know that the direction cosines of the secant (diagonal) \(PP'\) are proportional to

\[\Delta x,\quad \Delta y,\quad \Delta z;\]

or, dividing through by \(\Delta t\) and denoting the direction angles of the secant by \(\alpha'\), \(\beta'\), \(\gamma'\),

\[\cos\alpha' : \cos\beta' : \cos\gamma' :: \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} : \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta t} : \frac{\Delta z}{\Delta t}.\]

Now let \(P'\) approach \(P\) along the curve. Then \(\Delta t\), and therefore also \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\), \(\Delta z\), will approach zero as a limit, the secant \(PP'\) will approach the tangent line to the curve at \(P\) as a limiting position, and we shall have

\[\cos\alpha : \cos\beta : \cos\gamma :: \frac{dx}{dt} : \frac{dy}{dt} : \frac{dz}{dt},\]

where \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\) are the direction angles of the tangent (or curve) at \(P\). Hence the equations of the tangent line to the curve \[x=\phi(t), \quad y=\psi(t), \quad z=\chi(t)\] at the point \((x, y, z)\) are given by \[(69)\qquad \frac{X-x}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}}=\frac{Y-y}{\dfrac{dy}{dt}}=\frac{Z-z}{\dfrac{dz}{dt}};\] and the equation of the normal plane, i.e. the plane passing through \((x, y, z)\) perpendicular to the tangent, is \[(70)\qquad \frac{dx}{dt}(X-x)+\frac{dy}{dt}(Y-y)+\frac{dz}{dt}(Z-z)=0,\] \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) being the variable coördinates.

Illustrative Example 1. Find the equations of the tangent and the equation of the normal plane to the helix\(^*\) (\(\theta\) being the parameter) \[\left\{\begin{array}{l} x=a\cos\theta, \\ y=a\sin\theta, \\ z=b\theta, \end{array}\right.\] (a) at any point; (b) when \(\theta=2\pi\).

Solution. \(\dfrac{dx}{d\theta}=-a\sin\theta=-y, \quad \dfrac{dy}{d\theta}=a\cos\theta=x, \quad \dfrac{dz}{d\theta}=b.\)

Substituting in (69) and (70), we get at \((x, y, z)\) \[\frac{X-x}{-y}=\frac{Y-y}{x}=\frac{Z-z}{b}, \text{ tangent line;}\] and \(-y(X-x)+x(Y-y)+b(Z-z)=0\), normal plane.

When \(\theta=2\pi\), the point of contact is \((a, 0, 2b\pi)\), giving \[\frac{X-a}{0}=\frac{Y-0}{a}=\frac{Z-2b\pi}{b},\] or, \[X=a, \quad bY=aZ-2ab\pi,\] the equations of the tangent line; and \[aY+bZ-2b^2\pi=0,\] the equation of the normal plane.

\(^*\) The helix may be defined as a curve traced on a right circular cylinder so as to cut all the elements at the same angle.

Take \(OZ\) as the axis of the cylinder, and the point of starting in \(OX\) at \(P_0\). Let \(a=\) radius of base of cylinder and \(\theta=\) angle of rotation. By definition, \[\frac{PN}{SN}=\frac{PN}{\text{arc }P_0N}=\frac{z}{a\theta}=k\,\text{(const.)}, \quad\text{or}\quad z=ak\theta.\] Let \(ak=b\); then \(z=b\theta\). Also \(y=MN=a\sin\theta\), \(x=OM=a\cos\theta\).

EXAMPLES

Find the equations of the tangent line and the equation of the normal plane to each of the following skew curves at the point indicated:

1. \(x = 2\,t,\ y = t^2,\ z = 4\,t^4;\ t = 1.\) Ans. \(\dfrac{x-2}{2} = \dfrac{y-1}{2} = \dfrac{z-4}{16};\ x + y + 8\,z - 35 = 0.\)

2. \(x = t^2 - 1,\ y = t + 1,\ z = t^3;\ t = 2.\) Ans. \(\dfrac{x-3}{4} = \dfrac{y-3}{1} = \dfrac{z-8}{12};\ 4\,x + y + 12\,z - 111 = 0.\)

3. \(x = t^3 - 1,\ y = t + t^2,\ z = 4\,t^3 - 3\,t + 1;\ t = 1.\) Ans. \(\dfrac{x}{3} = \dfrac{y-2}{3} = \dfrac{z-2}{9};\ x + y + 3\,z - 8 = 0.\)

4. \(x = t,\ y = \sin t,\ z = \cos t;\ t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.\) Ans. \(\dfrac{4\,x - \pi}{4} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}\,y - 1}{1} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}\,z - 1}{-1};\ 16\,x + \sqrt{2}\,y - \sqrt{2}\,z - 4\,\pi = 0.\)

5. \(x = at,\ y = bt^2,\ z = ct^3;\ t = 1.\)

6. \(x = t,\ y = 1 - t^2,\ z = 3\,t^2 + 4\,t;\ t = -2.\)

7. \(x = t,\ y = e^t,\ z = e^{-t};\ t = 0.\)

8. \(x = a\sin t,\ y = b\cos t,\ z = t;\ t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.\)

9. Find the direction cosines of the tangent to the curve \(x = t^2,\ y = t^3,\ z = t^4\) at point \(x = 1\).

161. Tangent plane to a surface. A straight line is said to be tangent to a surface at a point \(P\) if it is the limiting position of a secant through \(P\) and a neighboring point \(P'\) on the surface, when \(P'\) is made to approach \(P\) along the surface. We now proceed to establish a theorem of fundamental importance.

Theorem. All tangent lines to a surface at a given point\({}^{*}\) lie in general in a plane called the tangent plane at that point.

Proof. Let

\[(A) \qquad\qquad F(x,\,y,\,z) = 0\]

be the equation of the given surface, and let \(P(x,\,y,\,z)\) be the given point on the surface. If now \(P'\) be made to approach \(P\) along a curve \(C\) lying on the surface and passing through \(P\) and \(P'\), then evidently the secant \(PP'\) approaches the position of a tangent to the curve \(C\) at \(P\). Now let the equations of the curve \(C\) be

\[(B) \qquad\qquad x = \phi(t),\quad y = \psi(t),\quad z = \chi(t).\]

\({}^{*}\) The point in question is assumed to be an ordinary (nonsingular) point of the surface, i.e. \(\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial x},\ \dfrac{\partial F}{\partial y},\ \dfrac{\partial F}{\partial z}\) are not all zero at the point.

Then the equation \((A)\) must be satisfied identically by these values, and since the total differential of \((A)\) when \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) are defined by \((B)\) must vanish, we have \[(C)\qquad \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt}+\frac{\partial F}{\partial z}\frac{dz}{dt}=0. \qquad \text{By (\textbf{52}), p.~196}\] This equation shows that the tangent line to \(C\), whose direction cosines are proportional to \[\frac{dx}{dt},\quad \frac{dy}{dt},\quad \frac{dz}{dt},\] is perpendicular \(^{*}\) to a line whose direction cosines are determined by the ratios \[\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}:\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}:\frac{\partial F}{\partial z};\] and since \(C\) is any curve on the surface through \(P\), it follows at once, if we replace the point \(P(x, y, z)\) by \(P_1(x_1, y_1, z_1)\), that all tangent lines to the surface at \(P_1\) lie in the plane \(^{\dagger}\) \[(71)\qquad \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}(x-x_1)+\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1}(y-y_1)+\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1}(z-z_1)=0,\ {}^{\ddagger}\] which is then the formula for finding the equation of a plane tangent at \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\) to a surface whose equation is given in the form \[F(x, y, z)=0.\] In case the equation of the surface is given in the form \(z=f(x, y)\), let \[(D)\qquad F(x, y, z)=f(x, y)-z=0.\] Then \[\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial x},\qquad \frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial z}{\partial y},\qquad \frac{\partial F}{\partial z}=-1.\]

\(^{*}\) From Solid Analytic Geometry we know that if two lines having the direction cosines \(\cos\alpha_1\), \(\cos\beta_1\), \(\cos\gamma_1\) and \(\cos\alpha_2\), \(\cos\beta_2\), \(\cos\gamma_2\) are perpendicular, then \[\cos\alpha_1\cos\alpha_2+\cos\beta_1\cos\beta_2+\cos\gamma_1\cos\gamma_2=0.\]

\(^{\dagger}\) The direction cosines of the normal to the plane (71) are proportional to \(\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}\), \(\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1}\), \(\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1}\). Hence from Analytic Geometry we see that \((C)\) is the condition that the tangents whose direction cosines are \(\cos\alpha\), \(\cos\beta\), \(\cos\gamma\) are perpendicular to the normal; i.e. the tangents must lie in the plane.

\(^{\ddagger}\) In agreement with our former practice, \[\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1},\quad \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1},\quad \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1},\quad \frac{\partial z_1}{\partial x_1},\quad \frac{\partial z_1}{\partial y_1}\] denote the values of the partial derivatives at the point \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\).

If we evaluate these at \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\) and substitute in (71), we get \[\frac{\partial z_1}{\partial x_1}(x - x_1) + \frac{\partial z_1}{\partial y_1}(y - y_1) - (z - z_1) = 0, \tag{72}\] which is then the formula for finding the equation of a plane tangent at \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\) to a surface whose equation is given in the form \(z = f(x, y)\).

In §126, p. 197, we found (55) the total differential of a function \(u\) (or \(z\)) of \(x\) and \(y\), namely, \[dz = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\,dx + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\,dy. \tag{E}\]

We have now a means of interpreting this result geometrically. For the tangent plane to the surface \(z = f(x, y)\) at \((x, y, z)\) is, from (72), \[Z - z = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}(X - x) + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}(Y - y), \tag{F}\] \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) denoting the variable coördinates at any point on the plane. If we substitute \[X = x + dx \quad\text{and}\quad Y = y + dy\] in \((F)\), there results \[Z - z = \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\,dx + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\,dy. \tag{G}\]

Comparing \((E)\) and \((G)\), we get \[dz = Z - z. \tag{H}\] Hence

Theorem. The total differential of a function \(f(x, y)\) corresponding to the increments \(dx\) and \(dy\) equals the corresponding increment of the \(z\)-coördinate of the tangent plane to the surface \(z = f(x, y)\).

Thus, in the figure, \(PP'\) is the plane tangent to surface \(PQ\) at \(P(x, y, z)\).

Let \[AB = dx \quad\text{and}\quad CD = dy;\] then \[dz = Z - z = DP' - DE = EP'.\]

162. Normal line to a surface. The normal line to a surface at a given point is the line passing through the point perpendicular to the tangent plane to the surface at that point.

The direction cosines of any line perpendicular to the tangent plane (71) are proportional to \[\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}, \qquad \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1}, \qquad \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1}.\] \[\therefore\ \frac{x - x_1}{\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}} = \frac{y - y_1}{\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1}} = \frac{z - z_1}{\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1}} \tag{73}\]

are the equations of the normal line\(^{*}\) to the surface \(F(x,\,y,\,z)=0\) at \((x_1,\,y_1,\,z_1)\).

Similarly, from (72), \[(74)\qquad \frac{x-x_1}{\dfrac{\partial z_1}{\partial x_1}}=\frac{y-y_1}{\dfrac{\partial z_1}{\partial y_1}}=\frac{z-z_1}{-1}\] are the equations of the normal line\(^{*}\) to the surface \(z=f(x,\,y)\) at \((x_1,\,y_1,\,z_1)\).

EXAMPLES

1. Find the equation of the tangent plane and the equations of the normal line to the sphere \(x^2+y^2+z^2=14\) at the point \((1,\,2,\,3)\).

Solution. Let \(F(x,\,y,\,z)=x^2+y^2+z^2-14\);

then \[\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=2\,x,\ \frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=2\,y,\ \frac{\partial F}{\partial z}=2\,z;\ x_1=1,\ y_1=2,\ z_1=3.\] \[\therefore\ \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}=2,\ \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1}=4,\ \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1}=6.\]

Substituting in (71), \(2\,(x-1)+4\,(y-2)+6\,(z-3)=0\), \(x+2\,y+3\,z=14\), the tangent plane.

Substituting in (73), \[\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-3}{6},\] giving \(z=3\,x\) and \(2\,z=3\,y\), equations of the normal line.

2. Find the equation of the tangent plane and the equations of the normal line to the ellipsoid \(4\,x^2+9\,y^2+36\,z^2=36\) at point of contact where \(x=2\), \(y=1\), and \(z\) is positive. Ans. Tangent plane, \(8\,(x-2)+9(y-1)+6\sqrt{11}\,(z-\tfrac{1}{6}\sqrt{11})=0\); normal line, \(\dfrac{x-2}{8}=\dfrac{y-1}{9}=\dfrac{z-\frac{1}{6}\sqrt{11}}{6\sqrt{11}}\).

3. Find the equation of the tangent plane to the elliptic parabola \(z=2\,x^2+4\,y^2\) at the point \((2,\,1,\,12)\). Ans. \(8\,x+8\,y-z=12\).

4. Find the equations of the normal line to the hyperboloid of one sheet \(x^2-4\,y^2+2\,z^2=6\) at \((2,\,2,\,3)\). Ans. \(y+4\,x=10\), \(3\,x-z=3\).

5. Find the equation of the tangent plane to the hyperboloid of two sheets \(\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}-\dfrac{z^2}{c^2}=1\) at \((x_1,\,y_1,\,z_1)\). Ans. \(\dfrac{x_1x}{a^2}-\dfrac{y_1y}{b^2}-\dfrac{z_1z}{c^2}=1\).

6. Find the equation of the tangent plane at the point \((x_1,\,y_1,\,z_1)\) on the surface \(ax^2+by^2+cz^2+d=0\). Ans. \(ax_1x+by_1y+cz_1z+d=0\).

7. Show that the equation of the plane tangent to the sphere \[x^2+y^2+z^2+2\,Lx+2\,My+2\,Nz+D=0\] at the point \((x_1,\,y_1,\,z_1)\) is \[x_1x+y_1y+z_1z+L\,(x+x_1)+M\,(y+y_1)+N\,(z+z_1)+D=0.\]

\(^{*}\) See second footnote, p. 265.

8. Find the equation of the tangent plane at any point of the surface \[x^{\frac{2}{3}} + y^{\frac{2}{3}} + z^{\frac{2}{3}} = a^{\frac{2}{3}},\] and show that the sum of the squares of the intercepts on the axes made by the tangent plane is constant.

9. Prove that the tetrahedron formed by the coördinate planes and any tangent plane to the surface \(xyz = a^3\) is of constant volume.

10. Find the equation of the tangent plane and the equations of the normal line to the following surfaces at the points indicated:

(a) \(2x^2 + 4y^2 - z = 0\); \((2, 1, 12)\).

(b) \(x^2 + 4y^2 - z^2 = 16\); \((1, 2, -1)\).

(c) \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 11\); \((3, 1, 1)\).

(d) \(3x^2 + y^2 - 2z = 0\); \(x = 1\), \(y = 1\).

(e) \(x^2y^2 + 2x + z^3 = 16\); \(x = 2\), \(y = 1\).

(f) \(x^2 + 3y^2 + 2z^2 = 9\); \(y = 1\), \(z = 1\).

163. Another form of the equations of the tangent line to a skew curve. If the curve in question be the curve of intersection \(AB\) of the two surfaces \(F(x, y, z) = 0\) and \(G(x, y, z) = 0\), the tangent line \(PT\) at \(P(x_1, y_1, z_1)\) is the intersection of the tangent planes \(CD\) and \(CE\) at that point, for it is also tangent to both surfaces and hence must lie in both tangent planes. The equations of the two tangent planes at \(P\) are, from (71),

\[\mathrm{(75)}\quad \left\{\begin{array}{l} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}(x - x_1) + \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1}(y - y_1) + \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1}(z - z_1) = 0, \\[2ex] \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial x_1}(x - x_1) + \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial y_1}(y - y_1) + \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial z_1}(z - z_1) = 0. \end{array}\right.\]

Taken simultaneously, the equations (75) are the equations of the tangent line \(PT\) to the skew curve \(AB\). Equations (75) in more compact form are

\[\mathrm{(76)}\quad \frac{x - x_1}{\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1}\dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial z_1} - \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1}\dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial y_1}} = \frac{y - y_1}{\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1}\dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial x_1} - \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}\dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial z_1}} = \frac{z - z_1}{\dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}\dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial y_1} - \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1}\dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial x_1}},\]

or,

\[\mathrm{(77)}\quad \frac{x - x_1}{\left|\begin{array}{cc} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1} & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1} \\[2ex] \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial y_1} & \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial z_1} \end{array}\right|} = \frac{y - y_1}{\left|\begin{array}{cc} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1} & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1} \\[2ex] \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial z_1} & \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial x_1} \end{array}\right|} = \frac{z - z_1}{\left|\begin{array}{cc} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1} \\[2ex] \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial y_1} \end{array}\right|},\]

using the notation of determinants.

164. Another form of the equation of the normal plane to a skew curve. The normal plane to a skew curve at a given point has already been defined as the plane passing through that point perpendicular to the tangent line to the curve at that point. Thus, in the above figure, \(PHI\) is the normal plane to the curve \(AB\) at \(P\). Since this plane is perpendicular to (77), we have at once

\[(78)\quad \left|\begin{array}{cc} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1} & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1} \\[2ex] \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial y_1} & \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial z_1} \end{array}\right| (x - x_1) + \left|\begin{array}{cc} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1} & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1} \\[2ex] \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial z_1} & \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial x_1} \end{array}\right| (y - y_1) + \left|\begin{array}{cc} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1} \\[2ex] \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial x_1} & \dfrac{\partial G_1}{\partial y_1} \end{array}\right| (z - z_1) = 0.\]

the equation of the normal plane to a skew curve.

Examples

1. Find the equations of the tangent line and the equation of the normal plane at \((r, r, r\sqrt{2})\) to the curve of intersection of the sphere and cylinder whose equations are respectively \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 4\,r^2\), \(x^2 + y^2 = 2\,rx\).

Solution. Let \(F = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 4\,r^2\) and \(G = x^2 + y^2 - 2\,rx\).

\[\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1} = 2\,r, \qquad \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1} = 2\,r, \qquad \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1} = 2\sqrt{2}\,r;\] \[\frac{\partial G_1}{\partial x_1} = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial G_1}{\partial y_1} = 2\,r, \qquad \frac{\partial G_1}{\partial z_1} = 0.\]

Substituting in (77),

\[\frac{x - r}{-\sqrt{2}} = \frac{y - r}{0} = \frac{z - r\sqrt{2}}{1};\]

or, \(\quad y = r, \; x + \sqrt{2}\,z = 3\,r,\)

the equations of the tangent \(PT\) at \(P\) to the curve of intersection.

Substituting in (78), we get the equation of the normal plane,

\[-\sqrt{2}\,(x - r) + 0\,(y - r) + (z - r\sqrt{2}) = 0,\]

or, \(\qquad \sqrt{2}\,x - z = 0.\)

2. Find the equations of the tangent line to the circle

\[x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 25,\] \[x + z = 5,\]

at the point \((2, 2\sqrt{3}, 3)\). Ans. \(2\,x + 2\sqrt{3}\,y + 3\,z = 25,\; x + z = 5.\)

3. Find the equation of the normal plane to the curve

\[x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = r^2,\] \[x^2 - rx + y^2 = 0,\]

at \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\). Ans. \(2\,y_1 z_1 x - (2\,x_1 - r)\,z_1 y - r y_1 z = 0.\)

4. Find the equations of the tangent line and the normal plane to the curve \[2\,x^2 + 3\,y^2 + z^2 = 9, \quad z^2 = 3\,x^2 + y^2\] at \((1, -1, 2)\).

5. Find the direction of the curve \[xyz = 1, \quad y^2 = x\] at the point \((1, 1, 1)\).

6. What is the direction of the tangent to the curve \[y = x^2, \quad z^2 = 1 - y\] at \((0, 0, 1)\)?

7. The equations of a helix (spiral) are \[x^2 + y^2 = r^2,\] \[y = x \tan \frac{z}{c}.\] Show that at the point \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\) the equations of the tangent line are \[c\,(x - x_1) + y_1\,(z - z_1) = 0,\] \[c\,(y - y_1) - x_1\,(z - z_1) = 0\,;\] and the equation of the normal plane is \[y_1 x - x_1 y - c\,(z - z_1) = 0.\]

8. A skew curve is formed by the intersection of the cone \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 0\) and the sphere \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = r^2\). Show that at the point \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\) the equations of the tangent line to the curve are \[c^2\,(a^2 - b^2)\,x_1\,(x - x_1) = -\,a^2\,(b^2 + c^2)\,z_1\,(z - z_1),\] \[c^2\,(a^2 - b^2)\,y_1\,(y - y_1) = +\,b^2\,(c^2 + a^2)\,z_1\,(z - z_1)\,;\] and the equation of the normal plane is \[a^2\,(b^2 + c^2)\,y_1 z_1 x - b^2\,(c^2 + a^2)\,z_1 x_1 y - c^2\,(a^2 - b^2)\,x_1 y_1 z = 0.\]

\chapter*{CHAPTER XXII: INTEGRATION. RULES FOR INTEGRATING STANDARD ELEMENTARY FORMS}

\begin{center}
{\Large INTEGRAL CALCULUS}
\end{center}

\textbf{165. Integration.} The student is already familiar with the mutually inverse operations of addition and subtraction, multiplication and division, involution and evolution. In the examples which follow, the second members of one column are respectively the inverse of the second members of the other column:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
y = x^2 + 1, & \qquad x = \pm\sqrt{y-1}; \\
y = a^x, & \qquad x = \log_a y; \\
y = \sin x, & \qquad x = \operatorname{arc\,sin} y.
\end{array}
\]

From the Differential Calculus we have learned how to calculate the derivative $f'(x)$ of a given function $f(x)$, an operation indicated by
\[
\frac{d}{dx} f(x) = f'(x),
\]
or, if we are using differentials, by
\[
df(x) = f'(x)\,dx.
\]

The problems of the Integral Calculus depend on the \textit{inverse operation}, namely:

\textit{To find a function $f(x)$ whose derivative}
\[
(A) \qquad f'(x) = \phi(x)
\]
\textit{is given.}

Or, since it is customary to use differentials in the Integral Calculus, we may write
\[
(B) \qquad df(x) = f'(x)\,dx = \phi(x)\,dx,
\]
and state the problem as follows:

\textit{Having given the differential of a function, to find the function itself.}

The function $f(x)$ thus found is called an \textit{integral}\,$^{*}$ of the given differential expression, the process of finding it is called \textit{integration}, and the operation is indicated by writing the \textit{integral sign}$^{\dagger}$ $\int$ in front of the given differential expression; thus
\[
(C)\qquad \int f'(x)\,dx^{\ddagger} = f(x),
\]
read \textit{an integral of $f'(x)\,dx$ equals $f(x)$}. The differential $dx$ indicates that $x$ is \textit{the variable of integration}. For example,

(a) If $f(x) = x^3$, then $f'(x)\,dx = 3\,x^2dx$, and
\[
\int 3\,x^2dx = x^3.
\]

(b) If $f(x) = \sin x$, then $f'(x)\,dx = \cos xdx$, and
\[
\int \cos xdx = \sin x.
\]

(c) If $f(x) = \text{arc tan}\,x$, then $f'(x)\,dx = \dfrac{dx}{1+x^2}$, and
\[
\int \frac{dx}{1+x^2} = \text{arc tan}\,x.
\]

Let us now emphasize what is apparent from the preceding explanations, namely, that

\textit{Differentiation and integration are inverse operations.}

Differentiating $(C)$ gives
\[
(D)\qquad d\int f'(x)\,dx = f'(x)\,dx.
\]

Substituting the value of $f'(x)\,dx\,[= df(x)]$ from $(B)$ in $(C)$, we get
\[
(E)\qquad \int df(x) = f(x).
\]

Therefore, considered as symbols of operation, $\dfrac{d}{dx}$ and $\int \cdots dx$ are \textit{inverse to each other}; or, if we are using differentials, $d$ and $\int$ are inverse to each other.

$^{*}$ Called \textit{anti-differential} by some writers.

$\dagger$ Historically this sign is a distorted $S$, the initial letter of the word \textit{sum}. Instead of defining integration as the inverse of differentiation, we may define it as a process of summation, a very important notion which we will consider in Chapter XXVIII.

$\ddagger$ Some authors write this $D_x^{-1}f'(x)$ when they wish to emphasize the fact that it is an inverse operation.

When $d$ is followed by $\int$ they annul each other, as in $(D)$, but when $\int$ is followed by $d$, as in $(E)$, that will not in general be the case unless we ignore the \textit{constant of integration}. The reason for this will appear at once from the definition of the constant of integration given in the next section.

\textbf{166. Constant of integration. Indefinite integral.} From the preceding section it follows that
\[ \text{since } d\,(x^3) \phantom{{}+2}= 3\,x^2dx, \text{ we have } \int 3\,x^2dx = x^3; \]
\[ \text{since } d\,(x^3+2) = 3\,x^2dx, \text{ we have } \int 3\,x^2dx = x^3+2; \]
\[ \text{since } d\,(x^3-7) = 3\,x^2dx, \text{ we have } \int 3\,x^2dx = x^3-7. \]
In fact, since
\[ d\,(x^3+C) = 3\,x^2dx, \]
where $C$ is any arbitrary constant, we have
\[ \int 3\,x^2dx = x^3+C. \]
A constant $C$ arising in this way is called a \textit{constant of integration}.$^{*}$ Since we can give $C$ as many values as we please, it follows that if a given differential expression has one integral, it has infinitely many differing only by constants. Hence
\[ \int f'(x)\,dx = f(x)+C; \]
and since $C$ is unknown and \textit{indefinite}, the expression
\[ f(x)+C \]
is called the \textit{indefinite integral of $f'(x)\,dx$}.

It is evident that if $\phi\,(x)$ is a function the derivative of which is $f(x)$, then $\phi\,(x)+C$, where $C$ is any constant whatever, is likewise a function the derivative of which is $f(x)$. Hence the

\textbf{Theorem.} \textit{If two functions differ by a constant, they have the same derivative.}

It is, however, not obvious that if $\phi\,(x)$ is a function the derivative of which is $f(x)$, then \textit{all} functions having the same derivative $f(x)$ are of the form
\[ \phi\,(x)+C, \]
where $C$ is any constant. In other words, there remains to be proved the

$^{*}$ Constant here means that it is independent of the \textit{variable of integration}.

\textbf{Converse theorem.} \textit{If two functions have the same derivative, their difference is a constant.}

\textbf{Proof.} Let $\phi(x)$ and $\psi(x)$ be two functions having the common derivative $f(x)$. Place
\[ F(x)=\phi(x)-\psi(x); \text{ then} \]
\[ (A)\qquad F'(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\left[\phi(x)-\psi(x)\right]=f(x)-f(x)=0. \quad \text{By hypothesis} \]

But from the Theorem of Mean Value \textbf{(46)}, p. 166, we have
\[ F(x+\Delta x)-F(x)=\Delta x\,F'(x+\theta\cdot\Delta x). \qquad 0<\theta<1 \]
\[ \therefore\ F(x+\Delta x)-F(x)=0, \]
[Since by $(A)$ the derivative of $F(x)$ is zero for all values of $x$.]

and
\[ F(x+\Delta x)=F(x). \]

This means that the function
\[ F(x)=\phi(x)-\psi(x) \]
does not change in value at all when $x$ takes on the increment $\Delta x$, i.e. $\phi(x)$ and $\psi(x)$ differ only by a constant.

In any given case the value of $C$ can be found when we know the value of the integral for some value of the variable, and this will be illustrated by numerous examples in the next chapter. For the present we shall content ourselves with first learning how to find the indefinite integrals of given differential expressions. In what follows we shall assume that \textit{every continuous function has an indefinite integral}, a statement the rigorous proof of which is beyond the scope of this book. For all elementary functions, however, the truth of the statement will appear in the chapters which follow.

In all cases of indefinite integration the test to be applied in verifying the results is that \textit{the differential of the integral must be equal to the given differential expression.}

\textbf{167. Rules for integrating standard elementary forms.} The Differential Calculus furnished us with a \textit{General Rule} for differentiation (p. 29). The Integral Calculus gives us no corresponding general rule that can be readily applied in practice for performing the inverse operation of integration.$^{*}$ Each case requires special treatment and we arrive at the integral of a given differential expression through

$^{*}$ Even though the integral of a given differential expression may be known to exist, yet it may not be possible for us actually to find it in terms of known functions, because there are functions other than the elementary functions whose derivatives are elementary functions.

our previous knowledge of the known results of differentiation. That is, we must be able to answer the question, \textit{What function, when differentiated, will yield the given differential expression?}

Integration then is essentially a tentative process, and to expedite the work, tables of known integrals are formed called \textit{standard forms.} To effect any integration we compare the given differential expression with these forms, and if it is found to be identical with one of them, the integral is known. If it is not identical with one of them, we strive to reduce it to one of the standard forms by various methods, many of which employ artifices which can be suggested by practice only. Accordingly a large portion of our treatise on the Integral Calculus will be devoted to the explanation of methods for integrating those functions which frequently appear in the process of solving practical problems.

From any result of differentiation may always be derived a formula for integration.

The following two rules are useful in reducing differential expressions to standard forms:

(a) \textit{The integral of any algebraic sum of differential expressions equals the same algebraic sum of the integrals of these expressions taken separately.}

\textbf{Proof.} Differentiating the expression
\[
\int du + \int dv - \int dw,
\]
$u, v, w$ being functions of a single variable, we get
\[
du + dv - dw. \qquad \text{By \textsc{iii}, p. 34}
\]
(1)
\[
\therefore \int (du + dv - dw) = \int du + \int dv - \int dw.
\]

(b) \textit{A constant factor may be written either before or after the integral sign.}

\textbf{Proof.} Differentiating the expression
\[
a \int dv
\]
gives
\[

On account of their importance we shall write the above two rules as formulas at the head of the following list of


\textsc{Standard Elementary Forms}

(1) \[ \int (du + dv - dw) = \int du + \int dv - \int dw. \]

(2) \[ \int a\,dv = a \int dv. \]

(3) \[ \int dx = x + C. \]

(4) \[ \int v^{n}dv = \frac{v^{n+1}}{n+1} + C. \qquad n \neq -1 \]

(5) \[ \begin{aligned}
\int \frac{dv}{v} &= \log v + C \\
&= \log v + \log c = \log cv.
\end{aligned} \]
[Placing $C = \log c$.]

(6) \[ \int a^{v}dv = \frac{a^{v}}{\log a} + C. \]

(7) \[ \int e^{v}dv = e^{v} + C. \]

(8) \[ \int \sin v \, dv = -\cos v + C. \]

(9) \[ \int \cos v \, dv = \sin v + C. \]

(10) \[ \int \sec^{2} v \, dv = \tan v + C. \]

(11) \[ \int \csc^{2} v \, dv = -\cot v + C. \]

(12) \[ \int \sec v \tan v \, dv = \sec v + C. \]

(13) \[ \int \csc v \cot v \, dv = -\csc v + C. \]

(14) \[ \int \tan v \, dv = \log \sec v + C. \]

(15) \[ \int \cot v \, dv = \log \sin v + C. \]

(16) \[ \int \sec v \, dv = \log (\sec v + \tan v) + C. \]

(17) \[ \int \csc v \, dv = \log (\csc v - \cot v) + C. \]


\[ \text{(18)}\qquad \int\frac{dv}{v^{2}+a^{2}}=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{v}{a}+C. \]
\[ \text{(19)}\qquad \int\frac{dv}{v^{2}-a^{2}}=\frac{1}{2\,a}\log\frac{v-a}{v+a}+C. \]
\[ \text{(20)}\qquad \int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{a^{2}-v^{2}}}=\operatorname{arc\,sin}\frac{v}{a}+C. \]
\[ \text{(21)}\qquad \int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}\pm a^{2}}}=\log\left(v+\sqrt{v^{2}\pm a^{2}}\right)+C. \]
\[ \text{(22)}\qquad \int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{2\,av-v^{2}}}=\operatorname{arc\,vers}\frac{v}{a}+C. \]
\[ \text{(23)}\qquad \int\frac{dv}{v\sqrt{v^{2}-a^{2}}}=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,sec}\frac{v}{a}+C. \]

\textbf{Proof of (3).} Since
\[ d(x+C)=dx, \qquad \textbf{II}\text{, p. 34} \]
we get
\[ \int dx=x+C. \]

\textbf{Proof of (4).} Since
\[ d\left(\frac{v^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\right)=v^{n}dv, \qquad \textbf{VI}\text{, p. 34} \]
we get
\[ \int v^{n}dv=\frac{v^{n+1}}{n+1}+C. \]

This holds true for all values of $n$ except $n=-1$. For, when $n=-1$, (4) gives
\[ \int v^{-1}dv=\frac{v^{-1+1}}{-1+1}+C=\frac{1}{0}+C=\infty+C, \]
which has no meaning.

The case when $n=-1$ comes under (5).

\textbf{Proof of (5).} Since
\[ d(\log v+C)=\frac{dv}{v}, \qquad \textbf{VIII}\ \textbf{\textit{a}}\text{, p. 35} \]
we get
\[ \int\frac{dv}{v}=\log v+C. \]

The results we get from (5) may be put in more compact form if we denote the constant of integration by $\log c$. Thus
\[ \int\frac{dv}{v}=\log v+\log c=\log cv. \]

Formula (5) states that \textit{if the expression under the integral sign is a fraction whose numerator is the differential of the denominator, then the integral is the natural logarithm of the denominator.}

\textbf{Proof of (14).}
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int \tan v\,dv &= \int \frac{\sin v\,dv}{\cos v} \\
&= -\int \frac{-\sin v\,dv}{\cos v} \\
&= -\int \frac{d(\cos v)}{\cos v} \\
&= -\log\cos v + C \qquad \text{by (5)} \\
&= \log\sec v + C.
\end{aligned}
\]
[Since $-\log\cos v = -\log\frac{1}{\sec v} = -\log 1 + \log\sec v = \log\sec v.$]

\textbf{Proof of (15).}
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int \cot v\,dv &= \int \frac{\cos v\,dv}{\sin v} = \int \frac{d(\sin v)}{\sin v} \\
&= \log\sin v + C. \qquad \text{By (5)}
\end{aligned}
\]

\textbf{Proof of (16).} Since
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sec v &= \sec v\,\frac{\sec v+\tan v}{\sec v+\tan v} \\
&= \frac{\sec v\tan v+\sec^{2}v}{\sec v+\tan v},
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int \sec v.dv &= \int \frac{\sec v\tan v+\sec^{2}v}{\sec v+\tan v}\,dv \\
&= \int \frac{d(\sec v+\tan v)}{\sec v+\tan v} \\
&= \log(\sec v+\tan v)+C. \qquad \text{By (5)}
\end{aligned}
\]

\textbf{Proof of (17).} Since
\[
\begin{aligned}
\csc v &= \csc v\,\frac{\csc v-\cot v}{\csc v-\cot v} \\
&= \frac{-\csc v\cot v+\csc^{2}v}{\csc v-\cot v},
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int \csc v\,dv &= \int \frac{-\csc v\cot v+\csc^{2}v}{\csc v-\cot v}\,dv \\
&= \int \frac{d(\csc v-\cot v)}{\csc v-\cot v} \\
&= \log(\csc v-\cot v)+C. \qquad \text{By (5)}
\end{aligned}
\]

\int \sin 2axdx &= \frac{1}{2a}\int \sin 2ax \cdot 2adx \\
&= \frac{1}{2a}\int \sin 2ax \cdot d(2ax) = \frac{1}{2a}\cdot -\cos 2ax + C. \qquad \text{By (8)} \\
&= -\frac{\cos 2ax}{2a} + C.

\]

\textbf{Proof of (18).} Since

\[
d\left(\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{v}{a}+C\right)=\frac{1}{a}\,\frac{d\left(\dfrac{v}{a}\right)}{1+\left(\dfrac{v}{a}\right)^{2}}=\frac{dv}{v^{2}+a^{2}},\qquad \text{by \textbf{XIII}, p. 35}
\]

we get
\[
\int\frac{dv}{v^{2}+a^{2}}=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{v}{a}+C.*
\]

\textbf{Proof of (19).} Since $\dfrac{1}{v^{2}-a^{2}}=\dfrac{1}{2a}\left(\dfrac{1}{v-a}-\dfrac{1}{v+a}\right),$$^{\dagger}$

\[
\int\frac{dv}{v^{2}-a^{2}}=\frac{1}{2a}\int\left(\frac{1}{v-a}-\frac{1}{v+a}\right)dv
\]
\[
=\frac{1}{2a}\{\log(v-a)-\log(v+a)\}+C \qquad \text{by (5)}
\]
\[
=\frac{1}{2a}\log\frac{v-a}{v+a}+C.
\]

$^{*}$ Also $d\left(\dfrac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,cot}\dfrac{v}{a}+C\right)=-\dfrac{dv}{v^{2}+a^{2}}$ and $\displaystyle\int\frac{dv}{v^{2}+a^{2}}=-\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,cot}\frac{v}{a}+C'.$ Hence

\[
\int\frac{dv}{v^{2}+a^{2}}=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{v}{a}+C=-\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,cot}\frac{v}{a}+C'.
\]

Since $\operatorname{arc\,tan}\dfrac{v}{a}+\operatorname{arc\,cot}\dfrac{v}{a}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, we see that one result may be easily transformed into the other. The same kind of discussion may be given for (20) involving $\operatorname{arc\,sin}\dfrac{v}{a}$ and $\operatorname{arc\,cos}\dfrac{v}{a}$, and for (23) involving $\operatorname{arc\,sec}\dfrac{v}{a}$ and $\operatorname{arc\,csc}\dfrac{v}{a}$.

$^{\dagger}$ By breaking the fraction up into partial fractions (see Case I, p. 325).

\textbf{Proof of (20).} Since
\[
d\left(\operatorname{arc\,sin}\frac{v}{a}+C\right)=\frac{d\left(\frac{v}{a}\right)}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{a}\right)^{2}}}=\frac{av}{\sqrt{a^{2}-v^{2}}},\qquad \text{by \textbf{XVIII}, p. 35}
\]
we get
\[
\int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{a^{2}-v^{2}}}=\operatorname{arc\,sin}\frac{v}{a}+C.
\]

\textbf{Proof of (21).} Assume $v=a\tan z$, where $z$ is a new variable; differentiating, $dv=a\sec^{2}z\,dz$. Hence, by substitution,
\[
\int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}+a^{2}}}=\int\frac{a\sec^{2}z\,dz}{\sqrt{a^{2}\tan^{2}z+a^{2}}}=\int\frac{\sec^{2}z\,dz}{\sqrt{\tan^{2}z+1}}
\]
\[
=\int\sec z\,dz=\log(\sec z+\tan z)+C\qquad\text{by (\textbf{16})}
\]
\[
=\log\left(\tan z+\sqrt{\tan^{2}z+1}\right)+c.\qquad\text{By 28, p. 2}
\]
But $\tan z=\frac{v}{a}$; hence,
\[
\int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}+a^{2}}}=\log\left(\frac{v}{a}+\sqrt{\frac{v^{2}}{a^{2}}+1}\right)+c
\]
\[
=\log\frac{v+\sqrt{v^{2}+a^{2}}}{a}+c
\]
\[
=\log\left(v+\sqrt{v^{2}+a^{2}}\right)-\log a+c.
\]
Placing $C=-\log a+c$, we get
\[
\int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}+a^{2}}}=\log\left(v+\sqrt{v^{2}+a^{2}}\right)+C.
\]
In the same manner, by assuming $v=a\sec z$, $dv=a\sec z\tan z\,dz$
we get
\[
\int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}-a^{2}}}=\int\frac{a\sec z\tan z\,dz}{\sqrt{a^{2}\sec^{2}z-a^{2}}}=\int\sec z\,dz
\]
\[
=\log(\sec z+\tan z)+c\qquad\text{by (\textbf{16})}
\]
\[
=\log\left(\sec z+\sqrt{\sec^{2}z-1}\right)+c\qquad\text{by 28, p. 2}
\]
\[
=\log\left(\frac{v}{a}+\sqrt{\frac{v^{2}}{a^{2}}-1}\right)+c=\log\left(v+\sqrt{v^{2}-a^{2}}\right)+C.
\]

\textbf{Proofs of (22) and (23).} These follow at once from the corresponding formulas for differentiation, \textbf{XXII} and \textbf{XXIV}, p. 36.

\textbf{168. Trigonometric differentials.} We shall now consider some trigonometric differentials of frequent occurrence which may be readily integrated by being transformed into standard forms by means of simple trigonometric reductions.

\textbf{Example I.} \textit{To find} $\int \sin^m x \cos^n x\,dx$.

When either $m$ or $n$ is a positive odd integer, no matter what the other may be, this integration may be performed by means of formula (\textbf{4}),
\[ \int v^n\,dv = \frac{v^{n+1}}{n+1}. \]

For the integral is reducible to the form
\[ \int (\textit{terms involving only cos } x)\,\textit{sin } x\,dx, \]
when \textit{sin x} has the odd exponent, and to the form
\[ \int (\textit{terms involving only sin } x)\,\textit{cos } x\,dx, \]
when \textit{cos x} has the odd exponent. We shall illustrate this by means of examples.

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Find $\int \sin^2 x \cos^5 x\,dx$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int \sin^2 x \cos^5 x\,dx &= \int \sin^2 x \cos^4 x \cos x\,dx \\
&= \int \sin^2 x\,(1-\sin^2 x)^2 \cos x\,dx \qquad \text{by 28, p. 2} \\
&= \int (\sin^2 x - 2\sin^4 x + \sin^6 x)\cos x\,dx \\
&= \int (\sin x)^2 \cos x\,dx - 2\int (\sin x)^4 \cos x\,dx + \int (\sin x)^6 \cos x\,dx \\
&= \frac{\sin^3 x}{3} - \frac{2\sin^5 x}{5} + \frac{\sin^7 x}{7} + C. \qquad \text{By (4)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here $v = \sin x$, $dv = \cos x\,dx$, and $n = 2$, 4, and 6 respectively.

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 2. Find $\int \cos^3 x\,dx$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int \cos^3 x\,dx &= \int \cos^2 x \cos x\,dx = \int (1-\sin^2 x)\cos x\,dx \\
&= \int \cos x\,dx - \int \sin^2 x \cos x\,dx \\
&= \sin x - \frac{\sin^3 x}{3} + C.
\end{aligned}
\]

\textsc{Examples}

1. $\int \sin^3 x\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\cos^3 x - \cos x + C.$

2. $\int \sin^2 x \cos x\,dx = \frac{\sin^3 x}{3} + C.$

3. $\int \sin x \cos x\,dx = \frac{\sin^2 x}{2} + C.*$

4. $\int \cos^2 \alpha \sin \alpha\,d\alpha = -\frac{\cos^3 \alpha}{3} + C.$

5. $\int \sin^3 6\theta \cos 6\theta\,d\theta = \frac{\sin^4 6\theta}{24} + C.$

6. $\int \cos^3 2\theta \sin 2\theta\,d\theta = -\frac{\cos^4 2\theta}{8} + C.$

7. $\int \frac{\cos^3 x\,dx}{\sin^4 x} = \csc x - \frac{1}{3}\csc^3 x + C.$

8. $\int \frac{\sin^3 \alpha\,d\alpha}{\cos^2 \alpha} = \sec \alpha + \cos \alpha + C.$

9. $\int \cos^4 x \sin^3 x\,dx = -\frac{1}{5}\cos^5 x + \frac{1}{7}\cos^7 x + C.$

10. $\int \sin^5 x\,dx = -\cos x + \frac{2}{3}\cos^3 x - \frac{\cos^5 x}{5} + C.$

11. $\int \cos^5 x\,dx = \sin x - \frac{2}{3}\sin^3 x + \frac{\sin^5 x}{5} + C.$

12. $\int \sin^{\frac{3}{7}} \phi \cos^3 \phi\,d\phi = \frac{7}{10}\sin^{\frac{10}{7}} \phi - \frac{7}{24}\sin^{\frac{24}{7}} \phi + C.$

$^{*}$ This was integrated by the power formula taking $n=1$, $v=\sin x$, $dv=\cos x\,dx$. To illustrate how an answer may take on different forms when more than one method of integration is possible, let us take $n=1$, $v=\cos x$, $dv=-\sin x\,dx$, and again integrate by the power formula. Then
\[
\int \sin x \cos x\,dx = -\int (\cos x)(-\sin x\,dx) = -\frac{\cos^2 x}{2} + C',
\]
a result which differs from the first one in the arbitrary constant only. For,
\[
-\frac{\cos^2 x}{2} + C' = -\frac{1-\sin^2 x}{2} + C' = -\frac{1}{2} + \frac{\sin^2 x}{2} + C' = \frac{\sin^2 x}{2} - \frac{1}{2} + C'.
\]
Hence, comparing the two answers, $C = -\frac{1}{2} + C'$.

13. $\int \sin^{\frac{2}{3}}\theta\,\cos^5\theta\,d\theta = \frac{3}{5}\sin^{\frac{5}{3}}\theta - \frac{6}{11}\sin^{\frac{11}{3}}\theta + \frac{3}{17}\sin^{\frac{17}{3}}\theta + C.$

14. $\int \frac{\sin^5 y}{\sqrt{\cos y}}\,dy = -2\sqrt{\cos y}\left(1 - \frac{2}{5}\cos^2 y + \frac{1}{9}\cos^4 y\right) + C.$

15. $\int \frac{\cos^5 t\,dt}{\sqrt[3]{\sin t}} = \frac{3}{2}\sin^{\frac{2}{3}} t\left(1 - \frac{1}{2}\sin^2 t + \frac{1}{7}\sin^4 t\right) + C.$

16. Integrate the following expressions and prove your results by differentiation:
(a) $\int \sin^3 2\theta\,d\theta.$
(b) $\int \cos^3\frac{\theta}{2}\,d\theta.$
(c) $\int \sin 2x\,\cos 2x\,dx.$
(d) $\int \sin^3 t\,\cos^3 t\,dt.$
(e) $\int \cos\frac{x}{a}\,\sin\frac{x}{a}\,dx.$
(f) $\int \cos^5 ax\,\sin ax\,dx.$
(g) $\int \sin^2\frac{2x}{3}\,\cos\frac{2x}{3}\,dx.$
(h) $\int \cos^2 3x\,\sin 3x\,dx.$
(i) $\int \sin^5 bs\,\cos bs\,ds.$
(j) $\int \cos^3\frac{\phi}{2}\,\sin^2\frac{\phi}{2}\,d\phi.$
(k) $\int \sin^3 mt\,\cos^2 mt\,dt.$
(l) $\int \sin^5 nt\,dt.$
(m) $\int \sin^4 x\,\cos x\,dx.$
(n) $\int \cos^4 y\,\sin y\,dy.$
(o) $\int \cos^3(a+bt)\,dt.$

\textbf{Example II.} \textit{To find} $\int \tan^n x\,dx$, \textit{or} $\int \cot^n x\,dx$.

These forms can be readily integrated, when $n$ is an integer, on somewhat the same plan as the previous examples.

\textsc{Illustrative Example 1.} Find $\int \tan^4 x\,dx$.

\textbf{Solution.} $\int \tan^4 x\,dx = \int \tan^2 x\,(\sec^2 x - 1)\,dx$ \hfill by 28, p. 2
\[ = \int \tan^2 x\,\sec^2 x\,dx - \int \tan^2 x\,dx \]
\[ = \int (\tan x)^2\,d(\tan x) - \int (\sec^2 x - 1)\,dx \]
\[ = \frac{\tan^3 x}{3} - \tan x + x + C. \]

\textbf{Example III.} \textit{To find} $\int \sec^n x\,dx$, \textit{or} $\int \csc^n x\,dx$.

These can be easily integrated when $n$ is a positive even integer, as follows:

\textsc{Illustrative Example 2.} Find $\int \sec^6 x\,dx$.

\textbf{Solution.} $\int \sec^6 x\,dx = \int (\tan^2 x + 1)^2\,\sec^2 x\,dx$ \hfill by 28, p. 2
\[ = \int (\tan x)^4\,\sec^2 x\,dx + 2\int (\tan x)^2\,\sec^2 x\,dx + \int \sec^2 x\,dx \]
\[ = \frac{\tan^5 x}{5} + 2\,\frac{\tan^3 x}{3} + \tan x + C. \]

When $n$ is an odd positive integer greater than unity, the best plan is to reduce to sine or cosine and then use reduction formulas on p. 303.


\textbf{Example IV.} \textit{To find} $\int \tan^m x \sec^n x\,dx$, \textit{or} $\int \cot^m x \csc^n x\,dx$.

When $n$ is a positive even integer we proceed as in Example III.

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 3. Find $\int \tan^6 x \sec^4 x\,dx$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int \tan^6 x \sec^4 x\,dx &= \int \tan^6 x\,(\tan^2 x + 1)\sec^2 x\,dx && \text{by 28, p. 2}\\
&= \int (\tan x)^8 \sec^2 x\,dx + \int \tan^6 x \sec^2 x\,dx\\
&= \frac{\tan^9 x}{9} + \frac{\tan^7 x}{7} + C. && \text{By (4)}
\end{aligned}
\]

Here $v = \tan x$, $dv = \sec^2 x\,dx$, etc.

When $m$ is odd we may proceed as in the following example.

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 4. Find $\int \tan^5 x \sec^3 x\,dx$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int \tan^5 x \sec^3 x\,dx &= \int \tan^4 x \sec^2 x \sec x \tan x\,dx\\
&= \int (\sec^2 x - 1)^2 \sec^2 x \sec x \tan x\,dx && \text{by 28, p. 2}\\
&= \int (\sec^6 x - 2\sec^4 x + \sec^2 x)\sec x \tan x\,dx\\
&= \frac{\sec^7 x}{7} - \frac{2\sec^5 x}{5} + \frac{\sec^3 x}{3} + C. && \text{By (4)}
\end{aligned}
\]

Here $v = \sec x$, $dv = \sec x \tan x\,dx$, etc.

\textbf{EXAMPLES} 

1. $\int \tan^3 x\,dx = \dfrac{\tan^2 x}{2} + \log \cos x + C.$

2. $\int \tan^2 2x\,dx = \dfrac{\tan 2x}{2} - x + C.$

3. $\int \cot^3 x\,dx = -\dfrac{\cot^2 x}{2} - \log \sin x + C$

4. $\int \cot^2 x\,dx = -\cot x - x + C.$

5. $\int \cot^4 \dfrac{x}{3}\,dx = -\cot^3 \dfrac{x}{3} + 3\cot \dfrac{x}{3} + x + C.$

6. $\int \cot^5 \alpha\,d\alpha = -\tfrac{1}{4}\cot^4 \alpha + \tfrac{1}{2}\cot^2 \alpha + \log \sin \alpha + C.$

7. $\int \tan^5 \dfrac{y}{4}\,dy = \tan^4 \dfrac{y}{4} - 2\tan^2 \dfrac{y}{4} + 4\log \sec \dfrac{y}{4} + C.$

8. $\int \sec^8 x\,dx = \dfrac{\tan^7 x}{7} + \dfrac{3\tan^5 x}{5} + \tan^3 x + \tan x + C.$

9. $\int \csc^6 x\,dx = -\cot x - \tfrac{2}{3}\cot^3 x - \tfrac{1}{5}\cot^5 x + C.$

10. $\int \tan^4 \phi \sec^4 \phi\,d\phi = \dfrac{\tan^7 \phi}{7} + \dfrac{\tan^5 \phi}{5} + C.$

11. $\int \tan^3 \theta \sec^5 \theta\,d\theta = \tfrac{1}{7}\sec^7 \theta - \tfrac{1}{5}\sec^5 \theta + C.$

12. $\int \cot^5 x \csc^4 x\,dx = -\dfrac{\cot^6 x}{6} - \dfrac{\cot^8 x}{8} + C.$

13. $\int \tan^{\frac{3}{2}} x \sec^4 x\,dx = \dfrac{2\tan^{\frac{5}{2}} x}{5} + \dfrac{2\tan^{\frac{9}{2}} x}{9} + C.$

14. $\displaystyle\int \tan^5 y\,\sec^{\frac{3}{2}} y\,dy = 2\sec^{\frac{3}{2}} y\left(\frac{\sec^4 y}{11} - \frac{2\sec^2 y}{7} + \frac{1}{3}\right) + C.$

15. $\displaystyle\int \frac{\sec^6\alpha\,d\alpha}{\tan^4\alpha} = \tan\alpha - 2\cot\alpha - \frac{\cot^3\alpha}{3} + C.$

16. $\displaystyle\int (\tan^2 z + \tan^4 z)\,dz = \tfrac{1}{3}\tan^3 z + C.$

17. $\displaystyle\int (\tan t + \cot t)^3\,dt = \tfrac{1}{2}(\tan^2 t - \cot^2 t) + \log\tan^2 t + C.$

18. Integrate the following expressions and prove your results by differentiation:
(a) $\displaystyle\int \tan^2 2t\,dt.$
(b) $\displaystyle\int \cot^2\frac{t}{2}\,dt.$
(c) $\displaystyle\int \tan^3 ax\,dx.$
(d) $\displaystyle\int \cot^3\frac{x}{a}\,dx.$
(e) $\displaystyle\int \frac{2\,dt}{\tan^4 t}.$
(f) $\displaystyle\int \frac{3\,d\theta}{\cot^2 4\theta}.$
(g) $\displaystyle\int \sec^2\theta\,\tan^2\theta\,d\theta.$
(h) $\displaystyle\int \csc^2\phi\,\cot^2\phi\,d\phi.$
(i) $\displaystyle\int \frac{a\,dx}{\tan^2 4x}.$
(j) $\displaystyle\int \tan^3 t\,\sec^2 t\,dt.$
(k) $\displaystyle\int \cot^5 y\,\csc^2 y\,dy.$
(l) $\displaystyle\int \frac{b\,d\theta}{\cot^3\theta}.$
(m) $\displaystyle\int \frac{\sqrt{\tan x}}{\cos^2 x}\,dx.$
(n) $\displaystyle\int \frac{\cot^{\frac{2}{3}} x}{\sin^2 x}\,dx.$
(o) $\displaystyle\int \sec^4 x\,dx.$
(p) $\displaystyle\int \csc^4 x\,dx.$
(q) $\displaystyle\int \tan x\,\sec^2 x\,dx.$
(r) $\displaystyle\int \cot x\,\csc^2 x\,dx.$

\textbf{Example V.} \textit{To find $\displaystyle\int \sin^m x\,\cos^n x\,dx$ by means of multiple angles.}

When either $m$ or $n$ is a positive odd integer, the shortest method is that shown in Example I, p. 298. When $m$ and $n$ are both positive even integers, the given differential expression may be transformed by suitable trigonometric substitutions into an expression involving sines and cosines of multiple angles, and then integrated. For this purpose we employ the following formulas:

\[ \sin u\cos u = \tfrac{1}{2}\sin 2u, \qquad \text{36, p. 2} \]
\[ \sin^2 u = \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}\cos 2u, \qquad \text{38, p. 2} \]
\[ \cos^2 u = \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}\cos 2u. \qquad \text{39, p. 2} \]

\textsc{Illustrative Example 1.} Find $\displaystyle\int \cos^2 x\,dx$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[ \int \cos^2 x\,dx = \int (\tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x)\,dx \qquad \text{38, p. 2} \]
\[ = \frac{1}{2}\int dx + \frac{1}{2}\int \cos 2x\,dx = \frac{x}{2} + \frac{1}{4}\sin 2x + C. \]

\textsc{Illustrative Example 2.} Find $\displaystyle\int \sin^2 x\,\cos^2 x\,dx$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[ \int \sin^2 x\cos^2 x\,dx = \tfrac{1}{4}\int \sin^2 2x\,dx \qquad \text{36, p. 2} \]
\[ = \tfrac{1}{4}\int (\tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}\cos 4x)\,dx \qquad \text{38, p. 2} \]
\[ = \frac{x}{8} - \frac{1}{32}\sin 4x + C. \]


\textsc{Illustrative Example 3.} Find $\int \sin^4 x \cos^2 x\,dx$.

\textbf{Solution.}
\[
\int \sin^4 x \cos^2 x\,dx = \int (\sin x \cos x)^2 \sin^2 x\,dx
\]
\[
= \int \tfrac{1}{4} \sin^2 2x\,(\tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x)\,dx \qquad \text{36, p. 2 ; 38, p. 2}
\]
\[
= \tfrac{1}{8}\int \sin^2 2x\,dx - \tfrac{1}{8}\int \sin^2 2x \cos 2x\,dx
\]
\[
= \tfrac{1}{8}\int (\tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{2}\cos 4x)\,dx - \tfrac{1}{8}\int \sin^2 2x \cos 2x\,dx
\]
\[
= \frac{x}{16} - \frac{\sin 4x}{64} - \frac{\sin^3 2x}{48} + C.
\]

\textbf{Example VI.} \textit{To find $\int \sin mx \cos nx\,dx$, $\int \sin mx \sin nx\,dx$, or $\int \cos mx \cos nx\,dx$, when $m \neq n$.}

By 41, p. 2, $\sin mx \cos nx = \tfrac{1}{2}\sin (m+n)x + \tfrac{1}{2}\sin (m-n)x$.
\[
\therefore \int \sin mx \cos nx\,dx = \tfrac{1}{2}\int \sin (m+n)x\,dx + \tfrac{1}{2}\int \sin (m-n)x\,dx
\]
\[
= -\frac{\cos (m+n)x}{2(m+n)} - \frac{\cos (m-n)x}{2(m-n)} + C.
\]

Similarly, we find
\[
\int \sin mx \sin nx\,dx = -\frac{\sin (m+n)x}{2(m+n)} + \frac{\sin (m-n)x}{2(m-n)} + C,
\]
\[
\int \cos mx \cos nx\,dx = \frac{\sin (m+n)x}{2(m+n)} + \frac{\sin (m-n)x}{2(m-n)} + C.
\]

\textbf{EXAMPLES} 

1. $\int \cos^2 x\,dx = \dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 2x + C.$

2. $\int \sin^4 x\,dx = \dfrac{3x}{8} - \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4} + \dfrac{\sin 4x}{32} + C.$

3. $\int \cos^4 x\,dx = \dfrac{3x}{8} + \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4} + \dfrac{\sin 4x}{32} + C.$

4. $\int \sin^6 x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{16}\left(5x - 4\sin 2x + \dfrac{\sin^3 2x}{3} + \dfrac{3}{4}\sin 4x\right) + C.$

5. $\int \cos^6 x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{16}\left(5x + 4\sin 2x - \dfrac{\sin^3 2x}{3} + \dfrac{3}{4}\sin 4x\right) + C.$

6. $\int \sin^4 \alpha \cos^2 \alpha\,d\alpha = -\dfrac{\sin^3 2\alpha}{48} + \dfrac{\alpha}{16} - \dfrac{\sin 4\alpha}{64} + C.$

7. $\int \sin^4 t \cos^4 t\,dt = \dfrac{1}{128}\left(3t - \sin 4t + \dfrac{\sin 8t}{8}\right) + C.$

8. $\int \cos^6 x \sin^2 x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{128}\left(5x + \dfrac{8}{3}\sin^3 2x - \sin 4x - \dfrac{\sin 8x}{8}\right) + C.$


9. $\displaystyle\int \cos 3y \sin 5y\,dy = -\frac{\cos 8y}{16} - \frac{\cos 2y}{4} + C.$

10. $\displaystyle\int \sin 5z \sin 6z\,dz = -\frac{\sin 11z}{22} + \frac{\sin z}{2} + C.$

11. $\displaystyle\int \cos 4s \cos 7s\,ds = \frac{\sin 11s}{22} + \frac{\sin 3s}{6} + C.$

\textbf{169. Integration of expressions containing $\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$ or $\sqrt{x^2 \pm a^2}$ by a trigonometric substitution.} In many cases the shortest method of integrating such expressions is to change the variable as follows:

\textit{When $\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$ occurs, let $x = a \sin z$.}

\textit{When $\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}$ occurs, let $x = a \tan z$.}

\textit{When $\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}$ occurs, let $x = a \sec z$.}$^{*}$

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Find $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{(a^2 - x^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.$

\textbf{Solution.} Let $x = a \sin z$; then $dx = a \cos z\,dz$, and
\[
\int \frac{dx}{(a^2 - x^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}} = \int \frac{a \cos z\,dz}{(a^2 - a^2 \sin^2 z)^{\frac{3}{2}}} = \int \frac{a \cos z\,dz}{a^3 \cos^3 z}
\]
\[
= \frac{1}{a^2}\int \frac{dz}{\cos^2 z} = \frac{1}{a^2}\int \sec^2 z\,dz = \frac{\tan z}{a^2} + C
\]
\[
= \frac{x}{a^2 \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}} + C.
\]

Since $\sin z = \frac{x}{a}$, draw a right triangle with $x$ as the opposite leg to the acute angle $z$, and $a$ as the hypotenuse. Then the adjacent leg will be $\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$ and $\tan z = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}}$.

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 2. Find $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}.$

\textbf{Solution.} Let $x = \tan z$ $\dagger$; then $dx = \sec^2 z\,dz$, and
\[
\int \frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^2 + 1}} = \int \frac{\sec^2 z\,dz}{\tan z\,\sqrt{\tan^2 z + 1}} = \int \frac{\sec^2 z\,dz}{\tan z \cdot \sec z}
\]
\[
= \int \frac{\sec z}{\tan z}\,dz = \int \frac{dz}{\sin z} = \int \csc z\,dz
\]
\[
= \log(\csc z - \cot z) = \log \frac{\sqrt{x^2 + 1} - 1}{x} + C.
\]

Since $\tan z = x$, $\cot z = \dfrac{1}{x}$, and $\csc z = \dfrac{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}}{x}$.

$^{*}$ We may also use the substitutions $x = a \cos z$, $x = a \cot z$, and $x = a \csc z$ respectively.

$\dagger$ In this example $a = 1$.


\textbf{EXAMPLES} 

1. $\displaystyle\int\frac{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}{x}\,dx=\sqrt{x^2-a^2}-a\operatorname{arc\,sec}\frac{x}{a}+C.$

2. $\displaystyle\int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx=\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^2-x^2}+\frac{a^2}{2}\arcsin\frac{x}{a}+C.$

3. $\displaystyle\int\frac{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}{x^2}\,dx=\log\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right)-\frac{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}{x}+C.$

4. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2\,dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}=\frac{1}{2}\arcsin x-\frac{x\sqrt{1-x^2}}{2}+C.$

5. $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^4\sqrt{x^2+1}}=\frac{(2x^2-1)\sqrt{x^2+1}}{3x^3}+C.$

6. $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}=-\frac{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}{a^2x}+C.$

7. $\displaystyle\int\frac{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}{x^4}\,dx=\frac{(x^2-a^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3a^2x^3}+C.$

\textbf{MISCELLANEOUS EXAMPLES} 

1. $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sin^4 x}.$

2. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(x^2+1)\,dx}{x+2}.$

\textbf{40.} The following functions have been obtained by differentiating certain functions. Find the functions and verify your results by differentiation.

(a) $5\,x^3 + \sin 2\,x$.

\textbf{Solution.} In this example $(5\,x^3 + \sin 2\,x)\,dx$ is the differential expression to be integrated. Thus
\[\int (5\,x^3 + \sin 2\,x)\,dx = \frac{5\,x^4}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\cos 2\,x + C. \quad \textit{Ans.}\]

\textit{Verification.}
\[\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{5\,x^4}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\cos 2\,x + C\right) = 5\,x^3 + \sin 2\,x.\]

# CHAPTER XXII: INTEGRATION. RULES FOR INTEGRATING STANDARD ELEMENTARY FORMS
INTEGRAL CALCULUS
**165. Integration.** The student is already familiar with the mutually inverse operations of addition and subtraction, multiplication and division, involution and evolution. In the examples which follow, the second members of one column are respectively the inverse of the second members of the other column: \begin{array}{ll} y = x^2 + 1, & \qquad x = \pm\sqrt{y-1}; \\ y = a^x, & \qquad x = \log_a y; \\ y = \sin x, & \qquad x = \operatorname{arc\,sin} y. \end{array} From the Differential Calculus we have learned how to calculate the derivative f'(x) of a given function f(x), an operation indicated \text{ by } \frac{d}{dx} f(x) = f'(x), or, if we are using differentials, by df(x) = f'(x)\,dx. The problems of the Integral Calculus depend on the *inverse operation*, namely: *To find a function f(x) whose derivative* (A) \qquad f'(x) = \phi(x) *is given.* Or, since it is customary to use differentials in the Integral Calculus, we may write (B) \qquad df(x) = f'(x)\,dx = \phi(x)\,dx, and state the problem as follows: *Having given the differential of a function, to find the function itself.* The function f(x) thus found is called an *integral* ^{*} of the given differential expression, the process of finding it is called *integration*, and the operation is indicated \text{ by } writing the *integral sign*^{\dagger} \int in front of the given differential expression; thus (C)\qquad \int f'(x)\,dx^{\ddagger} = f(x), read *an integral of f'(x)\,dx equals f(x)*. The differential dx indicates that x is *the variable of integration*. For example, \(a\) If f(x) = x^3, then f'(x)\,dx = 3\,x^2dx, and \int 3\,x^2dx = x^3. \(b\) If f(x) = \sin x, then f'(x)\,dx = \cos xdx, and \int \cos xdx = \sin x. \(c\) If f(x) = \text{arc tan}\,x, then f'(x)\,dx = \dfrac{dx}{1+x^2}, and \int \frac{dx}{1+x^2} = \text{arc tan}\,x. Let us now emphasize what is apparent from the preceding explanations, namely, that *Differentiation and integration are inverse operations.* Differentiating (C) gives (D)\qquad d\int f'(x)\,dx = f'(x)\,dx. Substituting the value of f'(x)\,dx\,[= df(x)] from (B) in (C), we get (E)\qquad \int df(x) = f(x). Therefore, considered as symbols of operation, \dfrac{d}{dx} and \int \cdots dx are *inverse to each other*; or, if we are using differentials, d and \int are inverse to each other. ^{*} Called *anti-differential* by some writers. \dagger Historically this sign is a distorted S, the initial letter of the word *sum*. Instead of defining integration as the inverse of differentiation, we may define it as a process of summation, a very important notion which we will consider in Chapter XXVIII. \ddagger Some authors write this D_x^{-1}f'(x) when they wish to emphasize the fact that it is an inverse operation. When d is followed \text{ by } \int they annul each other, as in (D), but when \int is followed \text{ by } d, as in (E), that will not in general be the case unless we ignore the *constant of integration*. The reason for this will appear at once from the definition of the constant of integration given in the next section. **166. Constant of integration. Indefinite integral.** From the preceding section it follows that \text{since } d\,(x^3) \phantom{{}+2}= 3\,x^2dx, \text{ we have } \int 3\,x^2dx = x^3; \text{since } d\,(x^3+2) = 3\,x^2dx, \text{ we have } \int 3\,x^2dx = x^3+2; \text{since } d\,(x^3-7) = 3\,x^2dx, \text{ we have } \int 3\,x^2dx = x^3-7. In fact, since d\,(x^3+C) = 3\,x^2dx, where C is any arbitrary constant, we have \int 3\,x^2dx = x^3+C. A constant C arising in this way is called a *constant of integration*.^{*} Since we can give C as many values as we please, it follows that if a given differential expression has one integral, it has infinitely many differing only \text{ by } constants. Hence \int f'(x)\,dx = f(x)+C; and since C is unknown and *indefinite*, the expression f(x)+C is called the *indefinite integral of f'(x)\,dx*. It is evident that if \phi\,(x) is a function the derivative of which is f(x), then \phi\,(x)+C, where C is any constant whatever, is likewise a function the derivative of which is f(x). Hence the **Theorem.** *If two functions differ \text{ by } a constant, they have the same derivative.* It is, however, not obvious that if \phi\,(x) is a function the derivative of which is f(x), then *all* functions having the same derivative f(x) are of the form \phi\,(x)+C, where C is any constant. In other words, there remains to be proved the ^{*} Constant here means that it is independent of the *variable of integration*. **Converse theorem.** *If two functions have the same derivative, their difference is a constant.* **Proof.** Let \phi(x) and \psi(x) be two functions having the common derivative f(x). Place F(x)=\phi(x)-\psi(x); \text{ then} (A)\qquad F'(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\left[\phi(x)-\psi(x)\right]=f(x)-f(x)=0. \quad \text{By hypothesis} But from the Theorem of Mean Value **(46)**, p. 166, we have F(x+\Delta x)-F(x)=\Delta x\,F'(x+\theta\cdot\Delta x). \qquad 0<\theta<1 \therefore\ F(x+\Delta x)-F(x)=0, \[Since \text{ by } (A) the derivative of F(x) is zero for all values of x.\] and $$F(x+\Delta x)=F(x).$$ This means that the function $$F(x)=\phi(x)-\psi(x)$$ does not change in value at all when $x$ takes on the increment $\Delta x$, i.e. $\phi(x)$ and $\psi(x)$ differ only by a constant. In any given case the value of $C$ can be found when we know the value of the integral for some value of the variable, and this will be illustrated by numerous examples in the next chapter. For the present we shall content ourselves with first learning how to find the indefinite integrals of given differential expressions. In what follows we shall assume that *every continuous function has an indefinite integral*, a statement the rigorous proof of which is beyond the scope of this book. For all elementary functions, however, the truth of the statement will appear in the chapters which follow. In all cases of indefinite integration the test to be applied in verifying the results is that *the differential of the integral must be equal to the given differential expression.* **167. Rules for integrating standard elementary forms.** The Differential Calculus furnished us with a *General Rule* for differentiation (p. 29). The Integral Calculus gives us no corresponding general rule that can be readily applied in practice for performing the inverse operation of integration.$^{*}$ Each case requires special treatment and we arrive at the integral of a given differential expression through $^{*}$ Even though the integral of a given differential expression may be known to exist, yet it may not be possible for us actually to find it in terms of known functions, because there are functions other than the elementary functions whose derivatives are elementary functions. our previous knowledge of the known results of differentiation. That is, we must be able to answer the question, *What function, when differentiated, will yield the given differential expression?* Integration then is essentially a tentative process, and to expedite the work, tables of known integrals are formed called *standard forms.* To effect any integration we compare the given differential expression with these forms, and if it is found to be identical with one of them, the integral is known. If it is not identical with one of them, we strive to reduce it to one of the standard forms by various methods, many of which employ artifices which can be suggested by practice only. Accordingly a large portion of our treatise on the Integral Calculus will be devoted to the explanation of methods for integrating those functions which frequently appear in the process of solving practical problems. From any result of differentiation may always be derived a formula for integration. The following two rules are useful in reducing differential expressions to standard forms: \(a\) *The integral of any algebraic sum of differential expressions equals the same algebraic sum of the integrals of these expressions taken separately.* **Proof.** Differentiating the expression $$\int du + \int dv - \int dw,$$ $u, v, w$ being functions of a single variable, we get $$du + dv - dw. \qquad \text{By \text{iii}, p. 34}$$ (1) $$\therefore \int (du + dv - dw) = \int du + \int dv - \int dw.$$ \(b\) *A constant factor may be written either before or after the integral sign.* **Proof.** Differentiating the expression $$a \int dv$$ gives $$a\,dv. \qquad \text{By \text{iv}, p. 34}$$ (2) $$\therefore \int a\,dv = a \int dv.$$ On account of their importance we shall write the above two rules as formulas at the head of the following list of Standard Elementary Forms \(1\) $$\int (du + dv - dw) = \int du + \int dv - \int dw.$$ \(2\) $$\int a\,dv = a \int dv.$$ \(3\) $$\int dx = x + C.$$ \(4\) $$\int v^{n}dv = \frac{v^{n+1}}{n+1} + C. \qquad n \neq -1$$ \(5\) $$\begin{aligned} \int \frac{dv}{v} &= \log v + C \\ &= \log v + \log c = \log cv. \end{aligned}$$ \[Placing C = \log c.\] \(6\) $$\int a^{v}dv = \frac{a^{v}}{\log a} + C.$$ \(7\) $$\int e^{v}dv = e^{v} + C.$$ \(8\) $$\int \sin v \, dv = -\cos v + C.$$ \(9\) $$\int \cos v \, dv = \sin v + C.$$ \(10\) $$\int \sec^{2} v \, dv = \tan v + C.$$ \(11\) $$\int \csc^{2} v \, dv = -\cot v + C.$$ \(12\) $$\int \sec v \tan v \, dv = \sec v + C.$$ \(13\) $$\int \csc v \cot v \, dv = -\csc v + C.$$ \(14\) $$\int \tan v \, dv = \log \sec v + C.$$ \(15\) $$\int \cot v \, dv = \log \sin v + C.$$ \(16\) $$\int \sec v \, dv = \log (\sec v + \tan v) + C.$$ \(17\) $$\int \csc v \, dv = \log (\csc v - \cot v) + C.$$ $$\text{(18)}\qquad \int\frac{dv}{v^{2}+a^{2}}=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{v}{a}+C.$$ $$\text{(19)}\qquad \int\frac{dv}{v^{2}-a^{2}}=\frac{1}{2\,a}\log\frac{v-a}{v+a}+C.$$ $$\text{(20)}\qquad \int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{a^{2}-v^{2}}}=\operatorname{arc\,sin}\frac{v}{a}+C.$$ $$\text{(21)}\qquad \int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}\pm a^{2}}}=\log\left(v+\sqrt{v^{2}\pm a^{2}}\right)+C.$$ $$\text{(22)}\qquad \int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{2\,av-v^{2}}}=\operatorname{arc\,vers}\frac{v}{a}+C.$$ $$\text{(23)}\qquad \int\frac{dv}{v\sqrt{v^{2}-a^{2}}}=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,sec}\frac{v}{a}+C.$$ **Proof of (3).** Since $$d(x+C)=dx, \qquad \textbf{II}\text{, p. 34}$$ we get $$\int dx=x+C.$$ **Proof of (4).** Since $$d\left(\frac{v^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\right)=v^{n}dv, \qquad \textbf{VI}\text{, p. 34}$$ we get $$\int v^{n}dv=\frac{v^{n+1}}{n+1}+C.$$ This holds true for all values of $n$ except $n=-1$. For, when $n=-1$, (4) gives $$\int v^{-1}dv=\frac{v^{-1+1}}{-1+1}+C=\frac{1}{0}+C=\infty+C,$$ which has no meaning. The case when $n=-1$ comes under (5). **Proof of (5).** Since $$d(\log v+C)=\frac{dv}{v}, \qquad \textbf{VIII}\ \textbf{\textit{a}}\text{, p. 35}$$ we get $$\int\frac{dv}{v}=\log v+C.$$ The results we get from (5) may be put in more compact form if we denote the constant of integration by $\log c$. Thus $$\int\frac{dv}{v}=\log v+\log c=\log cv.$$ Formula (5) states that *if the expression under the integral sign is a fraction whose numerator is the differential of the denominator, then the integral is the natural logarithm of the denominator.* **EXAMPLES**$^{*}$ For formulas (1)--(5). (v) $\int a^{\log x}\frac{dx}{x}$. **Proofs of (8)--(13).** These follow at once from the corresponding formulas for differentiation, **XI**, etc., p. 35. **Proof of (14).** $$\begin{aligned} \int \tan v\,dv &= \int \frac{\sin v\,dv}{\cos v} \\ &= -\int \frac{-\sin v\,dv}{\cos v} \\ &= -\int \frac{d(\cos v)}{\cos v} \\ &= -\log\cos v + C \qquad \text{by (5)} \\ &= \log\sec v + C. \end{aligned}$$ \[Since -\log\cos v = -\log\frac{1}{\sec v} = -\log 1 + \log\sec v = \log\sec v.\] **Proof of (15).** $$\begin{aligned} \int \cot v\,dv &= \int \frac{\cos v\,dv}{\sin v} = \int \frac{d(\sin v)}{\sin v} \\ &= \log\sin v + C. \qquad \text{By (5)} \end{aligned}$$ **Proof of (16).** Since $$\begin{aligned} \sec v &= \sec v\,\frac{\sec v+\tan v}{\sec v+\tan v} \\ &= \frac{\sec v\tan v+\sec^{2}v}{\sec v+\tan v}, \end{aligned}$$ $$\begin{aligned} \int \sec v.dv &= \int \frac{\sec v\tan v+\sec^{2}v}{\sec v+\tan v}\,dv \\ &= \int \frac{d(\sec v+\tan v)}{\sec v+\tan v} \\ &= \log(\sec v+\tan v)+C. \qquad \text{By (5)} \end{aligned}$$ **Proof of (17).** Since $$\begin{aligned} \csc v &= \csc v\,\frac{\csc v-\cot v}{\csc v-\cot v} \\ &= \frac{-\csc v\cot v+\csc^{2}v}{\csc v-\cot v}, \end{aligned}$$ $$\begin{aligned} \int \csc v\,dv &= \int \frac{-\csc v\cot v+\csc^{2}v}{\csc v-\cot v}\,dv \\ &= \int \frac{d(\csc v-\cot v)}{\csc v-\cot v} \\ &= \log(\csc v-\cot v)+C. \qquad \text{By (5)} \end{aligned}$$ **EXAMPLES** For formulas (8)--(17). If we now insert the factor $2a$ before $dx$ and the factor $\frac{1}{2a}$ before the integral sign, we get $$\begin{aligned} \int \sin 2axdx &= \frac{1}{2a}\int \sin 2ax \cdot 2adx \\ &= \frac{1}{2a}\int \sin 2ax \cdot d(2ax) = \frac{1}{2a}\cdot -\cos 2ax + C. \qquad \text{By (8)} \\ &= -\frac{\cos 2ax}{2a} + C. \end{aligned}$$ 2\. $\displaystyle\int \cos mxdx = \frac{1}{m}\sin mx + C.$ 3\. $\displaystyle\int \tan bxdx = \frac{1}{b}\log \sec bx + C.$ 4\. $\displaystyle\int \sec axdx = \frac{1}{a}\log(\sec ax + \tan ax) + C.$ 5\. $\displaystyle\int \csc\frac{x}{a}\,dx = a\log\left(\csc\frac{x}{a} - \cot\frac{x}{a}\right) + C.$ 6\. $\displaystyle\int \sec 3t\tan 3tdt = \tfrac{1}{3}\sec 3t + C.$ 7\. $\displaystyle\int \csc ay\cot aydy = -\frac{1}{a}\csc ay + C.$ 8\. $\displaystyle\int \csc^2 3xdx = -\tfrac{1}{3}\cot 3x + C.$ 9\. $\displaystyle\int \cot\frac{x}{2}\,dx = 2\log\sin\frac{x}{2} + C.$ 10\. $\displaystyle\int \sec^2 x^3 \cdot x^2dx = \tfrac{1}{3}\tan x^3 + C.$ 11\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{\sin^2 x} = -\cot x + C.$ 12\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{ds}{\cos^2 s} = \tan s + C.$ 13\. $\displaystyle\int (\tan\theta + \cot\theta)^2 d\theta = \tan\theta - \cot\theta + C.$ 14\. $\displaystyle\int (\sec\alpha - \tan\alpha)^2 d\alpha = 2(\tan\alpha - \sec\alpha) - \alpha + C.$ 15\. $\displaystyle\int (\tan 2s - 1)^2 ds = \tfrac{1}{2}\tan 2s + \log\cos 2s + C.$ 16\. $\displaystyle\int \left(\cos\frac{\theta}{3} - \sin 3\theta\right)d\theta = 3\sin\frac{\theta}{3} + \frac{1}{3}\cos 3\theta + C.$ 17\. $\displaystyle\int \left(\sin ax + \sin\frac{x}{a}\right)dx = -\frac{1}{a}\cos ax - a\cos\frac{x}{a} + C.$ 18\. $\displaystyle\int k\cos(a + by)\,dy = \frac{k}{b}\sin(a + by) + C.$ 19\. $\displaystyle\int \mathrm{cosec}^2 x^3 \cdot x^2dx = -\tfrac{1}{3}\cot x^3 + C.$ 20\. $\displaystyle\int \cos(\log x)\frac{dx}{x} = \sin(\log x) + C.$ 21\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{1 + \cos x} = -\cot x + \csc x + C = \tan\frac{x}{2} + C.$ Hint. $$=\frac{1}{2a}\{\log(v-a)-\log(v+a)\}+C \qquad \text{by (5)}$$ $$=\frac{1}{2a}\log\frac{v-a}{v+a}+C.$$ $^{*}$ Also $d\left(\dfrac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,cot}\dfrac{v}{a}+C\right)=-\dfrac{dv}{v^{2}+a^{2}}$ and $\displaystyle\int\frac{dv}{v^{2}+a^{2}}=-\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,cot}\frac{v}{a}+C'.$ Hence $$\int\frac{dv}{v^{2}+a^{2}}=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{v}{a}+C=-\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,cot}\frac{v}{a}+C'.$$ Since $\operatorname{arc\,tan}\dfrac{v}{a}+\operatorname{arc\,cot}\dfrac{v}{a}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, we see that one result may be easily transformed into the other. The same kind of discussion may be given for (20) involving $\operatorname{arc\,sin}\dfrac{v}{a}$ and $\operatorname{arc\,cos}\dfrac{v}{a}$, and for (23) involving $\operatorname{arc\,sec}\dfrac{v}{a}$ and $\operatorname{arc\,csc}\dfrac{v}{a}$. $^{\dagger}$ By breaking the fraction up into partial fractions (see Case I, p. 325). **Proof of (20).** Since $$d\left(\operatorname{arc\,sin}\frac{v}{a}+C\right)=\frac{d\left(\frac{v}{a}\right)}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{a}\right)^{2}}}=\frac{av}{\sqrt{a^{2}-v^{2}}},\qquad \text{by \textbf{XVIII}, p. 35}$$ we get $$\int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{a^{2}-v^{2}}}=\operatorname{arc\,sin}\frac{v}{a}+C.$$ **Proof of (21).** Assume $v=a\tan z$, where $z$ is a new variable; differentiating, $dv=a\sec^{2}z\,dz$. Hence, by substitution, $$\int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}+a^{2}}}=\int\frac{a\sec^{2}z\,dz}{\sqrt{a^{2}\tan^{2}z+a^{2}}}=\int\frac{\sec^{2}z\,dz}{\sqrt{\tan^{2}z+1}}$$ $$=\int\sec z\,dz=\log(\sec z+\tan z)+C\qquad\text{by (\textbf{16})}$$ $$=\log\left(\tan z+\sqrt{\tan^{2}z+1}\right)+c.\qquad\text{By 28, p. 2}$$ But $\tan z=\frac{v}{a}$; hence, $$\int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}+a^{2}}}=\log\left(\frac{v}{a}+\sqrt{\frac{v^{2}}{a^{2}}+1}\right)+c$$ $$=\log\frac{v+\sqrt{v^{2}+a^{2}}}{a}+c$$ $$=\log\left(v+\sqrt{v^{2}+a^{2}}\right)-\log a+c.$$ Placing $C=-\log a+c$, we get $$\int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}+a^{2}}}=\log\left(v+\sqrt{v^{2}+a^{2}}\right)+C.$$ In the same manner, by assuming $v=a\sec z$, $dv=a\sec z\tan z\,dz$ we get $$\int\frac{dv}{\sqrt{v^{2}-a^{2}}}=\int\frac{a\sec z\tan z\,dz}{\sqrt{a^{2}\sec^{2}z-a^{2}}}=\int\sec z\,dz$$ $$=\log(\sec z+\tan z)+c\qquad\text{by (\textbf{16})}$$ $$=\log\left(\sec z+\sqrt{\sec^{2}z-1}\right)+c\qquad\text{by 28, p. 2}$$ $$=\log\left(\frac{v}{a}+\sqrt{\frac{v^{2}}{a^{2}}-1}\right)+c=\log\left(v+\sqrt{v^{2}-a^{2}}\right)+C.$$ **Proofs of (22) and (23).** These follow at once from the corresponding formulas for differentiation, **XXII** and **XXIV**, p. 36.
