CHAPTER XXIV: THE DEFINITE INTEGRAL

173. Differential of an area. Consider the continuous function \(\phi(x)\), and let \[y = \phi(x)\] be the equation of the curve \(AB\). Let \(CD\) be a fixed and \(MP\) a variable ordinate, and let \(u\) be the measure of the area \(CMPD\).\(^{*}\) When \(x\) takes on a sufficiently small increment \(\Delta x\), \(u\) takes on an increment \(\Delta u\) (\(=\) area \(MNQP\)). Completing the rectangles \(MNRP\) and \(MNQS\), we see that

area \(MNRP <\) area \(MNQP <\) area \(MNQS\),

or, \[MP \cdot \Delta x < \Delta u < NQ \cdot \Delta x;\]

and, dividing by \(\Delta x\), \[MP < \frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} < NQ.^{\dagger}\]

Now let \(\Delta x\) approach zero as a limit; then since \(MP\) remains fixed and \(NQ\) approaches \(MP\) as a limit (since \(y\) is a continuous function of \(x\)), we get \[\frac{du}{dx} = y\,(= MP),\] or, using differentials, \[du = y\,dx.\]

Theorem. The differential of the area bounded by any curve, the axis of \(X\), and two ordinates is equal to the product of the ordinate terminating the area and the differential of the corresponding abscissa.

174. The definite integral. It follows from the theorem in the last section that if \(AB\) is the locus of \[y = \phi(x),\] then \[du = y\,dx, \text{ or}\] \[(A) \qquad du = \phi(x)\,dx,\]

\(^{*}\) We may suppose this area to be generated by a variable ordinate starting out from \(CD\) and moving to the right; hence \(u\) will be a function of \(x\) which vanishes when \(x = a\).

\(\dagger\) In this figure \(MP\) is less than \(NQ\); if \(MP\) happens to be greater than \(NQ\), simply reverse the inequality signs.

where \(du\) is the differential of the area between the curve, the axis of \(x\), and any two ordinates. Integrating \((A)\), we get \[u=\int \phi\,(x)\,dx.\] Since \(\int \phi\,(x)\,dx\) exists (it is here represented geometrically as an area), denote it by \(f(x)+C\).

\((B)\) \(\therefore\ u=f(x)+C.\)

We may determine \(C\), as in Chapter XXIII, if we know the value of \(u\) for some value of \(x\). If we agree to reckon the area from the axis of \(y\), i.e. when

\((C)\) \(x=a,\quad u=\text{area } OCDG,\)

and when \(x=b,\quad u=\text{area } OEFG,\) etc.,

it follows that if

\((D)\) \(x=0,\quad \text{then } u=0.\)

Substituting \((D)\) in \((B)\), we get \[u=f(0)+C,\quad \text{or,}\quad C=-f(0).\] Hence from \((B)\) we obtain

\((E)\) \(u=f(x)-f(0),\)

giving the area from the axis of \(y\) to any ordinate (as \(MP\)).

To find the area between the ordinates \(CD\) and \(EF\), substitute the values \((C)\) in \((E)\), giving

\((F)\) \(\text{area } OCDG=f(a)-f(0),\)

\((G)\) \(\text{area } OEFG=f(b)-f(0).\)

Subtracting \((F)\) from \((G)\),

\((H)\) \(\text{area } \mathbf{CEFD}=f(b)-f(a).\)\(^{*}\)

Theorem. The difference of the values of \(\int y\,dx\) for \(x=a\) and \(x=b\) gives the area bounded by the curve whose ordinate is \(y\), the axis of \(X\), and the ordinates corresponding to \(x=a\) and \(x=b\).

This difference is represented by the symbol \(\dagger\)

\((I)\) \(\displaystyle\int_a^b y\,dx,\quad \text{or,}\quad \int_a^b \phi\,(x)\,dx,\)

\(^{*}\) The student should observe that under the present hypothesis \(f(x)\) will be a single-valued function which changes continuously from \(f(a)\) to \(f(b)\) as \(x\) changes from \(a\) to \(b\).

\(\dagger\) This notation is due to Joseph Fourier (1768–1830).

and is read “the integral from \(a\) to \(b\) of \(y\,dx\).” The operation is called integration between limits, \(a\) being the lower and \(b\) the upper limit.\(^{*}\)

Since \((I)\) always has a definite value, it is called a definite integral. For, if \[\int \phi\,(x)\,dx = f(x)+C,\] then \[\int_a^b \phi\,(x)\,dx = \left[ f(x)+C \right]_a^b\] \[= [f(b)+C] - [f(a)+C],\] or \[\int_a^b \phi\,(x)\,dx = f(b)-f(a),\] the constant of integration having disappeared.

We may accordingly define the symbol \[\int_a^b \phi\,(x)\,dx \quad \text{or} \quad \int_a^b y\,dx\] as the numerical measure of the area bounded by the curve \(y = \phi\,(x)\),\(^{\dagger}\) the axis of \(X\), and the ordinates of the curve at \(x = a\), \(x = b\). This definition presupposes that these lines bound an area, i.e. the curve does not rise or fall to infinity, and both \(a\) and \(b\) are finite.

We have shown that the numerical value of the definite integral is always \(f(b)-f(a)\), but we shall see in Illustrative Example 2, p. 324, that \(f(b)-f(a)\) may be a number when the definite integral has no meaning.

175. Calculation of a definite integral. The process may be summarized as follows:

First Step. Find the indefinite integral of the given differential expression.

Second Step. Substitute in this indefinite integral first the upper limit and then the lower limit for the variable, and subtract the last result from the first.

It is not necessary to bring in the constant of integration, since it always disappears in subtracting.

\(^{*}\) The word limit in this connection means merely the value of the variable at one end of its range (end value), and should not be confused with the meaning of the word in the Theory of Limits.

\(\dagger\) \((x)\ \phi\) is continuous and single-valued throughout the interval \([a, b]\).

Illustrative Example 1. Find \(\int_1^4 x^2dx\).

Solution. \(\int_1^4 x^2dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^4 = \frac{64}{3} - \frac{1}{3} = 21.\) Ans.

Illustrative Example 2. Find \(\int_0^{\pi} \sin x dx\).

Solution. \(\int_0^{\pi} \sin x dx = \left[-\cos x\right]_0^{\pi} = \left[-(-1)\right] - \left[-1\right] = 2.\) Ans.

Illustrative Example 3. Find \(\int_0^a \frac{dx}{a^2+x^2}\).

Solution. \(\int_0^a \frac{dx}{a^2+x^2} = \left[\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{x}{a}\right]_0^a = \frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,tan} 1 - \frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arc\,tan} 0\) \[= \frac{\pi}{4a} - 0 = \frac{\pi}{4a}. \quad \textit{Ans.}\]

EXAMPLES

1. \(\int_2^3 6x^2dx = 38.\)

2. \(\int_0^a (a^2x - x^3)\,dx = \frac{a^4}{4}.\)

3. \(\int_1^4 \frac{dx}{x^{\frac{3}{2}}} = 1.\)

4. \(\int_1^e \frac{dx}{x} = 1.\)

5. \(\int_0^1 (x^2 - 2x + 2)(x - 1)\,dx = -\frac{3}{4}.\)

6. \(\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{3-2x}} = \sqrt{3} - 1.\)

7. \(\int_0^2 \frac{x^3dx}{x+1} = \frac{8}{3} - \log 3.\)

8. \(\int_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{2-3x^2}} = \frac{\pi}{4\sqrt{3}}.\)

9. \(\int_2^3 \frac{3xdx}{2\sqrt[4]{x^2-4}} = \sqrt[4]{125}.\)

10. \(\int_0^1 \frac{dy}{y^2-y+1} = \frac{2\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}.\)

11. \(\int_2^3 \frac{tdt}{1+t^2} = \frac{\log 2}{2}.\)

12. \(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin\phi d\phi = 1.\)

13. \(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \sec^4\theta d\theta = \frac{4}{3}.\)

14. \(\int_0^{2r} \frac{\sqrt{2r}}{\sqrt{x}}dx = 4r.\)

15. \(\int_0^5 \left(\frac{3}{5}\sqrt{t} - \frac{3}{25}t^2\right)dt = 2\sqrt{5} - 5.\)

16. \(\int_0^r \frac{rdx}{\sqrt{r^2-x^2}} = \frac{\pi r}{2}.\)

17. \(\int_0^{2r} \frac{2\sqrt{2r}dy}{\sqrt{2r-y}} = 8r.\)

18. \(\int_{-b}^{b} \frac{\pi}{a^4}(y^2-b^2)^4dy = \frac{256\pi b^9}{315a^4}.\)

19. \(2a\int_0^{\pi} (2 + 2\cos\theta)^{\frac{1}{2}}d\theta = 8a.\)

20. \(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin^3\alpha \cos^3\alpha d\alpha = \frac{1}{12}.\)

21. \(\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \tan\alpha d\alpha = 0.\)

22. \(\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \sec\theta d\theta = \log\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}\right).\)

23. \(\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{\cos\theta d\theta}{1+\sin^2\theta} = \frac{\pi}{4}.\)

176. Calculation of areas. On p. 316 it was shown that the area between a curve, the axis of \(X\), and the ordinates \(x=a\) and \(x=b\) is given by the formula \[\textbf{Area} = \int_a^b y\,dx,\] where the value of \(y\) in terms of \(x\) is substituted from the equation of the given curve.

Illustrative Example 1. Find the area bounded by the parabola \(y=x^2\), the axis of \(X\), and the ordinates \(x=2\) and \(x=4\).

Solution. Substituting in the formula \[\text{Area } ABDC = \int_2^4 x^2\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_2^4\] \[= \frac{64}{3} - \frac{8}{3} = \frac{56}{3} = 18\tfrac{2}{3}. \quad \textit{Ans.}\]

EXAMPLES

1. Find the area bounded by the parabola \(y=x^2\), the axis of \(X\), and the ordinate \(x=3\). Ans. \(9\).

2. Find the area above the axis of \(X\), under the parabola \(y^2=4x\), and included between the ordinates \(x=4\) and \(x=9\). Ans. \(25\frac{1}{3}\).

3. Find the area bounded by the equilateral hyperbola \(xy=a^2\), the axis of \(X\), and the ordinates \(x=a\) and \(x=2a\). Ans. \(a^2 \log 2\).

4. Find the area between the parabola \(y=4-x^2\) and the axis of \(X\). Ans. \(10\frac{2}{3}\).

5. Find the area intercepted between the coördinate axes and the parabola \(x^{\frac{1}{2}}+y^{\frac{1}{2}}=a^{\frac{1}{2}}\). Ans. \(\frac{a^2}{6}\).

6. Find the area by integration of the triangle bounded by the line \(y=5x\), the axis of \(X\), and the ordinate \(x=2\). Verify your result by finding the area as one half the product of the base and altitude.

7. Find the area by integration of the triangle bounded by the line \(y=2x+6\), the axis of \(X\), and the ordinate \(x=4\). Verify your result as in the last example.

8. Find the area by integration of the trapezoid bounded by the line \(x-y+4=0\), the axis of \(X\), and the ordinates \(x=-2\) and \(x=4\). Verify your result by finding the area as one half the product of the sum of the parallel sides and the altitude.

9. Find the area by integration of the trapezoid bounded by the line \(x+2y-6=0\), the axis of \(X\), and the ordinates \(x=0\) and \(x=3\). Verify your result as in the last example.

10. Find the area by integration of the rectangle bounded by the line \(y=5\), the axis of \(X\), and the ordinates \(x=2\) and \(x=6\). Verify your result geometrically.

11. Find by integration the area bounded by the lines \(x=0\), \(x=9\), \(y=0\), \(y=7\). Verify your result geometrically.

12. Find the area bounded by the semicubical parabola \(y^3=x^2\), the axis of \(X\), and the line \(x=4\). Ans. \(\frac{3}{5}\sqrt[3]{1024}\),

13. Find the area bounded by the cubical parabola \(y=x^3\), the axis of \(X\), and the ordinate \(x=4\). Ans. \(64\).

14. Find in each of the following cases the area bounded by the given curve, the axis of \(X\), and the given ordinates: (a) \(y=9-x^2\). \(x=-3,\ x=3\). Ans. \(36\). (b) \(y=\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}\). \(x=0,\ x=8\). \(\log\sqrt{65}\). (c) \(y=\sin x\). \(x=0,\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). \(1\). (d) \(y=x^3+3x^2+2x\). \(x=-3,\ x=3\). \(54\). (e) \(y=x^2+x+1\). \(x=2,\ x=3\). \(9\frac{5}{6}\). (f) \(y=x^4+4x^3+2x^2+3\). \(x=1,\ x=2\). \(28\frac{13}{15}\). (g) \(y^2=-4x\). \(x=-1,\ x=0\). \(-\frac{4}{3}\). (h) \(xy=k^2\). \(x=a,\ x=b\). \(k^2\log\dfrac{b}{a}\). (i) \(y=2x+3\). \(x=0,\ x=4\). (j) \(y^2=4x+16\). \(x=-2,\ x=0\). (k) \(y=x^2+4x\). \(x=-4,\ x=-2\). (l) \(y=\cos x\). \(x=0,\ x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\). (m) \(xy=12\). \(x=1,\ x=4\).

15. Find the area included between the parabolas \(y^2=4x\) and \(x^2=4y\). Ans. \(5\frac{1}{3}\).

16. Find the total area included between the cubical parabola \(y=x^3\) and the line \(y=2x\). Ans. \(2\).

17. Prove that the area bounded by a parabola and one of its double ordinates equals two thirds of the circumscribing rectangle having the double ordinate as one side.

18. Find the area included between the parabolas \(y^2=4+x\) and \(y^2=4-x\).

19. Find the area between the curve \(y=\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}\) and the line \(y=\dfrac{x}{4}\). Ans. \(\log 4-\frac{3}{4}\).

20. Find by integration the area of the triangle bounded by the lines \(x+3y-3=0\), \(5x-y-15=0\), \(x-y+1=0\). Ans. \(8\).

177. Geometrical representation of an integral. In the last section we represented the definite integral as an area. This does not necessarily mean that every integral is an area, for the physical interpretation of the result depends on the nature of the quantities represented by the abscissa and the ordinate. Thus, if \(x\) and \(y\) are considered as simply the coördinates of a point and nothing more, then the integral is indeed an area. But suppose the ordinate represents the speed of a moving point, and the corresponding abscissa the time at which the point has that speed; then the graph is the speed curve of the motion, and the area under it and between any two ordinates will represent the distance passed through in the corresponding interval of time. That is, the number which denotes the area equals the number which denotes the distance (or value of the integral).

Similarly, a definite integral standing for volume, surface, mass, force, etc., may be represented geometrically by an area. On p. 366 the algebraic sign of an area is interpreted.

178. Mean value of \(\phi(x)\). This is defined as follows:

\[\left.\begin{array}{l} \textbf{Mean value of } \phi(x)\\ \textbf{from } x=a \textbf{ to } x=b \end{array}\right\} = \frac{\displaystyle\int_a^b \phi(x)\,dx}{b-a}.\]

Since from the figure \[\int_a^b \phi(x)\,dx = \text{area } APQB,\] this definition means that if we construct on the base \(AB(=b-a)\) a rectangle (as \(ALMB\)) whose area equals the area of \(APQB\), then \[\text{mean value} = \frac{\text{area } ALMB}{b-a} = \frac{AB\cdot CR}{AB} = \text{altitude } CR.\]

179. Interchange of limits.

Since \[\int_a^b \phi(x)\,dx = f(b)-f(a),\] and \[\int_b^a \phi(x)\,dx = f(a)-f(b) = -[f(b)-f(a)],\] we have \[\int_a^b \phi(x)\,dx = -\int_b^a \phi(x)\,dx.\]

Theorem. Interchanging the limits is equivalent to changing the sign of the definite integral.

180. Decomposition of the interval of integration of the definite integral.

Since \[\int_a^{x_1} \phi(x)\,dx = f(x_1)-f(a),\] and \[\int_{x_1}^b \phi(x)\,dx = f(b)-f(x_1),\] we get, by addition, \[\int_a^{x_1} \phi(x)\,dx + \int_{x_1}^b \phi(x)\,dx = f(b)-f(a).\] But \[\int_a^b \phi(x)\,dx = f(b)-f(a);\] therefore, by comparing the last two expressions, we obtain \[\int_a^b \phi(x)\,dx = \int_a^{x_1} \phi(x)\,dx + \int_{x_1}^b \phi(x)\,dx.\]

Interpreting this theorem geometrically, as in §174, p. 315, we see that the integral on the left-hand side represents the whole area \(CEFD\), the first integral on the right-hand side the area \(CMPD\), and the second integral on the right-hand side the area \(MEFP\). The truth of the theorem is therefore obvious.

Even if \(x_1\) does not lie in the interval between \(a\) and \(b\), the truth of the theorem is apparent when the sign as well as the magnitude of the areas is taken into account. Evidently the definite integral may be decomposed into any number of separate definite integrals in this way.

181. The definite integral a function of its limits.

From \[\int_a^b \phi(x)\,dx = f(b) - f(a)\] we see that the definite integral is a function of its limits. Thus \(\int_a^b \phi(z)\,dz\) has precisely the same value as \(\int_a^b \phi(x)\,dx\).

Theorem. A definite integral is a function of its limits.

182. Infinite limits. So far the limits of the integral have been assumed as finite. Even in elementary work, however, it is sometimes desirable to remove this restriction and to consider integrals with infinite limits. This is possible in certain cases by making use of the following definitions.

When the upper limit is infinite, \[\int_a^{+\infty} \phi(x)\,dx = \mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{b=+\infty} \int_a^b \phi(x)\,dx,\] and when the lower limit is infinite, \[\int_{-\infty}^b \phi(x)\,dx = \mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{a=-\infty} \int_a^b \phi(x)\,dx,\] provided the limits exist.

Illustrative Example 1. Find \(\displaystyle\int_1^{+\infty} \frac{dx}{x^2}\).

Solution. \[\int_1^{\infty} \frac{dx}{x^2} = \mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{b=+\infty} \int_1^b \frac{dx}{x^2} = \mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{b=+\infty} \left[ -\frac{1}{x} \right]_1^b\] \[= \mathop{\mathrm{limit}}_{b=+\infty} \left[ -\frac{1}{b} + 1 \right] = 1. \quad \textit{Ans.}\]

Illustrative Example 2. Find \(\displaystyle\int_0^{+\infty}\frac{8\,a^3dx}{x^2+4\,a^2}\).

Solution. \[\int_0^{+\infty}\frac{8\,a^3dx}{x^2+4\,a^2} =\underset{b=+\infty}{\text{limit}}\int_0^{b}\frac{8\,a^3dx}{x^2+4\,a^2} =\underset{b=+\infty}{\text{limit}}\left[4\,a^2\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{x}{2\,a}\right]_0^{b}\] \[=\underset{b=+\infty}{\text{limit}}\left[4\,a^2\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{b}{2\,a}\right]=4\,a^2\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=2\,\pi a^2.\ \textit{Ans.}\]

Let us interpret this result geometrically. The graph of our function is the witch, the locus of \[y=\frac{8\,a^3}{x^2+4\,a^2}.\]

\[\text{area } OPQb=\int_0^{b}\frac{8\,a^3dx}{x^2+4\,a^2}=4\,a^2\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{b}{2\,a}.\]

Now as the ordinate \(Qb\) moves indefinitely to the right, \[4\,a^2\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{b}{2\,a}\] is always finite, and \[\underset{b=+\infty}{\text{limit}}\left[4\,a^2\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{b}{2\,a}\right]=2\,\pi a^2,\] which is also finite. In such cases we call the result the area bounded by the curve, the ordinate \(OP\), and \(OX\), although strictly speaking this area is not completely bounded.

Illustrative Example 3. Find \(\displaystyle\int_1^{+\infty}\frac{dx}{x}\).

Solution. \[\int_1^{+\infty}\frac{dx}{x}=\underset{b=+\infty}{\text{limit}}\int_1^{b}\frac{dx}{x}=\underset{b=+\infty}{\text{limit}}(\log b).\]

The limit of \(\log b\) as \(b\) increases without limit does not exist; hence the integral has in this case no meaning.

183. When \(y=\phi(x)\) is discontinuous. Let us now consider cases when the function to be integrated is discontinuous for isolated values of the variable lying within the limits of integration.

Consider first the case where the function to be integrated is continuous for all values of \(x\) between the limits \(a\) and \(b\) except \(x=a\).

If \(a<b\) and \(\epsilon\) is positive, we use the definition \[(A)\qquad \int_a^b\phi(x)\,dx=\underset{\epsilon=0}{\text{limit}}\int_{a+\epsilon}^{b}\phi(x)\,dx,\] and when \(\phi(x)\) is continuous except at \(x=b\), we use the definition \[(B)\qquad \int_a^b\phi(x)\,dx=\underset{\epsilon=0}{\text{limit}}\int_a^{b-\epsilon}\phi(x)\,dx,\] provided the limits are definite quantities.

Illustrative Example 1. Find \(\displaystyle\int_0^a \frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}\).

Solution. Here \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}\) becomes infinite for \(x=a\). Therefore, by \((B)\),

\[\int_0^a \frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}} = \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon=0}\int_0^{a-\epsilon}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}} = \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon=0}\left[\arcsin\frac{x}{a}\right]_0^{a-\epsilon}\] \[= \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon=0}\left[\arcsin\left(1-\frac{\epsilon}{a}\right)\right] = \arcsin 1 = \frac{\pi}{2}. \quad \textit{Ans.}\]

Illustrative Example 2. Find \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{dx}{x^2}\).

Solution. Here \(\dfrac{1}{x^2}\) becomes infinite for \(x=0\). Therefore, by \((A)\),

\[\int_0^1\frac{dx}{x^2} = \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon=0}\int_\epsilon^1\frac{dx}{x^2} = \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon=0}\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}-1\right).\]

In this case there is no limit and therefore the integral does not exist.

If \(c\) lies between \(a\) and \(b\), and \(\phi\,(x)\) is continuous except at \(x=c\), then, \(\epsilon\) and \(\epsilon'\) being positive numbers, the integral between \(a\) and \(b\) is defined by

\[(C)\qquad \int_a^b \phi\,(x)\,dx = \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon=0}\int_a^{c-\epsilon}\phi\,(x)\,dx + \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon'=0}\int_{c+\epsilon'}^b\phi\,(x)\,dx,\]

provided each separate limit is a definite quantity.

Illustrative Example 1. Find \(\displaystyle\int_0^{3a}\frac{2\,x\,dx}{(x^2-a^2)^{\frac{2}{3}}}\).

Solution. Here the function to be integrated becomes infinite for \(x=a\), i.e. for a value of \(x\) between the limits of integration 0 and \(3\,a\). Hence the above definition \((C)\) must be employed. Thus

\[\int_0^{3a}\frac{2\,x\,dx}{(x^2-a^2)^{\frac{2}{3}}} = \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon=0}\int_0^{a-\epsilon}\frac{2\,x\,dx}{(x^2-a^2)^{\frac{2}{3}}} + \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon'=0}\int_{a+\epsilon'}^{3a}\frac{2\,x\,dx}{(x^2-a^2)^{\frac{2}{3}}}\] \[= \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon=0}\left[3\,(x^2-a^2)^{\frac{1}{3}}\right]_0^{a-\epsilon} + \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon'=0}\left[3\,(x^2-a^2)^{\frac{1}{3}}\right]_{a+\epsilon'}^{3a}\] \[= \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon=0}\left[3\,\sqrt[3]{(a-\epsilon)^2-a^2}+3\,a^{\frac{2}{3}}\right] + \mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon'=0}\left[3\,\sqrt[3]{8\,a^2}-3\,\sqrt[3]{(a+\epsilon')^2-a^2}\right]\] \[= 3\,a^{\frac{2}{3}}+6\,a^{\frac{2}{3}} = 9\,a^{\frac{2}{3}}. \quad \textit{Ans.}\]

To interpret this geometrically, let us plot the graph, i.e. the locus, of

\[y = \frac{2\,x}{(x^2-a^2)^{\frac{2}{3}}},\]

and note that \(x=a\) is an asymptote.

\[\text{area } OPE = \int_0^{a-\epsilon}\frac{2\,x\,dx}{(x^2-a^2)^{\frac{2}{3}}}\] \[= 3\,\sqrt[3]{(a-\epsilon)^2-a^2}+3\,a^{\frac{2}{3}}.\]

Now as \(PE\) moves to the right toward the asymptote, i.e. as \(\epsilon\) approaches zero,

\[3\,\sqrt[3]{(a-\epsilon)^2-a^2}+3\,a^{\frac{2}{3}}\]

is always finite, and

\[\mathop{\text{limit}}_{\epsilon=0}\left[3\,\sqrt[3]{(a-\epsilon)^2-a^2}+3\,a^{\frac{2}{3}}\right] = 3\,a^{\frac{2}{3}},\]

which is also finite. As in Illustrative Example 1, p. 323, \(3\,a^{\frac{2}{3}}\) is called the area bounded by \(OP\), the asymptote, and \(OX\). Similarly, \[\text{area } E'QRG = \int_{a+\epsilon'}^{3a} \frac{2\,x\,dx}{(x^2-a^2)^{\frac{2}{3}}} = 3\sqrt[3]{8\,a^2} - 3\sqrt[3]{(a+\epsilon')^2-a^2}\] is always finite as \(QE'\) moves to the left toward the asymptote, and as \(\epsilon'\) approaches zero, the result \(6\,a^{\frac{2}{3}}\) is also finite. Hence \(6\,a^{\frac{2}{3}}\) is called the area between \(QR\), the asymptote, the ordinate \(x=3\,a\), and \(OX\). Adding these results, we get \(9\,a^{\frac{2}{3}}\), which is then called the area to the right of \(OY\) between the curve, the ordinate \(x=3\,a\), and \(OX\).

Illustrative Example 2. Find \(\displaystyle\int_0^{2a}\frac{dx}{(x-a)^2}\).

Solution. This function also becomes infinite between the limits of integration. Hence, by \((C)\), \[\int_0^{2a}\frac{dx}{(x-a)^2} = \underset{\epsilon=0}{\text{limit}}\int_0^{a-\epsilon}\frac{dx}{(x-a)^2} + \underset{\epsilon'=0}{\text{limit}}\int_{a+\epsilon}^{2a}\frac{dx}{(x-a)^2}\] \[= \underset{\epsilon=0}{\text{limit}}\left[-\frac{1}{x-a}\right]_0^{a-\epsilon} + \underset{\epsilon'=0}{\text{limit}}\left[-\frac{1}{x-a}\right]_{a+\epsilon'}^{2a}\] \[= \underset{\epsilon=0}{\text{limit}}\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}-\frac{1}{a}\right) + \underset{\epsilon'=0}{\text{limit}}\left(-\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{\epsilon'}\right).\]

In this case the limits do not exist and the integral has no meaning.

If we plot the graph of this function and note the limits, the condition of things appears very much the same as in the last example. It turns out, however, that the shaded portion cannot be properly spoken of as an area, and the integral sign has no meaning in this case.

That it is important to note whether or not the given function becomes infinite within the limits of integration will appear at once if we apply our integration formula without any investigation. Thus \[\int_0^{2a}\frac{dx}{(x-a)^2} = \left[-\frac{1}{x-a}\right]_0^{2a} = -\frac{2}{a},\] a result which is absurd in view of the above discussions.

Examples

1. \(\displaystyle\int_0^{+\infty}\frac{dx}{a^2+x^2}=\frac{\pi}{2\,a}\).

2. \(\displaystyle\int_1^{+\infty}\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{2\,x^2-1}}=\frac{\pi}{4}\).

3. \(\displaystyle\int_1^{+\infty}\frac{dx}{x^4}=\frac{1}{3}\).

4. \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\infty}\frac{dx}{a^2+b^2x^2}=\frac{\pi}{2\,ab}\).

5. \(\displaystyle\int_1^{\infty}\frac{dx}{x^2}=1\).

6. \(\displaystyle\int_0^{+\infty}e^{-x}dx=1\).

7. \(\displaystyle\int_0^{+\infty}e^{-ax}dx=\frac{1}{a}\).

8. \(\displaystyle\int_a^{+\infty}\frac{dx}{(a+x)^n}=\frac{1}{(n-1)(2\,a)^{n-1}}\).

9. \(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{1}e^{x}dx=e\).

10. \(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{dx}{x^2+2\,x+2}=\pi\).

11. \(\displaystyle\int_0^{a}x^2\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx=\frac{\pi a^4}{16}\).

12. \(\displaystyle\int_0^{a}\frac{x^3dx}{(a^2+x^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}=\frac{3\sqrt{2}-4}{2}\,a\).

\chapter*{CHAPTER XXV: INTEGRATION OF RATIONAL FRACTIONS}

\textbf{184. Introduction.} A rational fraction is a fraction the numerator and denominator of which are integral rational functions.$^{*}$ If the degree of the numerator is equal to or greater than that of the denominator, the fraction may be reduced to a mixed quantity by dividing the numerator by the denominator. For example,

\[
\frac{x^4+3x^3}{x^2+2x+1}=x^2+x-3+\frac{5x+3}{x^2+2x+1}.
\]

The last term is a fraction reduced to its lowest terms, having the degree of the numerator less than that of the denominator. It readily appears that the other terms are at once integrable, and hence we need consider only the fraction.

In order to integrate a differential expression involving such a fraction, it is often necessary to resolve it into simpler partial fractions, i.e. to replace it by the algebraic sum of fractions of forms such that we can complete the integration. That this is always possible when the denominator can be broken up into its real prime factors is shown in Algebra.$^{\dagger}$

\textbf{185. Case I.} \textit{When the factors of the denominators are all of the first degree and none repeated.}

To each nonrepeated linear factor, such as $x-a$, there corresponds a partial fraction of the form

\[
\frac{A}{x-a}.
\]

Such a partial fraction may be integrated at once as follows:

\[
\int\frac{A\,dx}{x-a}=A\int\frac{dx}{x-a}
\]
\[
=A\log(x-a)+C.
\]

$^{*}$ That is, the variable is not affected with fractional or negative exponents.

$\dagger$ See Chap. XIX in Hawkes's ``Advanced Algebra,'' Ginn and Company, Boston.


\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Find $\displaystyle\int \frac{(2\,x+3)\,dx}{x^{3}+x^{2}-2\,x}$.

\textbf{Solution.} The factors of the denominator being $x$, $x-1$, $x+2$, we assume $^{*}$

\[ (A)\qquad \frac{2\,x+3}{x(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-1}+\frac{C}{x+2}, \]

where $A$, $B$, $C$ are constants to be determined.

Clearing $(A)$ of fractions, we get

\[ (B)\qquad 2\,x+3=A(x-1)(x+2)+B(x+2)\,x+C(x-1)\,x, \]
\[ 2\,x+3=(A+B+C)\,x^{2}+(A+2\,B-C)\,x-2\,A. \]

Since this equation is an identity, we equate the coefficients of the like powers of $x$ in the two members according to the method of Undetermined Coefficients, and obtain three simultaneous equations

\[ (C)\qquad \left\{\begin{array}{l} A+B+C=0, \\ A+2\,B-C=2, \\ \phantom{A+2\,B}-2\,A=3. \end{array}\right. \]

Solving equations $(C)$, we get

\[ A=-\tfrac{3}{2},\quad B=\tfrac{5}{3},\quad C=-\tfrac{1}{6}. \]

Substituting these values in $(A)$,

\[ \frac{2\,x+3}{x(x-1)(x+2)}=-\frac{3}{2\,x}+\frac{5}{3(x-1)}-\frac{1}{6(x+2)}. \]
\[ \therefore\ \int\frac{2\,x+3}{x(x-1)(x+2)}\,dx=-\frac{3}{2}\int\frac{dx}{x}+\frac{5}{3}\int\frac{dx}{x-1}-\frac{1}{6}\int\frac{dx}{x+2} \]
\[ =-\tfrac{3}{2}\log x+\tfrac{5}{3}\log(x-1)-\tfrac{1}{6}\log(x+2)+\log c \]
\[ =\log\frac{c\,(x-1)^{\frac{5}{3}}}{x^{\frac{3}{2}}(x+2)^{\frac{1}{6}}}.\ \textit{Ans.} \]

A shorter method of finding the values of $A$, $B$, and $C$ from $(B)$ is the following

Let \quad factor $x=0$; then $3=-2\,A$, or \hfill $A=-\tfrac{3}{2}$.

Let \quad factor $x-1=0$, or $x=1$; then $5=3\,B$, or \hfill $B=\ \tfrac{5}{3}$.

Let \quad factor $x+2=0$, or $x=-2$; then $-1=6\,C$, or \hfill $C=-\tfrac{1}{6}$.

A useful exercise is to integrate without determining the constants $A$, $B$, $C$, etc. For instance, in the above example,

\[ \int\frac{(2\,x+3)\,dx}{x(x-1)(x+2)}=\int\frac{A\,dx}{x}+\int\frac{B\,dx}{x-1}+\int\frac{C\,dx}{x+2} \]
\[ =A\log x+B\log(x-1)+C\log(x+2). \]

$^{*}$ In the process of decomposing the fractional part of the given differential neither the integral sign nor $dx$ enters.


\textbf{EXAMPLES} 

1. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(2x-1)\,dx}{(x-1)(x-2)}=\log\frac{(x-2)^{3}}{x-1}+C.$

2. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x\,dx}{(x+1)(x+3)(x+5)}=\frac{1}{8}\log\frac{(x+3)^{6}}{(x+5)^{5}(x+1)}+C.$

3. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(x-1)\,dx}{x^{2}+6x+8}=\log\frac{c\,(x+4)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{(x+2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.$

4. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(3x-1)\,dx}{x^{2}+x-6}=\log\left[c\,(x+3)^{2}(x-2)\right].$

5. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(x^{2}+x-1)\,dx}{x^{3}+x^{2}-6x}=\log\sqrt[6]{x\,(x-2)^{3}(x+3)^{2}}+C.$

6. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(2x^{3}+1)\,dx}{x^{2}+3x+2}=x^{2}-6x+\log\frac{(x+2)^{15}}{x+1}+C.$

7. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^{5}+x^{4}-8}{x^{3}-4x}\,dx=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{x^{2}}{2}+4x+\log\frac{x^{2}(x-2)^{5}}{(x+2)^{3}}+C.$

8. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^{4}\,dx}{(x^{2}-1)(x+2)}=\frac{x^{2}}{2}-2x+\frac{1}{6}\log\frac{x-1}{(x+1)^{3}}+\frac{16}{3}\log(x+2)+C.$

9. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(a-b)\,y\,dy}{y^{2}-(a+b)\,y+ab}=\log\frac{(y-a)^{a}}{(y-b)^{b}}+C.$

10. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(t^{2}+pq)\,dt}{t(t-p)(t+q)}=\log\frac{(t-p)(t+q)}{t}+C.$

11. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(2z^{2}-5)\,dz}{z^{4}-5z^{2}+6}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\log\frac{z-\sqrt{2}}{z+\sqrt{2}}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\log\frac{z-\sqrt{3}}{z+\sqrt{3}}+C.$

12. $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dx}{x^{2}+4x}=\frac{1}{4}\log\frac{5}{3}.$

13. $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{5}\frac{dx}{1+3x+2x^{2}}=\log\frac{11}{6}.$

14. $\displaystyle\int_{3}^{4}\frac{(x^{2}+6x-8)\,dx}{x^{3}-4x}=\log\frac{200}{81}.$

\textbf{186. Case II.} \textit{When the factors of the denominator are all of the first degree and some repeated.}

To every $n$-fold linear factor, such as $(x-a)^{n}$, there corresponds the $n$ partial fractions

\[
\frac{A}{(x-a)^{n}}+\frac{B}{(x-a)^{n-1}}+\cdots+\frac{L}{x-a}.
\]

The last one is integrated as in Case I. The rest are all integrated by means of the power formula. Thus

\[
\int\frac{A\,dx}{(x-a)^{n}}=A\int(x-a)^{-n}\,dx=\frac{A}{(1-n)(x-a)^{n-1}}+C.
\]

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^3+1}{x(x-1)^3}\,dx$.

\textbf{Solution.} Since $x-1$ occurs three times as a factor, we assume
\[ \frac{x^3+1}{x(x-1)^3}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{(x-1)^3}+\frac{C}{(x-1)^2}+\frac{D}{x-1}. \]
Clearing of fractions,
\[ x^3+1=A(x-1)^3+Bx+Cx(x-1)+Dx(x-1)^2. \]
\[ x^3+1=(A+D)x^3+(-3A+C-2D)x^2+(3A+B-C+D)x-A. \]
Equating the coefficients of like powers of $x$, we get the simultaneous equations
\[ A+D=1, \]
\[ -3A+C-2D=0, \]
\[ 3A+B-C+D=0, \]
\[ -A=1. \]
Solving, $A=-1$, $B=2$, $C=1$, $D=2$, and
\[ \frac{x^3+1}{x(x-1)^3}=-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{2}{(x-1)^3}+\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}+\frac{2}{x-1}. \]
\[ \therefore\int\frac{x^3+1}{x(x-1)^3}\,dx=-\log x-\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}-\frac{1}{x-1}+2\log(x-1)+C \]
\[ =-\frac{x}{(x-1)^2}+\log\frac{(x-1)^2}{x}+C. \]

\textbf{EXAMPLES} 

1. $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x-1)^2(x-2)}=\frac{1}{x-1}+\log\frac{x-2}{x-1}+C.$

2. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2dx}{(x+2)^2(x+1)}=\frac{4}{x+2}+\log(x+1)+C.$

3. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(x-8)\,dx}{x^3-4x^2+4x}=\frac{3}{x-2}+\log\frac{(x-2)^2}{x^2}+C.$

4. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2+1}{(x-1)^3}\,dx=-\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}-\frac{2}{x-1}+\log(x-1)+C.$

5. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(x^5-x^3+1)\,dx}{x^4-x^3}=\frac{x^2}{2}+x+\frac{1}{2x^2}+\frac{1}{x}+\log\frac{x-1}{x}+C.$

6. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(3x+2)\,dx}{x(x+1)^3}=\frac{4x+3}{2(x+1)^2}+\log\frac{x^2}{(x+1)^2}+C.$

7. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2dx}{(x+2)^2(x+4)^2}=-\frac{5x+12}{x^2+6x+8}+\log\left(\frac{x+4}{x+2}\right)^2+C.$

8. $\displaystyle\int\frac{y^2dy}{y^3+5y^2+8y+4}=\frac{4}{y+2}+\log(y+1)+C.$

9. \[\int\frac{dt}{(t^2-2)^2}=-\frac{t}{4(t^2-2)}+\frac{1}{8\sqrt{2}}\log\frac{t+\sqrt{2}}{t-\sqrt{2}}+C.\]

10. \[\int\frac{as^2ds}{(s+a)^3}=a\log(s+a)+\frac{2a^2}{s+a}-\frac{a^3}{2(s+a)^2}+C.\]

11. \[\int\left(\frac{m}{z+m}-\frac{nz}{(z+n)^2}\right)dz=\log(z+m)^m(z+n)^{-n}-\frac{n^2}{z+n}+C.\]

12. \[\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{x^2(1+x)}=1-\log 2.\]

13. \[\int_1^\infty\frac{dt}{t(1+t)^2}=\log 2-\frac{1}{2}.\]

14. \[\int_1^4\frac{(1+3x)\,dx}{x+2x^2+x^3}=\log\frac{8}{5}+\frac{3}{5}.\]

\textbf{187. Case III.} \textit{When the denominator contains factors of the second degree but none repeated.}

To every nonrepeated quadratic factor, such as $x^2+px+q$, there corresponds a partial fraction of the form
\[\frac{Ax+B}{x^2+px+q}.\]
This may be integrated as follows:
\[\int\frac{(Ax+B)\,dx}{x^2+px+q}=\int\frac{\left(Ax+\frac{Ap}{2}-\frac{Ap}{2}+B\right)dx}{x^2+px+q}\]
[Adding and subtracting $\frac{Ap}{2}$ in the numerator.]
\[=\int\frac{\left(Ax+\frac{Ap}{2}\right)dx}{x^2+px+q}+\int\frac{\left(-\frac{Ap}{2}+B\right)dx}{x^2+px+q}\]
\[=\frac{A}{2}\int\frac{(2x+p)\,dx}{x^2+px+q}+\left(\frac{2B-Ap}{2}\right)\int\frac{dx}{\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^2+\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)}\]
[Completing the square in the denominator of the second integral.]
\[=\frac{A}{2}\log(x^2+px+q)+\frac{2B-Ap}{\sqrt{4q-p^2}}\arctan\frac{2x+p}{\sqrt{4q-p^2}}+C.\]

Since $x^2+px+q=0$ has imaginary roots, we know from 3, p. 1, that $4q-p^2>0$.


\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Find $\displaystyle\int \frac{4\,dx}{x^3 + 4x}$.

\textbf{Solution.} Assume
\[ \frac{4}{x\,(x^2 + 4)} = \frac{A}{x} + \frac{Bx + C}{x^2 + 4}. \]

Clearing of fractions, $4 = A\,(x^2 + 4) + x\,(Bx + C) = (A + B)x^2 + Cx + 4A$.
Equating the coefficients of like powers of $x$, we get
\[ A + B = 0, \quad C = 0, \quad 4A = 4. \]

This gives $A = 1$, $B = -1$, $C = 0$, so that $\dfrac{4}{x\,(x^2 + 4)} = \dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 4}$.
\[ \therefore \int \frac{4\,dx}{x\,(x^2 + 4)} = \int \frac{dx}{x} - \int \frac{x\,dx}{x^2 + 4} \]
\[ = \log x - \frac{1}{2}\log\,(x^2 + 4) + \log c = \log \frac{cx}{\sqrt{x^2 + 4}}. \quad \textit{Ans.} \]

\textbf{EXAMPLES} 

1. $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{x\,(x^2 + 1)} = \log \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}} + C.$

2. $\displaystyle\int \frac{x\,dx}{(x + 1)\,(x^2 + 4)} = \frac{1}{10}\log \frac{x^2 + 4}{(x + 1)^2} + \frac{2}{5}\arctan \frac{x}{2} + C.$

3. $\displaystyle\int \frac{(2x^2 - 3x - 3)\,dx}{(x - 1)\,(x^2 - 2x + 5)} = \log \frac{(x^2 - 2x + 5)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{x - 1} + \frac{1}{2}\arctan \frac{x - 1}{2} + C.$

4. $\displaystyle\int \frac{x^2 dx}{1 - x^4} = \frac{1}{4}\log \frac{1 + x}{1 - x} - \frac{1}{2}\arctan x + C.$

5. $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{(x^2 + 1)\,(x^2 + x)} = \frac{1}{4}\log \frac{x^4}{(x + 1)^2\,(x^2 + 1)} - \frac{1}{2}\arctan x + C.$

6. $\displaystyle\int \frac{(x^3 - 6)\,dx}{x^4 + 6x^2 + 8} = \log \frac{x^2 + 4}{\sqrt{x^2 + 2}} + \frac{3}{2}\arctan \frac{x}{2} - \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\arctan \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} + C.$

7. $\displaystyle\int \frac{(5x^2 - 1)\,dx}{(x^2 + 3)(x^2 - 2x + 5)} = \log \frac{x^2 - 2x + 5}{x^2 + 3} + \frac{5}{2}\arctan \frac{x - 1}{2} - \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan \frac{x}{\sqrt{3}} + C.$

8. $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{x^3 + 1} = \frac{1}{6}\log \frac{(x + 1)^2}{x^2 - x + 1} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan \frac{2x - 1}{\sqrt{3}} + C.$

9. $\displaystyle\int \frac{z^2 dz}{z^4 + z^2 - 2} = \frac{1}{6}\log \left(\frac{z - 1}{z + 1}\right) + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\arctan \frac{z}{\sqrt{2}} + C.$

10. $\displaystyle\int \frac{4\,dt}{t^4 + 1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\log \frac{t^2 + t\sqrt{2} + 1}{t^2 - t\sqrt{2} + 1} + \sqrt{2}\arctan \frac{t\sqrt{2}}{1 - t^2} + C.$

11. $\displaystyle\int \frac{dy}{1 - y^3} = \frac{1}{6}\log \frac{y^2 + y + 1}{y^2 - 2y + 1} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan \frac{2y + 1}{\sqrt{3}} + C.$

12. $\displaystyle\int_0^3 \frac{2x\,dx}{(1 + x^2)\,(3 + x^2)} = \log \sqrt{\frac{5}{2}}.$

13. $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \frac{2x^2 + x + 3}{(x + 1)\,(x^2 + 1)}\,dx = \log 4 + \frac{\pi}{4}.$

\textbf{188. Case IV.} \textit{When the denominator contains factors of the second degree some of which are repeated.}

To every $n$-fold quadratic factor, such as $(x^2+px+q)^n$, there correspond the $n$ partial fractions

\[
(A)\quad \frac{Ax+B}{(x^2+px+q)^n}+\frac{Cx+D}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}+\cdots+\frac{Lx+M}{x^2+px+q}.
\]

To derive a formula for integrating the first one we proceed as follows:

\[
\int\frac{Ax+B}{(x^2+px+q)^n}\,dx=\int\frac{\left(Ax+\frac{Ap}{2}-\frac{Ap}{2}+B\right)dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}
\]

[Adding and subtracting $\frac{Ap}{2}$ in the numerator.]

\[
=\int\frac{\left(Ax+\frac{Ap}{2}\right)dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}+\int\frac{\left(-\frac{Ap}{2}+B\right)dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}
\]

\[
=\frac{A}{2}\int(x^2+px+q)^{-n}(2x+p)\,dx+\left(\frac{2B-Ap}{2}\right)\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}.
\]

The first one of these may be integrated by \textbf{(4)} p. 284; hence

\[
(B)\quad \int\frac{Ax+B}{(x^2+px+q)^n}\,dx=\frac{A}{2(1-n)(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}
\]
\[
+\left(\frac{2B-Ap}{2}\right)\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}.
\]

Let us now differentiate the function $\dfrac{\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}$. Thus

\[
\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x+\frac{p}{2}}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}\right)=\frac{1}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}-\frac{2(n-1)\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^2}{(x^2+px+q)^n},\ \text{or}
\]

\[
(C)\quad d\left(\frac{x+\frac{p}{2}}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}\right)=\left(\frac{-(2n-3)}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}+\frac{2(n-1)\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)}{(x^2+px+q)^n}\right)dx.
\]

[Since $x^2+px+q=\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^2+\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)$, and $\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^2=(x^2+px+q)-\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)$.]


Integrating both sides of $(C)$,
\[
\frac{x+\frac{p}{2}}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}} = -(2n-3)\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}
+ 2(n-1)\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^{n}},
\]
or, solving for the last integral,
\[
(D)\quad \int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n} = \frac{x+\frac{p}{2}}{2(n-1)\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}
+ \frac{2n-3}{2(n-1)\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)}\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}.
\]
Substituting this result in the second member of $(B)$, we get $^{*}$
\[
(E)\quad \int\frac{(Ax+B)\,dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n} = \frac{A(p^2-4q)+(2B-Ap)(2x+p)}{2(n-1)(4q-p^2)(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}
+ \frac{(2B-Ap)(2n-3)}{(n-1)(4q-p^2)}\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}.
\]
It is seen that our integral has been made to depend on the integration of a rational fraction of the same type in which, however, the quadratic factor occurs only $n-1$ times. By applying the formula $(E)$ $n-1$ times successively it is evident that our integral may be made ultimately to depend on
\[
\int\frac{dx}{x^2+px+q},
\]
and this may be integrated by completing the square, as shown on p. 296.

In the same manner all but the last fraction of $(A)$ may be integrated. But this last fraction, namely,
\[
\frac{Lx+M}{x^2+px+q},
\]
may be integrated by the method already given under the previous case (p. 329).

$^{*}$ $4q-p^2>0$, since $x^2+px+q=0$ has imaginary roots.


\textsc{Illustrative Example} 1. Find $\int \frac{(x^3 + x^2 + 2)\,dx}{(x^2 + 2)^2}$.

\textbf{Solution.} Since $x^2 + 2$ occurs twice as a factor, we assume
\[
\frac{x^3 + x^2 + 2}{(x^2 + 2)^2} = \frac{Ax + B}{(x^2 + 2)^2} + \frac{Cx + D}{x^2 + 2}.
\]
Clearing of fractions, we get
\[
x^3 + x^2 + 2 = Ax + B + (Cx + D)(x^2 + 2).
\]
\[
x^3 + x^2 + 2 = Cx^3 + Dx^2 + (A + 2\,C)x + B + 2\,D.
\]
Equating the coefficients of like powers of $x$,
\[
C = 1, \quad D = 1, \quad A + 2\,C = 0, \quad B + 2\,D = 2.
\]
This gives
\[
A = -2, \quad B = 0, \quad C = 1, \quad D = 1.
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{x^3 + x^2 + 2}{(x^2 + 2)^2} = -\frac{2\,x}{(x^2 + 2)^2} + \frac{x + 1}{x^2 + 2}, \text{ and}
\]
\[
\int \frac{(x^3 + x^2 + 2)\,dx}{(x^2 + 2)^2} = -\int \frac{2\,x\,dx}{(x^2 + 2)^2} + \int \frac{x\,dx}{x^2 + 2} + \int \frac{dx}{x^2 + 2}
\]
\[
= \frac{1}{x^2 + 2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \operatorname{arc\,tan} \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{2} \log (x^2 + 2) + C.
\]

\textsc{Illustrative Example} 2. Find $\int \frac{2\,x^3 + x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx$.

\textbf{Solution.} Since $x^2 + 1$ occurs twice as a factor, we assume
\[
\frac{2\,x^3 + x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2} = \frac{Ax + B}{(x^2 + 1)^2} + \frac{Cx + D}{x^2 + 1}.
\]
Clearing of fractions,
\[
2\,x^3 + x + 3 = Ax + B + (Cx + D)(x^2 + 1).
\]
Equating the coefficients of like powers of $x$ and solving, we get
\[
A = -1, \quad B = 3, \quad C = 2, \quad D = 0.
\]
Hence
\[
\int \frac{2\,x^3 + x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx = \int \frac{-x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx + \int \frac{2\,x\,dx}{x^2 + 1}
\]
\[
= \log (x^2 + 1) + \int \frac{-x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx.
\]
Now apply formula $(E)$, p. 332, to the remaining integral. Here
\[
A = -1, \quad B = 3, \quad p = 0, \quad q = 1, \quad n = 2.
\]
Substituting, we get
\[
\int \frac{-x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx = \frac{1 + 3x}{2\,(x^2 + 1)} + \frac{3}{2} \int \frac{dx}{x^2 + 1} = \frac{1 + 3x}{2\,(x^2 + 1)} + \frac{3}{2} \operatorname{arc\,tan} x.
\]
Therefore
\[
\int \frac{2\,x^3 + x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx = \log (x^2 + 1) + \frac{1 + 3x}{2\,(x^2 + 1)} + \frac{3}{2} \operatorname{arc\,tan} x + C.
\]


\textbf{EXAMPLES} 

1. $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+1)^2}=\frac{x}{2(x^2+1)}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arc\,tan}x+C.$

2. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^3+x-1}{(x^2+2)^2}\,dx=\frac{2-x}{4(x^2+2)}+\log(x^2+2)^{\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}+C.$

3. $\displaystyle\int\frac{2\,x\,dx}{(1+x)(1+x^2)^2}=\frac{1}{4}\log\frac{x^2+1}{(x+1)^2}+\frac{x-1}{2(x^2+1)}+C.$

4. $\displaystyle\int\left(\frac{x^2-a^2}{x^2+a^2}\right)^2dx=x+\frac{2\,a^2x}{x^2+a^2}-2\,a\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{x}{a}+C.$

5. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(4\,x+3)\,dx}{(4\,x^2+3)^3}=\frac{4\,x^3+5\,x-2}{8(4\,x^2+3)^2}+\frac{1}{16\sqrt{3}}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{2\,x}{\sqrt{3}}+C.$

6. $\displaystyle\int\frac{9\,x^3\,dx}{(x^3+1)^2}=-\frac{3\,x}{x^3+1}+\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2-x+1}+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{2\,x-1}{\sqrt{3}}+C.$

7. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^7+x^5+x^3+x}{(x^2+2)^2(x^2+3)^2}\,dx=\frac{5}{2(x^2+2)}+\frac{10}{x^2+3}+\frac{19}{2}\log(x^2+2)-9\log(x^2+3)+C.$

8. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(4\,x^2-8\,x)\,dx}{(x-1)^2(x^2+1)^2}=\frac{3\,x^2-x}{(x-1)(x^2+1)}+\log\frac{(x-1)^2}{x^2+1}+\operatorname{arc\,tan}x+C.$

9. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(3\,x+2)\,dx}{(x^2-3\,x+3)^2}=\frac{13\,x-24}{3(x^2-3\,x+3)}+\frac{26}{3\sqrt{3}}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{2\,x-3}{\sqrt{3}}+C.$

Since a rational function may always be reduced to the quotient of two integral rational functions, i.e. to a rational fraction, it follows from the preceding sections in this chapter that any rational function whose denominator can be broken up into real quadratic and linear factors may be expressed as the algebraic sum of integral rational functions and partial fractions. The terms of this sum have forms all of which we have shown how to integrate. Hence the

\textbf{Theorem.} \textit{The integral of every rational function whose denominator can be broken up into real quadratic and linear factors may be found, and is expressible in terms of algebraic, logarithmic, and inverse-trigonometric functions ; that is, in terms of the elementary functions.}
chapters.text_markdown: # CHAPTER XXV: INTEGRATION OF RATIONAL FRACTIONS **184. Introduction.** A rational fraction is a fraction the numerator and denominator of which are integral rational functions.$^{*}$ If the degree of the numerator is equal to or greater than that of the denominator, the fraction may be reduced to a mixed quantity by dividing the numerator by the denominator. For example, $$\frac{x^4+3x^3}{x^2+2x+1}=x^2+x-3+\frac{5x+3}{x^2+2x+1}.$$ The last term is a fraction reduced to its lowest terms, having the degree of the numerator less than that of the denominator. It readily appears that the other terms are at once integrable, and hence we need consider only the fraction. In order to integrate a differential expression involving such a fraction, it is often necessary to resolve it into simpler partial fractions, i.e. to replace it by the algebraic sum of fractions of forms such that we can complete the integration. That this is always possible when the denominator can be broken up into its real prime factors is shown in Algebra.$^{\dagger}$ **185. Case I.** *When the factors of the denominators are all of the first degree and none repeated.* To each nonrepeated linear factor, such as $x-a$, there corresponds a partial fraction of the form $$\frac{A}{x-a}.$$ Such a partial fraction may be integrated at once as follows: $$\int\frac{A\,dx}{x-a}=A\int\frac{dx}{x-a}$$ $$=A\log(x-a)+C.$$ $^{*}$ That is, the variable is not affected with fractional or negative exponents. $\dagger$ See Chap. XIX in Hawkes's "Advanced Algebra," Ginn and Company, Boston. Illustrative Example 1. Find $\displaystyle\int \frac{(2\,x+3)\,dx}{x^{3}+x^{2}-2\,x}$. **Solution.** The factors of the denominator being $x$, $x-1$, $x+2$, we assume $^{*}$ $$(A)\qquad \frac{2\,x+3}{x(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-1}+\frac{C}{x+2},$$ where $A$, $B$, $C$ are constants to be determined. Clearing $(A)$ of fractions, we get $$(B)\qquad 2\,x+3=A(x-1)(x+2)+B(x+2)\,x+C(x-1)\,x,$$ $$2\,x+3=(A+B+C)\,x^{2}+(A+2\,B-C)\,x-2\,A.$$ Since this equation is an identity, we equate the coefficients of the like powers of $x$ in the two members according to the method of Undetermined Coefficients, and obtain three simultaneous equations $$(C)\qquad \left\{\begin{array}{l} A+B+C=0, \\ A+2\,B-C=2, \\ \phantom{A+2\,B}-2\,A=3. \end{array}\right.$$ Solving equations $(C)$, we get $$A=-\tfrac{3}{2},\quad B=\tfrac{5}{3},\quad C=-\tfrac{1}{6}.$$ Substituting these values in $(A)$, $$\frac{2\,x+3}{x(x-1)(x+2)}=-\frac{3}{2\,x}+\frac{5}{3(x-1)}-\frac{1}{6(x+2)}.$$ $$\therefore\ \int\frac{2\,x+3}{x(x-1)(x+2)}\,dx=-\frac{3}{2}\int\frac{dx}{x}+\frac{5}{3}\int\frac{dx}{x-1}-\frac{1}{6}\int\frac{dx}{x+2}$$ $$=-\tfrac{3}{2}\log x+\tfrac{5}{3}\log(x-1)-\tfrac{1}{6}\log(x+2)+\log c$$ $$=\log\frac{c\,(x-1)^{\frac{5}{3}}}{x^{\frac{3}{2}}(x+2)^{\frac{1}{6}}}.\ \textit{Ans.}$$ A shorter method of finding the values of $A$, $B$, and $C$ from $(B)$ is the following Let factor $x=0$; then $3=-2\,A$, or $A=-\tfrac{3}{2}$. Let factor $x-1=0$, or $x=1$; then $5=3\,B$, or $B=\ \tfrac{5}{3}$. Let factor $x+2=0$, or $x=-2$; then $-1=6\,C$, or $C=-\tfrac{1}{6}$. A useful exercise is to integrate without determining the constants $A$, $B$, $C$, etc. For instance, in the above example, $$\int\frac{(2\,x+3)\,dx}{x(x-1)(x+2)}=\int\frac{A\,dx}{x}+\int\frac{B\,dx}{x-1}+\int\frac{C\,dx}{x+2}$$ $$=A\log x+B\log(x-1)+C\log(x+2).$$ $^{*}$ In the process of decomposing the fractional part of the given differential neither the integral sign nor $dx$ enters. **EXAMPLES** 1\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(2x-1)\,dx}{(x-1)(x-2)}=\log\frac{(x-2)^{3}}{x-1}+C.$ 2\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x\,dx}{(x+1)(x+3)(x+5)}=\frac{1}{8}\log\frac{(x+3)^{6}}{(x+5)^{5}(x+1)}+C.$ 3\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(x-1)\,dx}{x^{2}+6x+8}=\log\frac{c\,(x+4)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{(x+2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.$ 4\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(3x-1)\,dx}{x^{2}+x-6}=\log\left[c\,(x+3)^{2}(x-2)\right].$ 5\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(x^{2}+x-1)\,dx}{x^{3}+x^{2}-6x}=\log\sqrt[6]{x\,(x-2)^{3}(x+3)^{2}}+C.$ 6\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(2x^{3}+1)\,dx}{x^{2}+3x+2}=x^{2}-6x+\log\frac{(x+2)^{15}}{x+1}+C.$ 7\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^{5}+x^{4}-8}{x^{3}-4x}\,dx=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{x^{2}}{2}+4x+\log\frac{x^{2}(x-2)^{5}}{(x+2)^{3}}+C.$ 8\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^{4}\,dx}{(x^{2}-1)(x+2)}=\frac{x^{2}}{2}-2x+\frac{1}{6}\log\frac{x-1}{(x+1)^{3}}+\frac{16}{3}\log(x+2)+C.$ 9\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(a-b)\,y\,dy}{y^{2}-(a+b)\,y+ab}=\log\frac{(y-a)^{a}}{(y-b)^{b}}+C.$ 10\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(t^{2}+pq)\,dt}{t(t-p)(t+q)}=\log\frac{(t-p)(t+q)}{t}+C.$ 11\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(2z^{2}-5)\,dz}{z^{4}-5z^{2}+6}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\log\frac{z-\sqrt{2}}{z+\sqrt{2}}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\log\frac{z-\sqrt{3}}{z+\sqrt{3}}+C.$ 12\. $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dx}{x^{2}+4x}=\frac{1}{4}\log\frac{5}{3}.$ 13\. $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{5}\frac{dx}{1+3x+2x^{2}}=\log\frac{11}{6}.$ 14\. $\displaystyle\int_{3}^{4}\frac{(x^{2}+6x-8)\,dx}{x^{3}-4x}=\log\frac{200}{81}.$ **186. Case II.** *When the factors of the denominator are all of the first degree and some repeated.* To every $n$-fold linear factor, such as $(x-a)^{n}$, there corresponds the $n$ partial fractions $$\frac{A}{(x-a)^{n}}+\frac{B}{(x-a)^{n-1}}+\cdots+\frac{L}{x-a}.$$ The last one is integrated as in Case I. The rest are all integrated by means of the power formula. Thus $$\int\frac{A\,dx}{(x-a)^{n}}=A\int(x-a)^{-n}\,dx=\frac{A}{(1-n)(x-a)^{n-1}}+C.$$ Illustrative Example 1. Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^3+1}{x(x-1)^3}\,dx$. **Solution.** Since $x-1$ occurs three times as a factor, we assume $$\frac{x^3+1}{x(x-1)^3}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{(x-1)^3}+\frac{C}{(x-1)^2}+\frac{D}{x-1}.$$ Clearing of fractions, $$x^3+1=A(x-1)^3+Bx+Cx(x-1)+Dx(x-1)^2.$$ $$x^3+1=(A+D)x^3+(-3A+C-2D)x^2+(3A+B-C+D)x-A.$$ Equating the coefficients of like powers of $x$, we get the simultaneous equations $$A+D=1,$$ $$-3A+C-2D=0,$$ $$3A+B-C+D=0,$$ $$-A=1.$$ Solving, $A=-1$, $B=2$, $C=1$, $D=2$, and $$\frac{x^3+1}{x(x-1)^3}=-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{2}{(x-1)^3}+\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}+\frac{2}{x-1}.$$ $$\therefore\int\frac{x^3+1}{x(x-1)^3}\,dx=-\log x-\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}-\frac{1}{x-1}+2\log(x-1)+C$$ $$=-\frac{x}{(x-1)^2}+\log\frac{(x-1)^2}{x}+C.$$ **EXAMPLES** 1\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x-1)^2(x-2)}=\frac{1}{x-1}+\log\frac{x-2}{x-1}+C.$ 2\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2dx}{(x+2)^2(x+1)}=\frac{4}{x+2}+\log(x+1)+C.$ 3\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(x-8)\,dx}{x^3-4x^2+4x}=\frac{3}{x-2}+\log\frac{(x-2)^2}{x^2}+C.$ 4\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2+1}{(x-1)^3}\,dx=-\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}-\frac{2}{x-1}+\log(x-1)+C.$ 5\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(x^5-x^3+1)\,dx}{x^4-x^3}=\frac{x^2}{2}+x+\frac{1}{2x^2}+\frac{1}{x}+\log\frac{x-1}{x}+C.$ 6\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(3x+2)\,dx}{x(x+1)^3}=\frac{4x+3}{2(x+1)^2}+\log\frac{x^2}{(x+1)^2}+C.$ 7\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2dx}{(x+2)^2(x+4)^2}=-\frac{5x+12}{x^2+6x+8}+\log\left(\frac{x+4}{x+2}\right)^2+C.$ 8\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{y^2dy}{y^3+5y^2+8y+4}=\frac{4}{y+2}+\log(y+1)+C.$ 9\. $$\int\frac{dt}{(t^2-2)^2}=-\frac{t}{4(t^2-2)}+\frac{1}{8\sqrt{2}}\log\frac{t+\sqrt{2}}{t-\sqrt{2}}+C.$$ 10\. $$\int\frac{as^2ds}{(s+a)^3}=a\log(s+a)+\frac{2a^2}{s+a}-\frac{a^3}{2(s+a)^2}+C.$$ 11\. $$\int\left(\frac{m}{z+m}-\frac{nz}{(z+n)^2}\right)dz=\log(z+m)^m(z+n)^{-n}-\frac{n^2}{z+n}+C.$$ 12\. $$\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{x^2(1+x)}=1-\log 2.$$ 13\. $$\int_1^\infty\frac{dt}{t(1+t)^2}=\log 2-\frac{1}{2}.$$ 14\. $$\int_1^4\frac{(1+3x)\,dx}{x+2x^2+x^3}=\log\frac{8}{5}+\frac{3}{5}.$$ **187. Case III.** *When the denominator contains factors of the second degree but none repeated.* To every nonrepeated quadratic factor, such as $x^2+px+q$, there corresponds a partial fraction of the form $$\frac{Ax+B}{x^2+px+q}.$$ This may be integrated as follows: $$\int\frac{(Ax+B)\,dx}{x^2+px+q}=\int\frac{\left(Ax+\frac{Ap}{2}-\frac{Ap}{2}+B\right)dx}{x^2+px+q}$$ \[Adding and subtracting $\frac{Ap}{2}$ in the numerator.\] $$=\int\frac{\left(Ax+\frac{Ap}{2}\right)dx}{x^2+px+q}+\int\frac{\left(-\frac{Ap}{2}+B\right)dx}{x^2+px+q}$$ $$=\frac{A}{2}\int\frac{(2x+p)\,dx}{x^2+px+q}+\left(\frac{2B-Ap}{2}\right)\int\frac{dx}{\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^2+\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)}$$ \[Completing the square in the denominator of the second integral.\] $$=\frac{A}{2}\log(x^2+px+q)+\frac{2B-Ap}{\sqrt{4q-p^2}}\arctan\frac{2x+p}{\sqrt{4q-p^2}}+C.$$ Since $x^2+px+q=0$ has imaginary roots, we know from 3, p. 1, that $4q-p^2>0$. Illustrative Example 1. Find $\displaystyle\int \frac{4\,dx}{x^3 + 4x}$. **Solution.** Assume $$\frac{4}{x\,(x^2 + 4)} = \frac{A}{x} + \frac{Bx + C}{x^2 + 4}.$$ Clearing of fractions, $4 = A\,(x^2 + 4) + x\,(Bx + C) = (A + B)x^2 + Cx + 4A$. Equating the coefficients of like powers of $x$, we get $$A + B = 0, \quad C = 0, \quad 4A = 4.$$ This gives $A = 1$, $B = -1$, $C = 0$, so that $\dfrac{4}{x\,(x^2 + 4)} = \dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 4}$. $$\therefore \int \frac{4\,dx}{x\,(x^2 + 4)} = \int \frac{dx}{x} - \int \frac{x\,dx}{x^2 + 4}$$ $$= \log x - \frac{1}{2}\log\,(x^2 + 4) + \log c = \log \frac{cx}{\sqrt{x^2 + 4}}. \quad \textit{Ans.}$$ **EXAMPLES** 1\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{x\,(x^2 + 1)} = \log \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}} + C.$ 2\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{x\,dx}{(x + 1)\,(x^2 + 4)} = \frac{1}{10}\log \frac{x^2 + 4}{(x + 1)^2} + \frac{2}{5}\arctan \frac{x}{2} + C.$ 3\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{(2x^2 - 3x - 3)\,dx}{(x - 1)\,(x^2 - 2x + 5)} = \log \frac{(x^2 - 2x + 5)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{x - 1} + \frac{1}{2}\arctan \frac{x - 1}{2} + C.$ 4\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{x^2 dx}{1 - x^4} = \frac{1}{4}\log \frac{1 + x}{1 - x} - \frac{1}{2}\arctan x + C.$ 5\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{(x^2 + 1)\,(x^2 + x)} = \frac{1}{4}\log \frac{x^4}{(x + 1)^2\,(x^2 + 1)} - \frac{1}{2}\arctan x + C.$ 6\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{(x^3 - 6)\,dx}{x^4 + 6x^2 + 8} = \log \frac{x^2 + 4}{\sqrt{x^2 + 2}} + \frac{3}{2}\arctan \frac{x}{2} - \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\arctan \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} + C.$ 7\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{(5x^2 - 1)\,dx}{(x^2 + 3)(x^2 - 2x + 5)} = \log \frac{x^2 - 2x + 5}{x^2 + 3} + \frac{5}{2}\arctan \frac{x - 1}{2} - \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan \frac{x}{\sqrt{3}} + C.$ 8\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{x^3 + 1} = \frac{1}{6}\log \frac{(x + 1)^2}{x^2 - x + 1} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan \frac{2x - 1}{\sqrt{3}} + C.$ 9\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{z^2 dz}{z^4 + z^2 - 2} = \frac{1}{6}\log \left(\frac{z - 1}{z + 1}\right) + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\arctan \frac{z}{\sqrt{2}} + C.$ 10\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{4\,dt}{t^4 + 1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\log \frac{t^2 + t\sqrt{2} + 1}{t^2 - t\sqrt{2} + 1} + \sqrt{2}\arctan \frac{t\sqrt{2}}{1 - t^2} + C.$ 11\. $\displaystyle\int \frac{dy}{1 - y^3} = \frac{1}{6}\log \frac{y^2 + y + 1}{y^2 - 2y + 1} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan \frac{2y + 1}{\sqrt{3}} + C.$ 12\. $\displaystyle\int_0^3 \frac{2x\,dx}{(1 + x^2)\,(3 + x^2)} = \log \sqrt{\frac{5}{2}}.$ 13\. $\displaystyle\int_0^1 \frac{2x^2 + x + 3}{(x + 1)\,(x^2 + 1)}\,dx = \log 4 + \frac{\pi}{4}.$ **188. Case IV.** *When the denominator contains factors of the second degree some of which are repeated.* To every $n$-fold quadratic factor, such as $(x^2+px+q)^n$, there correspond the $n$ partial fractions $$(A)\quad \frac{Ax+B}{(x^2+px+q)^n}+\frac{Cx+D}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}+\cdots+\frac{Lx+M}{x^2+px+q}.$$ To derive a formula for integrating the first one we proceed as follows: $$\int\frac{Ax+B}{(x^2+px+q)^n}\,dx=\int\frac{\left(Ax+\frac{Ap}{2}-\frac{Ap}{2}+B\right)dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}$$ \[Adding and subtracting $\frac{Ap}{2}$ in the numerator.\] $$=\int\frac{\left(Ax+\frac{Ap}{2}\right)dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}+\int\frac{\left(-\frac{Ap}{2}+B\right)dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}$$ $$=\frac{A}{2}\int(x^2+px+q)^{-n}(2x+p)\,dx+\left(\frac{2B-Ap}{2}\right)\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}.$$ The first one of these may be integrated by **(4)** p. 284; hence $$(B)\quad \int\frac{Ax+B}{(x^2+px+q)^n}\,dx=\frac{A}{2(1-n)(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}$$ $$+\left(\frac{2B-Ap}{2}\right)\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}.$$ Let us now differentiate the function $\dfrac{\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}$. Thus $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x+\frac{p}{2}}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}\right)=\frac{1}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}-\frac{2(n-1)\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^2}{(x^2+px+q)^n},\ \text{or}$$ $$(C)\quad d\left(\frac{x+\frac{p}{2}}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}\right)=\left(\frac{-(2n-3)}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}+\frac{2(n-1)\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)}{(x^2+px+q)^n}\right)dx.$$ \[Since $x^2+px+q=\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^2+\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)$, and $\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^2=(x^2+px+q)-\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)$.\] Integrating both sides of $(C)$, $$\frac{x+\frac{p}{2}}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}} = -(2n-3)\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}} + 2(n-1)\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^{n}},$$ or, solving for the last integral, $$(D)\quad \int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n} = \frac{x+\frac{p}{2}}{2(n-1)\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}} + \frac{2n-3}{2(n-1)\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)}\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}.$$ Substituting this result in the second member of $(B)$, we get $^{*}$ $$(E)\quad \int\frac{(Ax+B)\,dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n} = \frac{A(p^2-4q)+(2B-Ap)(2x+p)}{2(n-1)(4q-p^2)(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}} + \frac{(2B-Ap)(2n-3)}{(n-1)(4q-p^2)}\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}.$$ It is seen that our integral has been made to depend on the integration of a rational fraction of the same type in which, however, the quadratic factor occurs only $n-1$ times. By applying the formula $(E)$ $n-1$ times successively it is evident that our integral may be made ultimately to depend on $$\int\frac{dx}{x^2+px+q},$$ and this may be integrated by completing the square, as shown on p. 296. In the same manner all but the last fraction of $(A)$ may be integrated. But this last fraction, namely, $$\frac{Lx+M}{x^2+px+q},$$ may be integrated by the method already given under the previous case (p. 329). $^{*}$ $4q-p^2>0$, since $x^2+px+q=0$ has imaginary roots. Illustrative Example 1. Find $\int \frac{(x^3 + x^2 + 2)\,dx}{(x^2 + 2)^2}$. **Solution.** Since $x^2 + 2$ occurs twice as a factor, we assume $$\frac{x^3 + x^2 + 2}{(x^2 + 2)^2} = \frac{Ax + B}{(x^2 + 2)^2} + \frac{Cx + D}{x^2 + 2}.$$ Clearing of fractions, we get $$x^3 + x^2 + 2 = Ax + B + (Cx + D)(x^2 + 2).$$ $$x^3 + x^2 + 2 = Cx^3 + Dx^2 + (A + 2\,C)x + B + 2\,D.$$ Equating the coefficients of like powers of $x$, $$C = 1, \quad D = 1, \quad A + 2\,C = 0, \quad B + 2\,D = 2.$$ This gives $$A = -2, \quad B = 0, \quad C = 1, \quad D = 1.$$ Hence $$\frac{x^3 + x^2 + 2}{(x^2 + 2)^2} = -\frac{2\,x}{(x^2 + 2)^2} + \frac{x + 1}{x^2 + 2}, \text{ and}$$ $$\int \frac{(x^3 + x^2 + 2)\,dx}{(x^2 + 2)^2} = -\int \frac{2\,x\,dx}{(x^2 + 2)^2} + \int \frac{x\,dx}{x^2 + 2} + \int \frac{dx}{x^2 + 2}$$ $$= \frac{1}{x^2 + 2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \operatorname{arc\,tan} \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{2} \log (x^2 + 2) + C.$$ Illustrative Example 2. Find $\int \frac{2\,x^3 + x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx$. **Solution.** Since $x^2 + 1$ occurs twice as a factor, we assume $$\frac{2\,x^3 + x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2} = \frac{Ax + B}{(x^2 + 1)^2} + \frac{Cx + D}{x^2 + 1}.$$ Clearing of fractions, $$2\,x^3 + x + 3 = Ax + B + (Cx + D)(x^2 + 1).$$ Equating the coefficients of like powers of $x$ and solving, we get $$A = -1, \quad B = 3, \quad C = 2, \quad D = 0.$$ Hence $$\int \frac{2\,x^3 + x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx = \int \frac{-x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx + \int \frac{2\,x\,dx}{x^2 + 1}$$ $$= \log (x^2 + 1) + \int \frac{-x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx.$$ Now apply formula $(E)$, p. 332, to the remaining integral. Here $$A = -1, \quad B = 3, \quad p = 0, \quad q = 1, \quad n = 2.$$ Substituting, we get $$\int \frac{-x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx = \frac{1 + 3x}{2\,(x^2 + 1)} + \frac{3}{2} \int \frac{dx}{x^2 + 1} = \frac{1 + 3x}{2\,(x^2 + 1)} + \frac{3}{2} \operatorname{arc\,tan} x.$$ Therefore $$\int \frac{2\,x^3 + x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx = \log (x^2 + 1) + \frac{1 + 3x}{2\,(x^2 + 1)} + \frac{3}{2} \operatorname{arc\,tan} x + C.$$ **EXAMPLES** 1\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+1)^2}=\frac{x}{2(x^2+1)}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arc\,tan}x+C.$ 2\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^3+x-1}{(x^2+2)^2}\,dx=\frac{2-x}{4(x^2+2)}+\log(x^2+2)^{\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}+C.$ 3\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{2\,x\,dx}{(1+x)(1+x^2)^2}=\frac{1}{4}\log\frac{x^2+1}{(x+1)^2}+\frac{x-1}{2(x^2+1)}+C.$ 4\. $\displaystyle\int\left(\frac{x^2-a^2}{x^2+a^2}\right)^2dx=x+\frac{2\,a^2x}{x^2+a^2}-2\,a\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{x}{a}+C.$ 5\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(4\,x+3)\,dx}{(4\,x^2+3)^3}=\frac{4\,x^3+5\,x-2}{8(4\,x^2+3)^2}+\frac{1}{16\sqrt{3}}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{2\,x}{\sqrt{3}}+C.$ 6\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{9\,x^3\,dx}{(x^3+1)^2}=-\frac{3\,x}{x^3+1}+\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2-x+1}+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{2\,x-1}{\sqrt{3}}+C.$ 7\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^7+x^5+x^3+x}{(x^2+2)^2(x^2+3)^2}\,dx=\frac{5}{2(x^2+2)}+\frac{10}{x^2+3}+\frac{19}{2}\log(x^2+2)-9\log(x^2+3)+C.$ 8\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(4\,x^2-8\,x)\,dx}{(x-1)^2(x^2+1)^2}=\frac{3\,x^2-x}{(x-1)(x^2+1)}+\log\frac{(x-1)^2}{x^2+1}+\operatorname{arc\,tan}x+C.$ 9\. $\displaystyle\int\frac{(3\,x+2)\,dx}{(x^2-3\,x+3)^2}=\frac{13\,x-24}{3(x^2-3\,x+3)}+\frac{26}{3\sqrt{3}}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{2\,x-3}{\sqrt{3}}+C.$ Since a rational function may always be reduced to the quotient of two integral rational functions, i.e. to a rational fraction, it follows from the preceding sections in this chapter that any rational function whose denominator can be broken up into real quadratic and linear factors may be expressed as the algebraic sum of integral rational functions and partial fractions. The terms of this sum have forms all of which we have shown how to integrate. Hence the **Theorem.** *The integral of every rational function whose denominator can be broken up into real quadratic and linear factors may be found, and is expressible in terms of algebraic, logarithmic, and inverse-trigonometric functions ; that is, in terms of the elementary functions.*

CHAPTER XXV: INTEGRATION OF RATIONAL FRACTIONS

184. Introduction. A rational fraction is a fraction the numerator and denominator of which are integral rational functions.\(^{*}\) If the degree of the numerator is equal to or greater than that of the denominator, the fraction may be reduced to a mixed quantity by dividing the numerator by the denominator. For example,

\[\frac{x^4+3x^3}{x^2+2x+1}=x^2+x-3+\frac{5x+3}{x^2+2x+1}.\]

The last term is a fraction reduced to its lowest terms, having the degree of the numerator less than that of the denominator. It readily appears that the other terms are at once integrable, and hence we need consider only the fraction.

In order to integrate a differential expression involving such a fraction, it is often necessary to resolve it into simpler partial fractions, i.e. to replace it by the algebraic sum of fractions of forms such that we can complete the integration. That this is always possible when the denominator can be broken up into its real prime factors is shown in Algebra.\(^{\dagger}\)

185. Case I. When the factors of the denominators are all of the first degree and none repeated.

To each nonrepeated linear factor, such as \(x-a\), there corresponds a partial fraction of the form

\[\frac{A}{x-a}.\]

Such a partial fraction may be integrated at once as follows:

\[\int\frac{A\,dx}{x-a}=A\int\frac{dx}{x-a}\] \[=A\log(x-a)+C.\]

\(^{*}\) That is, the variable is not affected with fractional or negative exponents.

\(\dagger\) See Chap. XIX in Hawkes’s “Advanced Algebra,” Ginn and Company, Boston.

Illustrative Example 1. Find \(\displaystyle\int \frac{(2\,x+3)\,dx}{x^{3}+x^{2}-2\,x}\).

Solution. The factors of the denominator being \(x\), \(x-1\), \(x+2\), we assume \(^{*}\)

\[(A)\qquad \frac{2\,x+3}{x(x-1)(x+2)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-1}+\frac{C}{x+2},\]

where \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) are constants to be determined.

Clearing \((A)\) of fractions, we get

\[(B)\qquad 2\,x+3=A(x-1)(x+2)+B(x+2)\,x+C(x-1)\,x,\] \[2\,x+3=(A+B+C)\,x^{2}+(A+2\,B-C)\,x-2\,A.\]

Since this equation is an identity, we equate the coefficients of the like powers of \(x\) in the two members according to the method of Undetermined Coefficients, and obtain three simultaneous equations

\[(C)\qquad \left\{\begin{array}{l} A+B+C=0, \\ A+2\,B-C=2, \\ \phantom{A+2\,B}-2\,A=3. \end{array}\right.\]

Solving equations \((C)\), we get

\[A=-\tfrac{3}{2},\quad B=\tfrac{5}{3},\quad C=-\tfrac{1}{6}.\]

Substituting these values in \((A)\),

\[\frac{2\,x+3}{x(x-1)(x+2)}=-\frac{3}{2\,x}+\frac{5}{3(x-1)}-\frac{1}{6(x+2)}.\] \[\therefore\ \int\frac{2\,x+3}{x(x-1)(x+2)}\,dx=-\frac{3}{2}\int\frac{dx}{x}+\frac{5}{3}\int\frac{dx}{x-1}-\frac{1}{6}\int\frac{dx}{x+2}\] \[=-\tfrac{3}{2}\log x+\tfrac{5}{3}\log(x-1)-\tfrac{1}{6}\log(x+2)+\log c\] \[=\log\frac{c\,(x-1)^{\frac{5}{3}}}{x^{\frac{3}{2}}(x+2)^{\frac{1}{6}}}.\ \textit{Ans.}\]

A shorter method of finding the values of \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) from \((B)\) is the following

Let factor \(x=0\); then \(3=-2\,A\), or \(A=-\tfrac{3}{2}\).

Let factor \(x-1=0\), or \(x=1\); then \(5=3\,B\), or \(B=\ \tfrac{5}{3}\).

Let factor \(x+2=0\), or \(x=-2\); then \(-1=6\,C\), or \(C=-\tfrac{1}{6}\).

A useful exercise is to integrate without determining the constants \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), etc. For instance, in the above example,

\[\int\frac{(2\,x+3)\,dx}{x(x-1)(x+2)}=\int\frac{A\,dx}{x}+\int\frac{B\,dx}{x-1}+\int\frac{C\,dx}{x+2}\] \[=A\log x+B\log(x-1)+C\log(x+2).\]

\(^{*}\) In the process of decomposing the fractional part of the given differential neither the integral sign nor \(dx\) enters.

EXAMPLES

1. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(2x-1)\,dx}{(x-1)(x-2)}=\log\frac{(x-2)^{3}}{x-1}+C.\)

2. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x\,dx}{(x+1)(x+3)(x+5)}=\frac{1}{8}\log\frac{(x+3)^{6}}{(x+5)^{5}(x+1)}+C.\)

3. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(x-1)\,dx}{x^{2}+6x+8}=\log\frac{c\,(x+4)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{(x+2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}.\)

4. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(3x-1)\,dx}{x^{2}+x-6}=\log\left[c\,(x+3)^{2}(x-2)\right].\)

5. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(x^{2}+x-1)\,dx}{x^{3}+x^{2}-6x}=\log\sqrt[6]{x\,(x-2)^{3}(x+3)^{2}}+C.\)

6. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(2x^{3}+1)\,dx}{x^{2}+3x+2}=x^{2}-6x+\log\frac{(x+2)^{15}}{x+1}+C.\)

7. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^{5}+x^{4}-8}{x^{3}-4x}\,dx=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{x^{2}}{2}+4x+\log\frac{x^{2}(x-2)^{5}}{(x+2)^{3}}+C.\)

8. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^{4}\,dx}{(x^{2}-1)(x+2)}=\frac{x^{2}}{2}-2x+\frac{1}{6}\log\frac{x-1}{(x+1)^{3}}+\frac{16}{3}\log(x+2)+C.\)

9. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(a-b)\,y\,dy}{y^{2}-(a+b)\,y+ab}=\log\frac{(y-a)^{a}}{(y-b)^{b}}+C.\)

10. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(t^{2}+pq)\,dt}{t(t-p)(t+q)}=\log\frac{(t-p)(t+q)}{t}+C.\)

11. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(2z^{2}-5)\,dz}{z^{4}-5z^{2}+6}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\log\frac{z-\sqrt{2}}{z+\sqrt{2}}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\log\frac{z-\sqrt{3}}{z+\sqrt{3}}+C.\)

12. \(\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\frac{dx}{x^{2}+4x}=\frac{1}{4}\log\frac{5}{3}.\)

13. \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{5}\frac{dx}{1+3x+2x^{2}}=\log\frac{11}{6}.\)

14. \(\displaystyle\int_{3}^{4}\frac{(x^{2}+6x-8)\,dx}{x^{3}-4x}=\log\frac{200}{81}.\)

186. Case II. When the factors of the denominator are all of the first degree and some repeated.

To every \(n\)-fold linear factor, such as \((x-a)^{n}\), there corresponds the \(n\) partial fractions

\[\frac{A}{(x-a)^{n}}+\frac{B}{(x-a)^{n-1}}+\cdots+\frac{L}{x-a}.\]

The last one is integrated as in Case I. The rest are all integrated by means of the power formula. Thus

\[\int\frac{A\,dx}{(x-a)^{n}}=A\int(x-a)^{-n}\,dx=\frac{A}{(1-n)(x-a)^{n-1}}+C.\]

Illustrative Example 1. Find \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^3+1}{x(x-1)^3}\,dx\).

Solution. Since \(x-1\) occurs three times as a factor, we assume \[\frac{x^3+1}{x(x-1)^3}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{(x-1)^3}+\frac{C}{(x-1)^2}+\frac{D}{x-1}.\] Clearing of fractions, \[x^3+1=A(x-1)^3+Bx+Cx(x-1)+Dx(x-1)^2.\] \[x^3+1=(A+D)x^3+(-3A+C-2D)x^2+(3A+B-C+D)x-A.\] Equating the coefficients of like powers of \(x\), we get the simultaneous equations \[A+D=1,\] \[-3A+C-2D=0,\] \[3A+B-C+D=0,\] \[-A=1.\] Solving, \(A=-1\), \(B=2\), \(C=1\), \(D=2\), and \[\frac{x^3+1}{x(x-1)^3}=-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{2}{(x-1)^3}+\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}+\frac{2}{x-1}.\] \[\therefore\int\frac{x^3+1}{x(x-1)^3}\,dx=-\log x-\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}-\frac{1}{x-1}+2\log(x-1)+C\] \[=-\frac{x}{(x-1)^2}+\log\frac{(x-1)^2}{x}+C.\]

EXAMPLES

1. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x-1)^2(x-2)}=\frac{1}{x-1}+\log\frac{x-2}{x-1}+C.\)

2. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2dx}{(x+2)^2(x+1)}=\frac{4}{x+2}+\log(x+1)+C.\)

3. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(x-8)\,dx}{x^3-4x^2+4x}=\frac{3}{x-2}+\log\frac{(x-2)^2}{x^2}+C.\)

4. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2+1}{(x-1)^3}\,dx=-\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}-\frac{2}{x-1}+\log(x-1)+C.\)

5. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(x^5-x^3+1)\,dx}{x^4-x^3}=\frac{x^2}{2}+x+\frac{1}{2x^2}+\frac{1}{x}+\log\frac{x-1}{x}+C.\)

6. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(3x+2)\,dx}{x(x+1)^3}=\frac{4x+3}{2(x+1)^2}+\log\frac{x^2}{(x+1)^2}+C.\)

7. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2dx}{(x+2)^2(x+4)^2}=-\frac{5x+12}{x^2+6x+8}+\log\left(\frac{x+4}{x+2}\right)^2+C.\)

8. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{y^2dy}{y^3+5y^2+8y+4}=\frac{4}{y+2}+\log(y+1)+C.\)

9. \[\int\frac{dt}{(t^2-2)^2}=-\frac{t}{4(t^2-2)}+\frac{1}{8\sqrt{2}}\log\frac{t+\sqrt{2}}{t-\sqrt{2}}+C.\]

10. \[\int\frac{as^2ds}{(s+a)^3}=a\log(s+a)+\frac{2a^2}{s+a}-\frac{a^3}{2(s+a)^2}+C.\]

11. \[\int\left(\frac{m}{z+m}-\frac{nz}{(z+n)^2}\right)dz=\log(z+m)^m(z+n)^{-n}-\frac{n^2}{z+n}+C.\]

12. \[\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{x^2(1+x)}=1-\log 2.\]

13. \[\int_1^\infty\frac{dt}{t(1+t)^2}=\log 2-\frac{1}{2}.\]

14. \[\int_1^4\frac{(1+3x)\,dx}{x+2x^2+x^3}=\log\frac{8}{5}+\frac{3}{5}.\]

187. Case III. When the denominator contains factors of the second degree but none repeated.

To every nonrepeated quadratic factor, such as \(x^2+px+q\), there corresponds a partial fraction of the form \[\frac{Ax+B}{x^2+px+q}.\] This may be integrated as follows: \[\int\frac{(Ax+B)\,dx}{x^2+px+q}=\int\frac{\left(Ax+\frac{Ap}{2}-\frac{Ap}{2}+B\right)dx}{x^2+px+q}\] [Adding and subtracting \(\frac{Ap}{2}\) in the numerator.] \[=\int\frac{\left(Ax+\frac{Ap}{2}\right)dx}{x^2+px+q}+\int\frac{\left(-\frac{Ap}{2}+B\right)dx}{x^2+px+q}\] \[=\frac{A}{2}\int\frac{(2x+p)\,dx}{x^2+px+q}+\left(\frac{2B-Ap}{2}\right)\int\frac{dx}{\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^2+\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)}\] [Completing the square in the denominator of the second integral.] \[=\frac{A}{2}\log(x^2+px+q)+\frac{2B-Ap}{\sqrt{4q-p^2}}\arctan\frac{2x+p}{\sqrt{4q-p^2}}+C.\]

Since \(x^2+px+q=0\) has imaginary roots, we know from 3, p. 1, that \(4q-p^2>0\).

Illustrative Example 1. Find \(\displaystyle\int \frac{4\,dx}{x^3 + 4x}\).

Solution. Assume \[\frac{4}{x\,(x^2 + 4)} = \frac{A}{x} + \frac{Bx + C}{x^2 + 4}.\]

Clearing of fractions, \(4 = A\,(x^2 + 4) + x\,(Bx + C) = (A + B)x^2 + Cx + 4A\). Equating the coefficients of like powers of \(x\), we get \[A + B = 0, \quad C = 0, \quad 4A = 4.\]

This gives \(A = 1\), \(B = -1\), \(C = 0\), so that \(\dfrac{4}{x\,(x^2 + 4)} = \dfrac{1}{x} - \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 4}\). \[\therefore \int \frac{4\,dx}{x\,(x^2 + 4)} = \int \frac{dx}{x} - \int \frac{x\,dx}{x^2 + 4}\] \[= \log x - \frac{1}{2}\log\,(x^2 + 4) + \log c = \log \frac{cx}{\sqrt{x^2 + 4}}. \quad \textit{Ans.}\]

EXAMPLES

1. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{x\,(x^2 + 1)} = \log \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 1}} + C.\)

2. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{x\,dx}{(x + 1)\,(x^2 + 4)} = \frac{1}{10}\log \frac{x^2 + 4}{(x + 1)^2} + \frac{2}{5}\arctan \frac{x}{2} + C.\)

3. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{(2x^2 - 3x - 3)\,dx}{(x - 1)\,(x^2 - 2x + 5)} = \log \frac{(x^2 - 2x + 5)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{x - 1} + \frac{1}{2}\arctan \frac{x - 1}{2} + C.\)

4. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{x^2 dx}{1 - x^4} = \frac{1}{4}\log \frac{1 + x}{1 - x} - \frac{1}{2}\arctan x + C.\)

5. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{(x^2 + 1)\,(x^2 + x)} = \frac{1}{4}\log \frac{x^4}{(x + 1)^2\,(x^2 + 1)} - \frac{1}{2}\arctan x + C.\)

6. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{(x^3 - 6)\,dx}{x^4 + 6x^2 + 8} = \log \frac{x^2 + 4}{\sqrt{x^2 + 2}} + \frac{3}{2}\arctan \frac{x}{2} - \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\arctan \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} + C.\)

7. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{(5x^2 - 1)\,dx}{(x^2 + 3)(x^2 - 2x + 5)} = \log \frac{x^2 - 2x + 5}{x^2 + 3} + \frac{5}{2}\arctan \frac{x - 1}{2} - \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan \frac{x}{\sqrt{3}} + C.\)

8. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{x^3 + 1} = \frac{1}{6}\log \frac{(x + 1)^2}{x^2 - x + 1} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan \frac{2x - 1}{\sqrt{3}} + C.\)

9. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{z^2 dz}{z^4 + z^2 - 2} = \frac{1}{6}\log \left(\frac{z - 1}{z + 1}\right) + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\arctan \frac{z}{\sqrt{2}} + C.\)

10. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{4\,dt}{t^4 + 1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\log \frac{t^2 + t\sqrt{2} + 1}{t^2 - t\sqrt{2} + 1} + \sqrt{2}\arctan \frac{t\sqrt{2}}{1 - t^2} + C.\)

11. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{dy}{1 - y^3} = \frac{1}{6}\log \frac{y^2 + y + 1}{y^2 - 2y + 1} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan \frac{2y + 1}{\sqrt{3}} + C.\)

12. \(\displaystyle\int_0^3 \frac{2x\,dx}{(1 + x^2)\,(3 + x^2)} = \log \sqrt{\frac{5}{2}}.\)

13. \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 \frac{2x^2 + x + 3}{(x + 1)\,(x^2 + 1)}\,dx = \log 4 + \frac{\pi}{4}.\)

188. Case IV. When the denominator contains factors of the second degree some of which are repeated.

To every \(n\)-fold quadratic factor, such as \((x^2+px+q)^n\), there correspond the \(n\) partial fractions

\[(A)\quad \frac{Ax+B}{(x^2+px+q)^n}+\frac{Cx+D}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}+\cdots+\frac{Lx+M}{x^2+px+q}.\]

To derive a formula for integrating the first one we proceed as follows:

\[\int\frac{Ax+B}{(x^2+px+q)^n}\,dx=\int\frac{\left(Ax+\frac{Ap}{2}-\frac{Ap}{2}+B\right)dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}\]

[Adding and subtracting \(\frac{Ap}{2}\) in the numerator.]

\[=\int\frac{\left(Ax+\frac{Ap}{2}\right)dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}+\int\frac{\left(-\frac{Ap}{2}+B\right)dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}\]

\[=\frac{A}{2}\int(x^2+px+q)^{-n}(2x+p)\,dx+\left(\frac{2B-Ap}{2}\right)\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}.\]

The first one of these may be integrated by (4) p. 284; hence

\[(B)\quad \int\frac{Ax+B}{(x^2+px+q)^n}\,dx=\frac{A}{2(1-n)(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}\] \[+\left(\frac{2B-Ap}{2}\right)\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n}.\]

Let us now differentiate the function \(\dfrac{\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}\). Thus

\[\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x+\frac{p}{2}}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}\right)=\frac{1}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}-\frac{2(n-1)\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^2}{(x^2+px+q)^n},\ \text{or}\]

\[(C)\quad d\left(\frac{x+\frac{p}{2}}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}\right)=\left(\frac{-(2n-3)}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}+\frac{2(n-1)\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)}{(x^2+px+q)^n}\right)dx.\]

[Since \(x^2+px+q=\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^2+\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)\), and \(\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^2=(x^2+px+q)-\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)\).]

Integrating both sides of \((C)\), \[\frac{x+\frac{p}{2}}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}} = -(2n-3)\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}} + 2(n-1)\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^{n}},\] or, solving for the last integral, \[(D)\quad \int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n} = \frac{x+\frac{p}{2}}{2(n-1)\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}} + \frac{2n-3}{2(n-1)\left(q-\frac{p^2}{4}\right)}\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}.\] Substituting this result in the second member of \((B)\), we get \(^{*}\) \[(E)\quad \int\frac{(Ax+B)\,dx}{(x^2+px+q)^n} = \frac{A(p^2-4q)+(2B-Ap)(2x+p)}{2(n-1)(4q-p^2)(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}} + \frac{(2B-Ap)(2n-3)}{(n-1)(4q-p^2)}\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+px+q)^{n-1}}.\] It is seen that our integral has been made to depend on the integration of a rational fraction of the same type in which, however, the quadratic factor occurs only \(n-1\) times. By applying the formula \((E)\) \(n-1\) times successively it is evident that our integral may be made ultimately to depend on \[\int\frac{dx}{x^2+px+q},\] and this may be integrated by completing the square, as shown on p. 296.

In the same manner all but the last fraction of \((A)\) may be integrated. But this last fraction, namely, \[\frac{Lx+M}{x^2+px+q},\] may be integrated by the method already given under the previous case (p. 329).

\(^{*}\) \(4q-p^2>0\), since \(x^2+px+q=0\) has imaginary roots.

Illustrative Example 1. Find \(\int \frac{(x^3 + x^2 + 2)\,dx}{(x^2 + 2)^2}\).

Solution. Since \(x^2 + 2\) occurs twice as a factor, we assume \[\frac{x^3 + x^2 + 2}{(x^2 + 2)^2} = \frac{Ax + B}{(x^2 + 2)^2} + \frac{Cx + D}{x^2 + 2}.\] Clearing of fractions, we get \[x^3 + x^2 + 2 = Ax + B + (Cx + D)(x^2 + 2).\] \[x^3 + x^2 + 2 = Cx^3 + Dx^2 + (A + 2\,C)x + B + 2\,D.\] Equating the coefficients of like powers of \(x\), \[C = 1, \quad D = 1, \quad A + 2\,C = 0, \quad B + 2\,D = 2.\] This gives \[A = -2, \quad B = 0, \quad C = 1, \quad D = 1.\] Hence \[\frac{x^3 + x^2 + 2}{(x^2 + 2)^2} = -\frac{2\,x}{(x^2 + 2)^2} + \frac{x + 1}{x^2 + 2}, \text{ and}\] \[\int \frac{(x^3 + x^2 + 2)\,dx}{(x^2 + 2)^2} = -\int \frac{2\,x\,dx}{(x^2 + 2)^2} + \int \frac{x\,dx}{x^2 + 2} + \int \frac{dx}{x^2 + 2}\] \[= \frac{1}{x^2 + 2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \operatorname{arc\,tan} \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{2} \log (x^2 + 2) + C.\]

Illustrative Example 2. Find \(\int \frac{2\,x^3 + x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx\).

Solution. Since \(x^2 + 1\) occurs twice as a factor, we assume \[\frac{2\,x^3 + x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2} = \frac{Ax + B}{(x^2 + 1)^2} + \frac{Cx + D}{x^2 + 1}.\] Clearing of fractions, \[2\,x^3 + x + 3 = Ax + B + (Cx + D)(x^2 + 1).\] Equating the coefficients of like powers of \(x\) and solving, we get \[A = -1, \quad B = 3, \quad C = 2, \quad D = 0.\] Hence \[\int \frac{2\,x^3 + x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx = \int \frac{-x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx + \int \frac{2\,x\,dx}{x^2 + 1}\] \[= \log (x^2 + 1) + \int \frac{-x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx.\] Now apply formula \((E)\), p. 332, to the remaining integral. Here \[A = -1, \quad B = 3, \quad p = 0, \quad q = 1, \quad n = 2.\] Substituting, we get \[\int \frac{-x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx = \frac{1 + 3x}{2\,(x^2 + 1)} + \frac{3}{2} \int \frac{dx}{x^2 + 1} = \frac{1 + 3x}{2\,(x^2 + 1)} + \frac{3}{2} \operatorname{arc\,tan} x.\] Therefore \[\int \frac{2\,x^3 + x + 3}{(x^2 + 1)^2}\,dx = \log (x^2 + 1) + \frac{1 + 3x}{2\,(x^2 + 1)} + \frac{3}{2} \operatorname{arc\,tan} x + C.\]

EXAMPLES

1. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+1)^2}=\frac{x}{2(x^2+1)}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arc\,tan}x+C.\)

2. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^3+x-1}{(x^2+2)^2}\,dx=\frac{2-x}{4(x^2+2)}+\log(x^2+2)^{\frac{1}{2}}-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}+C.\)

3. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{2\,x\,dx}{(1+x)(1+x^2)^2}=\frac{1}{4}\log\frac{x^2+1}{(x+1)^2}+\frac{x-1}{2(x^2+1)}+C.\)

4. \(\displaystyle\int\left(\frac{x^2-a^2}{x^2+a^2}\right)^2dx=x+\frac{2\,a^2x}{x^2+a^2}-2\,a\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{x}{a}+C.\)

5. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(4\,x+3)\,dx}{(4\,x^2+3)^3}=\frac{4\,x^3+5\,x-2}{8(4\,x^2+3)^2}+\frac{1}{16\sqrt{3}}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{2\,x}{\sqrt{3}}+C.\)

6. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{9\,x^3\,dx}{(x^3+1)^2}=-\frac{3\,x}{x^3+1}+\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2-x+1}+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{2\,x-1}{\sqrt{3}}+C.\)

7. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^7+x^5+x^3+x}{(x^2+2)^2(x^2+3)^2}\,dx=\frac{5}{2(x^2+2)}+\frac{10}{x^2+3}+\frac{19}{2}\log(x^2+2)-9\log(x^2+3)+C.\)

8. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(4\,x^2-8\,x)\,dx}{(x-1)^2(x^2+1)^2}=\frac{3\,x^2-x}{(x-1)(x^2+1)}+\log\frac{(x-1)^2}{x^2+1}+\operatorname{arc\,tan}x+C.\)

9. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{(3\,x+2)\,dx}{(x^2-3\,x+3)^2}=\frac{13\,x-24}{3(x^2-3\,x+3)}+\frac{26}{3\sqrt{3}}\operatorname{arc\,tan}\frac{2\,x-3}{\sqrt{3}}+C.\)

Since a rational function may always be reduced to the quotient of two integral rational functions, i.e. to a rational fraction, it follows from the preceding sections in this chapter that any rational function whose denominator can be broken up into real quadratic and linear factors may be expressed as the algebraic sum of integral rational functions and partial fractions. The terms of this sum have forms all of which we have shown how to integrate. Hence the

Theorem. The integral of every rational function whose denominator can be broken up into real quadratic and linear factors may be found, and is expressible in terms of algebraic, logarithmic, and inverse-trigonometric functions ; that is, in terms of the elementary functions.
