excerpts.why: Shows the reduction step that lets a repeated quadratic factor be handled by recursion on its power.

excerpts.latex: The integral of every rational function whose denominator can be broken up into real quadratic and linear factors may be found, and is expressible in terms of algebraic, logarithmic, and inverse-trigonometric functions ; that is, in terms of the elementary functions.
excerpts.markdown: The integral of every rational function whose denominator can be broken up into real quadratic and linear factors may be found, and is expressible in terms of algebraic, logarithmic, and inverse-trigonometric functions ; that is, in terms of the elementary functions.
excerpts.why: States the chapter's main result in one sentence, tying the methods to the class of elementary functions.

excerpts.location: INTEGRATION BY SUBSTITUTION OF A NEW VARIABLE. RATIONALIZATION
excerpts.latex: The method of integrating a function that is not rational by substituting for the old variable such a function of a new variable that the result is a rational function is sometimes called \textit{integration by rationalization.} This is a very important artifice in integration and we will now take up some of the more important cases coming under this head.
excerpts.markdown: The method of integrating a function that is not rational by substituting for the old variable such a function of a new variable that the result is a rational function is sometimes called *integration by rationalization.* This is a very important artifice in integration and we will now take up some of the more important cases coming under this head.
excerpts.why: Defines rationalization in the book's own words and tells the learner it is a central trick of integration.

excerpts.location: INTEGRATION BY SUBSTITUTION OF A NEW VARIABLE. RATIONALIZATION
excerpts.latex: Of algebraic functions which are \textit{not rational}, that is, such as contain radicals, only a small number, relatively speaking, can be integrated in terms of elementary functions.
excerpts.markdown: Of algebraic functions which are *not rational*, that is, such as contain radicals, only a small number, relatively speaking, can be integrated in terms of elementary functions.
excerpts.why: Explains why substitution is needed at all: most radical integrands have no elementary integral without a change of variable.

excerpts.location: INTEGRATION BY SUBSTITUTION OF A NEW VARIABLE. RATIONALIZATION
excerpts.latex: The relation between the old and the new variable should be such that to each value of one within the limits of integration there is always one, and only one, finite value of the other.
excerpts.markdown: The relation between the old and the new variable should be such that to each value of one within the limits of integration there is always one, and only one, finite value of the other.
excerpts.why: A warning that a substitution must map the limits one-to-one, so learners do not apply a many-valued substitution blindly.

excerpts.location: INTEGRATION BY SUBSTITUTION OF A NEW VARIABLE. RATIONALIZATION
excerpts.latex: When integrating between limits, however, we may avoid the process of restoring the original variable by changing the limits to correspond with the new variable.
excerpts.markdown: When integrating between limits, however, we may avoid the process of restoring the original variable by changing the limits to correspond with the new variable.
excerpts.why: Shows learners they can convert the limits and skip substituting back, which saves work in definite integrals.

excerpts.location: INTEGRATION BY SUBSTITUTION OF A NEW VARIABLE. RATIONALIZATION
excerpts.latex: In a great number of cases, however, integrations may be effected by means of substitutions which do not rationalize the given differential, but no general rule can be given, and the experience gained in working out a large number of problems must be our guide.
excerpts.markdown: In a great number of cases, however, integrations may be effected by means of substitutions which do not rationalize the given differential, but no general rule can be given, and the experience gained in working out a large number of problems must be our guide.
excerpts.why: Honest statement that substitution is a matter of judgement, which invites learners to practise rather than memorise a rule.

excerpts.location: INTEGRATION BY SUBSTITUTION OF A NEW VARIABLE. RATIONALIZATION
excerpts.latex: It is evident that if a trigonometric differential involves $\tan x$, $\cot x$, $\sec x$, $\csc x$ rationally only, it will be included in the above theorem, since these four functions can be expressed rationally in terms of $\sin x$, or $\cos x$, or both.
excerpts.markdown: It is evident that if a trigonometric differential involves $\tan x$, $\cot x$, $\sec x$, $\csc x$ rationally only, it will be included in the above theorem, since these four functions can be expressed rationally in terms of $\sin x$, or $\cos x$, or both.
excerpts.why: Explains why the half-angle substitution covers tangent, cotangent, secant and cosecant as well as sine and cosine.

excerpts.latex: This method of \textit{integration by parts} is one of the most useful in the Integral Calculus.
excerpts.markdown: This method of *integration by parts* is one of the most useful in the Integral Calculus.
excerpts.why: It tells a learner at once why this technique is worth mastering before any example is worked.

excerpts.latex: This formula makes the integration of $udv$, which we may not be able to integrate directly, depend on the integration of $dv$ and $vdu$, which may be in such form as to be readily integrable.
excerpts.markdown: This formula makes the integration of $udv$, which we may not be able to integrate directly, depend on the integration of $dv$ and $vdu$, which may be in such form as to be readily integrable.
excerpts.why: It explains in plain terms what the formula achieves: a hard integral is traded for two easier ones.

excerpts.latex: But $x^2e^{ax}dx$ is not as simple to integrate as $xe^{ax}dx$, which fact indicates that we did not choose our factors suitably.
excerpts.markdown: But $x^2e^{ax}dx$ is not as simple to integrate as $xe^{ax}dx$, which fact indicates that we did not choose our factors suitably.
excerpts.why: It shows a common mistake in choosing u and dv and how to recognise it from the result.

excerpts.latex: While it is not desirable for the student to memorize these formulas, he should know what each one will do and when each one fails.
excerpts.markdown: While it is not desirable for the student to memorize these formulas, he should know what each one will do and when each one fails.
excerpts.why: It gives learners a practical habit: know what each reduction formula does and where it breaks down.

excerpts.latex: In working out the examples which follow, the student is advised not to use the above results as formulas, but to follow the method by which they were obtained.
excerpts.markdown: In working out the examples which follow, the student is advised not to use the above results as formulas, but to follow the method by which they were obtained.
excerpts.why: It urges learners to rederive a result by method rather than memorise it.

excerpts.latex: Evidently we may consider a solid of revolution as generated by a moving circle of varying radius whose center lies on the axis of revolution and whose plane is perpendicular to it.
excerpts.markdown: Evidently we may consider a solid of revolution as generated by a moving circle of varying radius whose center lies on the axis of revolution and whose plane is perpendicular to it.
excerpts.why: It gives learners a clear picture of how a solid of revolution is built from a moving circle before any integral is set up.

excerpts.latex: Suppose we divide the solid shown in our figure into $n$ slices by sections perpendicular to $OX$ and take the origin as our fixed point.
excerpts.markdown: Suppose we divide the solid shown in our figure into $n$ slices by sections perpendicular to $OX$ and take the origin as our fixed point.
excerpts.why: It shows the slicing step that turns a volume into a sum of prism volumes, which is the core idea of integration by sections.

excerpts.latex: The pressure of a fluid on any given horizontal surface equals the weight of a column of the fluid standing on that surface as a base and of height equal to the distance of this surface below the surface of the fluid.
excerpts.markdown: The pressure of a fluid on any given horizontal surface equals the weight of a column of the fluid standing on that surface as a base and of height equal to the distance of this surface below the surface of the fluid.
excerpts.why: It states the physical rule that lets a learner convert fluid pressure into a weight-times-depth sum.

excerpts.latex: Work done in lifting equals the weight multiplied by the vertical height.
excerpts.markdown: Work done in lifting equals the weight multiplied by the vertical height.
excerpts.why: It gives the single physical principle behind every work integral in the reservoir problems.

excerpts.latex: The total attraction between the particle at $P$ and the rod being the limit of the sum of all such elements between $x = 0$ and $x = l$, we have
excerpts.markdown: The total attraction between the particle at $P$ and the rod being the limit of the sum of all such elements between $x = 0$ and $x = l$, we have
excerpts.why: It shows plainly that a total force is the limit of a sum of element contributions, which is the integration idea in another setting.

excerpts.latex: By the \textit{length of a straight line} we commonly mean the number of times we can superpose upon it another straight line employed as a unit of length, as when the carpenter measures the length of a board by making end-to-end applications of his foot rule.
excerpts.markdown: By the *length of a straight line* we commonly mean the number of times we can superpose upon it another straight line employed as a unit of length, as when the carpenter measures the length of a board by making end-to-end applications of his foot rule.
excerpts.why: It grounds the idea of length in a familiar act of measuring, so a learner sees why a curve needs a different method.

excerpts.latex: Since it is impossible to make a straight line coincide with an arc of a curve, we cannot measure curves in the same manner as we measure straight lines.
excerpts.markdown: Since it is impossible to make a straight line coincide with an arc of a curve, we cannot measure curves in the same manner as we measure straight lines.
excerpts.why: It states the difficulty that motivates the limiting definition of arc length.

excerpts.latex: The length of the curve is defined as the limit of the sum of the chords as the number of points of division increases without limit in such a way that at the same time each chord separately approaches zero as a limit.
excerpts.markdown: The length of the curve is defined as the limit of the sum of the chords as the number of points of division increases without limit in such a way that at the same time each chord separately approaches zero as a limit.
excerpts.why: It gives the precise definition of arc length as a limit of inscribed chord sums, the core idea of the section.

excerpts.latex: The student will observe that as $\Delta x_1$ approaches zero as a limit, $\epsilon_1$ also approaches the limit zero.
excerpts.markdown: The student will observe that as $\Delta x_1$ approaches zero as a limit, $\epsilon_1$ also approaches the limit zero.
excerpts.why: It warns that a small correction term must be shown to vanish in the limit before the sum can be replaced by an integral.

excerpts.latex: The lateral area of the frustum of a cone of revolution is equal to the circumference of the middle section multiplied by the slant height.
excerpts.markdown: The lateral area of the frustum of a cone of revolution is equal to the circumference of the middle section multiplied by the slant height.
excerpts.why: It gives the rule that makes each band of a revolved surface computable as a product of circumference and slant height.

excerpts.latex: This formula is easily remembered if we consider a slice or disk of the solid between two planes perpendicular to the axis of revolution as an element of the volume, and regard it as a cylinder of infinitesimal altitude $dx$ and with a base of area $\pi y^2$, and hence of volume $\pi y^2 dx$.
excerpts.markdown: This formula is easily remembered if we consider a slice or disk of the solid between two planes perpendicular to the axis of revolution as an element of the volume, and regard it as a cylinder of infinitesimal altitude $dx$ and with a base of area $\pi y^2$, and hence of volume $\pi y^2 dx$.
excerpts.why: It shows how the volume integral comes from a thin cylinder of infinitesimal thickness, a picture learners can reuse.

excerpts.latex: Since this limit will also be the measure of the length of some straight line, the finding of the length of a curve is also called ``the rectification of the curve.''
excerpts.markdown: Since this limit will also be the measure of the length of some straight line, the finding of the length of a curve is also called “the rectification of the curve.”
excerpts.why: It records the older name for arc length, which a reader meeting the term in older books will need.

excerpts.latex: In fact, the Integral Calculus was invented in the attempt to calculate the area bounded by curves, by supposing the given area to be divided into an ``infinite number of infinitesimal parts called \textit{elements}, the sum of all these elements being the area required.''
excerpts.markdown: In fact, the Integral Calculus was invented in the attempt to calculate the area bounded by curves, by supposing the given area to be divided into an “infinite number of infinitesimal parts called *elements*, the sum of all these elements being the area required.”
excerpts.why: It gives the historical motivation for integration as summation, so learners see why the area is built from thin pieces.

excerpts.latex: The importance of this theorem results from the fact that \textit{we are able to calculate by integration a magnitude which is the limit of a sum of the form $(C)$.}
excerpts.markdown: The importance of this theorem results from the fact that *we are able to calculate by integration a magnitude which is the limit of a sum of the form $(C)$.*
excerpts.why: It states plainly what the fundamental theorem buys a student: a way to evaluate limits of sums.

excerpts.latex: Then the limiting value of this sum when $n$ increases without limit, and each subinterval approaches zero as a limit, equals the value of the definite integral
excerpts.markdown: Then the limiting value of this sum when $n$ increases without limit, and each subinterval approaches zero as a limit, equals the value of the definite integral
excerpts.why: It is the core statement of the theorem in words, which a teacher can read aloud before showing the formula.

excerpts.latex: Equation $(A)$ is readily memorized by observing that $y\,dx$ represents the area of a rectangle (as $CR$) of base $dx$ and altitude $y$.
excerpts.markdown: Equation $(A)$ is readily memorized by observing that $y\,dx$ represents the area of a rectangle (as $CR$) of base $dx$ and altitude $y$.
excerpts.why: It gives a memorable picture of the strip whose area is y dx, which helps learners set up area integrals.

excerpts.latex: \textit{This area lies below the axis of $x$ and has a negative sign} because the ordinates are negative.
excerpts.markdown: *This area lies below the axis of $x$ and has a negative sign* because the ordinates are negative.
excerpts.why: It warns that an area below the x-axis integrates to a negative value, a common source of sign mistakes.

excerpts.latex: This last result takes into account the signs of the two separate areas composing the whole. The total area regardless of these signs equals 4.
excerpts.markdown: This last result takes into account the signs of the two separate areas composing the whole. The total area regardless of these signs equals 4.
excerpts.why: It shows that a signed integral can give zero while the true total area is positive, so learners must split at zeros.

excerpts.latex: Historically, the integral sign is merely the long $S$, used by early writers to indicate ``sum.''
excerpts.markdown: Historically, the integral sign is merely the long $S$, used by early writers to indicate “sum.”
excerpts.why: It links the integral sign to its origin as an S for sum, which makes the summation idea memorable.

excerpts.latex: In general, a \textit{multiple integral} requires two or more successive integrations. As before, if there are no limits assigned, as in the above example, the integral is indefinite; if there are limits assigned for each successive integration, the integral is definite.
excerpts.markdown: In general, a *multiple integral* requires two or more successive integrations. As before, if there are no limits assigned, as in the above example, the integral is indefinite; if there are limits assigned for each successive integration, the integral is definite.
excerpts.why: It tells the learner in one place what makes a multiple integral and what separates an indefinite integral from a definite one.

excerpts.latex: But since $y$ was regarded as constant during this integration, it may happen that $\phi$ involves $y$ in some way; in fact, $\phi$ will in general be a function of $y$.
excerpts.markdown: But since $y$ was regarded as constant during this integration, it may happen that $\phi$ involves $y$ in some way; in fact, $\phi$ will in general be a function of $y$.
excerpts.why: It explains why the constant of integration in partial integration becomes an arbitrary function of the variables held fixed.

excerpts.latex: Before attempting to apply partial integration to practical problems it is best that the student should acquire by practice some facility in evaluating definite multiple integrals.
excerpts.markdown: Before attempting to apply partial integration to practical problems it is best that the student should acquire by practice some facility in evaluating definite multiple integrals.
excerpts.why: It gives the learner a clear order of study: practise evaluating the integrals before applying them.

excerpts.latex: Consider a column of infinitesimal base $dydx$ and altitude $z$ as an element of the volume. Summing up all such elements from $y = DF$ to $y = DG$, $x$ in the meanwhile being constant (say $= OD$), gives the volume of an indefinitely thin slice having $FGHI$ as one face.
excerpts.markdown: Consider a column of infinitesimal base $dydx$ and altitude $z$ as an element of the volume. Summing up all such elements from $y = DF$ to $y = DG$, $x$ in the meanwhile being constant (say $= OD$), gives the volume of an indefinitely thin slice having $FGHI$ as one face.
excerpts.why: It pictures a double integral as a column, then a slice, then a solid, which makes the nested limits intuitive.

excerpts.latex: The area of any region is the value of the double integral of the function $f(x,\,y)=1$ taken over that region.
excerpts.markdown: The area of any region is the value of the double integral of the function $f(x,\,y)=1$ taken over that region.
excerpts.why: It states plainly that an area is a double integral of the constant function 1, a link learners can remember.

excerpts.latex: These are easily remembered if we think of the elements (checks) as being rectangles with dimensions $\rho\,d\theta$ and $d\rho$, and hence of area $\rho\,d\theta\,d\rho$.
excerpts.markdown: These are easily remembered if we think of the elements (checks) as being rectangles with dimensions $\rho\,d\theta$ and $d\rho$, and hence of area $\rho\,d\theta\,d\rho$.
excerpts.why: It gives the learner a memory aid for the area element in polar coordinates, showing why the two orders of integration carry different factors.

excerpts.latex: Since the element of area ($= \Delta y\Delta x = \rho\Delta\rho\Delta\theta$) is essentially positive and $x^2$, $y^2$, $\rho^2$ are always positive, it follows that moment of inertia is never zero, but always a positive number.
excerpts.markdown: Since the element of area ($= \Delta y\Delta x = \rho\Delta\rho\Delta\theta$) is essentially positive and $x^2$, $y^2$, $\rho^2$ are always positive, it follows that moment of inertia is never zero, but always a positive number.
excerpts.why: It explains in one step why a moment of inertia can never vanish, a point learners often find surprising.

excerpts.latex: The center of area of a thin homogeneous plate or lamina is the same as its \textit{center of mass} (or \textit{center of gravity}).
excerpts.markdown: The center of area of a thin homogeneous plate or lamina is the same as its *center of mass* (or *center of gravity*).
excerpts.why: It connects a purely geometric quantity to the physical balance point of a thin plate, giving the centroid a concrete meaning.

excerpts.latex: The polar moment of inertia of a plane area with respect to any point equals the sum of its moments of inertia with respect to any two perpendicular axes through that point.
excerpts.markdown: The polar moment of inertia of a plane area with respect to any point equals the sum of its moments of inertia with respect to any two perpendicular axes through that point.
excerpts.why: It states the perpendicular axes theorem in one sentence, letting a learner compute a polar moment from two simpler integrals.

excerpts.latex: \textit{To find the projection of the area required on the $XOY$-plane, eliminate $z$ between the equations of the surfaces whose intersections form the boundary of the area.}
excerpts.markdown: *To find the projection of the area required on the $XOY$-plane, eliminate $z$ between the equations of the surfaces whose intersections form the boundary of the area.*
excerpts.why: It gives the rule for finding integration limits on a surface, the step where learners most often go wrong.

excerpts.latex: If a coördinate axis is an axis of symmetry of the area, it is evident that the corresponding coördinate of the center of area will be zero.
excerpts.markdown: If a coördinate axis is an axis of symmetry of the area, it is evident that the corresponding coördinate of the center of area will be zero.
excerpts.why: It lets a learner skip a calculation whenever a symmetry of the region is present.

excerpts.latex: Moments of inertia arise frequently in engineering problems, the principal application being to the calculation of the energy of a rotating body.
excerpts.markdown: Moments of inertia arise frequently in engineering problems, the principal application being to the calculation of the energy of a rotating body.
excerpts.why: It shows the historical and engineering purpose behind a definition that can otherwise look like an arbitrary integral.

excerpts.latex: Since the required surface lies on the cylinder, the partial derivatives required for formula $(C)$, p. 415, must be found from the equation of the cylinder.
excerpts.markdown: Since the required surface lies on the cylinder, the partial derivatives required for formula $(C)$, p. 415, must be found from the equation of the cylinder.
excerpts.why: It is a worked-example rule about which equation to differentiate, which decides whether the surface integral is tractable.

excerpts.latex: Thus, by extension of the principle of \S\ 218, p. 401, we speak of volume as the result of integrating the function $f(x,\, y,\, z) = 1$ \textit{throughout a given region.}
excerpts.markdown: Thus, by extension of the principle of 218, p. 401, we speak of volume as the result of integrating the function $f(x,\, y,\, z) = 1$ *throughout a given region.*
excerpts.why: It shows a learner that volume is simply the integral of the constant function 1 over a region, which links volume to integration.

excerpts.latex: The method of evaluating this triple integral is precisely analogous to that already explained for double integrals in \S\ 218, p. 401.
excerpts.markdown: The method of evaluating this triple integral is precisely analogous to that already explained for double integrals in 218, p. 401.
excerpts.why: It tells a learner that a triple integral is evaluated the same way as a double integral, so the earlier method carries over.

excerpts.latex: The volume $V$ of the solid will then be the limit of this triple sum as $\Delta z$, $\Delta y$, $\Delta x$ each approaches zero as a limit.
excerpts.markdown: The volume $V$ of the solid will then be the limit of this triple sum as $\Delta z$, $\Delta y$, $\Delta x$ each approaches zero as a limit.
excerpts.why: It states the idea behind the whole chapter: volume is a limit of sums of small boxes.

excerpts.latex: Integrating first with respect to $z$, we sum up all such elements in a column (as $RS$), the $z$-limits being zero [from (2)] and $TR = c\sqrt{1-\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}}$ [from (1) by solving for $z$].
excerpts.markdown: Integrating first with respect to $z$, we sum up all such elements in a column (as $RS$), the $z$-limits being zero [from (2)] and $TR = c\sqrt{1-\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}}$ [from (1) by solving for $z$].
excerpts.why: This worked step shows how each limit is read off from a bounding surface, the central skill for setting up a triple integral.

excerpts.latex: Therefore the volume of the entire ellipsoid is $\dfrac{4\pi abc}{3}$.
excerpts.markdown: Therefore the volume of the entire ellipsoid is $\dfrac{4\pi abc}{3}$.
excerpts.why: It gives a memorable result that a learner can check against the familiar volume formula for a sphere when a=b=c.

excerpts.latex: A differential equation is an equation involving derivatives or differentials.
excerpts.markdown: A differential equation is an equation involving derivatives or differentials.
excerpts.why: It gives the learner the one-sentence definition that every later type in the chapter depends on.

excerpts.latex: The \textit{order} of a differential equation is that of the highest derivative (or differential) in it.
excerpts.markdown: The *order* of a differential equation is that of the highest derivative (or differential) in it.
excerpts.why: It defines order by the highest derivative; flag: the text's list then places equation (2), whose highest derivative is d^2y/dx^2, in the third order, which looks like an erratum (it is second order).

excerpts.latex: A solution such as $(E)$, which contains a number of arbitrary essential constants equal to the order of the equation (in this case two), is called the \textit{general solution} or the \textit{complete integral.}
excerpts.markdown: A solution such as $(E)$, which contains a number of arbitrary essential constants equal to the order of the equation (in this case two), is called the *general solution* or the *complete integral.*
excerpts.why: It ties the number of arbitrary constants to the order, so a learner can check whether a family of solutions is general.

excerpts.latex: Solutions obtained therefrom by giving particular values to the constants are called \textit{particular solutions} or \textit{particular integrals.}
excerpts.markdown: Solutions obtained therefrom by giving particular values to the constants are called *particular solutions* or *particular integrals.*
excerpts.why: It separates a particular solution from the general one by fixing the constants, which is the step a student takes next.

excerpts.latex: \textit{Clear of fractions, and if the equation involves derivatives, multiply through by the differential of the independent variable.}
excerpts.markdown: *Clear of fractions, and if the equation involves derivatives, multiply through by the differential of the independent variable.*
excerpts.why: It states the first step of the separation rule in plain words a student can follow before the terms are collected.

excerpts.latex: In solving examples coming under this head the student is advised to find the solution by following the method illustrated above, rather than by using $(G)$ as a formula.
excerpts.markdown: In solving examples coming under this head the student is advised to find the solution by following the method illustrated above, rather than by using $(G)$ as a formula.
excerpts.why: It warns that memorising the general formula is weaker than following the method step by step, which is the lesson a learner needs.

excerpts.latex: The solution of the auxiliary equation of the new derived differential equation is facilitated by observing that the left-hand member of that equation is exactly divisible by the left-hand member of the auxiliary equation used in finding the complementary function.
excerpts.markdown: The solution of the auxiliary equation of the new derived differential equation is facilitated by observing that the left-hand member of that equation is exactly divisible by the left-hand member of the auxiliary equation used in finding the complementary function.
excerpts.why: It gives a shortcut for factoring the higher-order auxiliary equation by reusing the one already solved.

excerpts.latex: A check on the accuracy of the work is found in the fact that the first three steps must give $n$ independent solutions.
excerpts.markdown: A check on the accuracy of the work is found in the fact that the first three steps must give $n$ independent solutions.
excerpts.why: It gives the learner a self-check: the count of independent solutions must equal the order of the equation.

excerpts.markdown: *For the same abscissa $x_1$ the number giving the length of the ordinate of the integral curve $(B)$ is the same as the number that gives the area between the original curve, the axes, and the ordinate corresponding to this abscissa.*
excerpts.why: It states the central idea of integral curves in one sentence a learner can check against a graph.

excerpts.markdown: It is clear that the greater the number of intervals (i.e. the smaller $\Delta x$ is) the closer will the sum of the areas of the trapezoids approach the area under the curve.
excerpts.why: It explains why refining the subdivision improves a numerical estimate of an integral.

excerpts.latex: As in the case of the trapezoidal rule, the greater the number of parts into which $M_0M_n$ is divided, the closer will the result be to the area under the curve.
excerpts.markdown: As in the case of the trapezoidal rule, the greater the number of parts into which $M_0M_n$ is divided, the closer will the result be to the area under the curve.
excerpts.why: It carries the same error-reduction idea over to Simpson's rule for comparison.

excerpts.latex: By integration, $\displaystyle\int_0^{10} x^3dx = \left[\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^{10} = 2500$, so that in this example Simpson's rule happens to give an exact result.
excerpts.markdown: By integration, $\displaystyle\int_0^{10} x^3dx = \left[\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^{10} = 2500$, so that in this example Simpson’s rule happens to give an exact result.
excerpts.why: It shows a worked check of an approximate rule against the exact antiderivative, with the caveat that exactness is not general.

excerpts.latex: Evidently the origin is a point of inflection of the integral curve and a point with minimum ordinate on the original curve.
excerpts.markdown: Evidently the origin is a point of inflection of the integral curve and a point with minimum ordinate on the original curve.
excerpts.why: It links an inflection on the integral curve to a minimum on the original curve, a pattern learners can verify on a sketch.

equations.name: Binomial Theorem

equations.name: cosine curve

equations.name: limaçon
equations.statement: In polar coordinates the limaçon has rho equal to b minus a times the cosine of theta.

equations.name: strophoid
equations.statement: The strophoid is the curve in which y squared equals x squared times the ratio of a plus x to a minus x.

equations.name: spiral of Archimedes
equations.statement: In polar coordinates the spiral of Archimedes has rho equal to a times theta.

equations.name: equiangular spiral

equations.name: equiangular spiral

equations.name: hyperbolic spiral

equations.name: lituus
equations.statement: The lituus has rho squared times theta equal to a constant squared.

equations.name: parabolic spiral
equations.statement: The parabolic spiral is the curve in which the square of rho minus a equals four a c times theta.

equations.name: logarithmic curve
equations.statement: The logarithmic curve is the graph of the ordinate equal to the logarithm of the abscissa.

equations.name: exponential curve
equations.statement: The exponential curve is the graph of the ordinate equal to e raised to the abscissa.

equations.name: probability curve

equations.name: secant curve

equations.name: tangent curve

problems.markdown: Given $f(x, y) \equiv Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2$, expand $f(x + h, y + k)$ in powers of $h$ and $k$.
answer_markdown: **Solution.** $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2\,Ax + By, \quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = Bx + 2\,Cy;$$ $$\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} = 2\,A, \quad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y} = B, \quad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} = 2\,C.$$ The third and higher partial derivatives are all zero. Substituting in (67), $$\begin{array}{c} f(x + h, y + k) \equiv Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + (2\,Ax + By)\,h + (Bx + 2\,Cy)\,k \\ + Ah^2 + Bhk + Ck^2. \quad \textit{Ans.} \end{array}$$

answer_markdown: **Solution.** $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2\,Ax, \quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2\,By, \quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} = 2\,Cz;$$ $$\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} = 2\,A, \quad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} = 2\,B, \quad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} = 2\,C, \quad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \partial z} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z \partial x} = 0.$$ The third and higher partial derivatives are all zero. problems.problem_latex: Find the equation of the tangent plane and the equations of the normal line to the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=14$ at the point $(1,\,2,\,3)$.
problems.markdown: Find the equation of the tangent plane and the equations of the normal line to the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=14$ at the point $(1,\,2,\,3)$.
answer_latex:
\textbf{Solution.} Let $F(x,\,y,\,z)=x^2+y^2+z^2-14$;

then
\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=2\,x,\ \frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=2\,y,\ \frac{\partial F}{\partial z}=2\,z;\ x_1=1,\ y_1=2,\ z_1=3.
\]
\[
\therefore\ \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}=2,\ \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1}=4,\ \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1}=6.
\]

Substituting in (71), $2\,(x-1)+4\,(y-2)+6\,(z-3)=0$, $x+2\,y+3\,z=14$, the tangent plane.

Substituting in (73),
\[
\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-3}{6},
\]
giving $z=3\,x$ and $2\,z=3\,y$, equations of the normal line.
answer_markdown: **Solution.** Let $F(x,\,y,\,z)=x^2+y^2+z^2-14$; then $$\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=2\,x,\ \frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=2\,y,\ \frac{\partial F}{\partial z}=2\,z;\ x_1=1,\ y_1=2,\ z_1=3.$$ $$\therefore\ \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x_1}=2,\ \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y_1}=4,\ \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial z_1}=6.$$ Substituting in (71), $2\,(x-1)+4\,(y-2)+6\,(z-3)=0$, $x+2\,y+3\,z=14$, the tangent plane. Substituting in (73), $$\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-3}{6},$$ giving $z=3\,x$ and $2\,z=3\,y$, equations of the normal line.

(b) when $25\sqrt{2}$ rods north of $OX$? \quad Southeast or northeast.
(c) when 30 rods west of $OY$? \quad E. $36^\circ\,52'\,12''$ N. or W. $36^\circ\,52'\,12''$ N.
(d) when 40 rods south of $OX$?
(e) when 10 rods east of $OY$?
